entries.title: ROM 1:2
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-A promised gospel. It sometimes happens that a blewng long promised, loudly heralded, and warmly ex.tolled, loses thereby something of its charm, and suffers in the warmness of its welcome when it appears. That must be a vast and pricelboon which will bear to be promised and expected generation after generation. Expectation is aroused, the flame of hope is fanned, desire stands on tip-toe and strains her eyes, And wh.au the gift comes, it must be of surpassing value, if no dLsappointment follow. The gospel of Jesus Christ was foretold for centuries. It had become" the desire of all nations." But when it came, it was more glorious and welcome than all hope, all imagination, could have dreamed. I. IT WAS TAUGHT DY CHRIST A~'D JIIB Al'OSTLES THAT THE GOSPEL WAS a. BLESSING PROMISED FB0]I[ ANCIENT TIME. Here are three direct proofs of this. 1. Our Lord, in his conversation with the disciples on the way to Emmaus, reproached them as " slow of heart to believe all that the prophets had spoken; " and, " beginning at Moses and all the.prophets, expounded unto them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself." 2. Upon the Day of Pentecost Pdler instanced the resurrection of Christ ae a fulfilment of Hebrew propheoy; David, being a prophet, and knuwing that Goel had sworn to raise up hie descendant to sit on his throno, "se~in~ this bd"c,ro, epa.lrn of the rosurrootion of Christ." 3. When beforo Agrippa t\ll,L 1''ei;tu:,, P,ml allinnod th11t, in his witnessiug, be !!IUd "none other things thll.ll thO&J which ti.t.i 18 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [on. 1. l-at,

prophett: and Moses did say Bbould oome : tl11tt Christ should suffer, and that he should be t,be fi~t that should rise from the dead, and should show light unto the people, and w the Gentile..," Add to these the many instances in which the writers of the New Teslllment declare the gospel to be the fulfilment of Old 'l'est&ment prophecy, nnd it becomes apparent that the Founder and first preaohers of Christianity all claim thab the Hebrew Scriptures testified beforehand to their glorious theme. Il. THE KEN BY WHOM THE GOSPEL WAS FORETOLD WERE GoD1B PBOPIIETB, They were so oa.lled because they uttered forth, s.s bis representatives, the mind and will of God. And they fulfilled this office, not only with a view to the time then present, it.I circumstances and duties, but with a view to a time to come. Thus prophecy and prediction were closely linked together. With God is neither past, present, nor future. The promise was first made to our first parents, and through .Adam to his posterity. The l!88d. of the wom.&n should bruise the serpent's head. .Abraham, in whom the human race t.ook a new departure, was assured that in hie seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed. This declaration, made to the father of the faithful, was believed by him, and his faith was accounted as righteousness. Through him it became the property of his desoendant.s; for it was evidently so understood by Jacob. To Moses the promise was given, and by him it was recorded, that God should raise up a prophet like unto himself. But Moses prophesied of Christ rather in the ordinances he iastitut.ed than in the words he uttered. The sacrifices especially of the Jewish dispensation were an earnest of him who in due time should die for the ungodly. In the Psalms of Damd are several passages in which the Holy Spirit s.ssured to the lsraelitish monarch a successor to more than his own dignity and dominion. Isaiah spoke of a sulfering and victorioUB Messiah. And others of the goodly fellowship, especia.lly Jeremiah, Zechariah, Malachi, and Daniel, announced beforehand the advent or Israel's and the world's Deliverer. Ill. TEE 5CRIPrURES WJm.E THE BECOBD IN WHICH THE PROMISE OJ!' THE GOSPEL wA.S PRESERVED. Admire the wisdom of God manifested in this provision. Men have sneered &ta "book-revelation;" but it should be remembered that the only alternative to this, so far 11S we can see, was tradition-shifting, untrustworthy tradition. The Hebrews valuea their sacred writings, and they had good reason for doing so. The Lord Jesus bade his opponents" search the Scriptures," knowing that these testified of him. The apostles always appealed, when reasoning with the Jews; to the books they justly deemed inspired. These books contained a treasure which those who knew only their letter, not their spirit, often failed to discern and value. "Holy," because inspired by the Holy Ghost; because written by the pens of holy men; _because containing holy doctrine ; because tending to foster a holy character and hfe, to leaven society with holy doctrines and principles. Above all, holy because witnessing to him who was the" Holy One and the Just," God's" holy Child Jesus," The Scrip- ~es are the casket, and Christ the Divine Jewel within. IV. CoxsmEB THE PURPOSES FOB wmcm: THE GQBPEL WAS THUS FORETOLD AND PUBLI6HED, with growing clearness in the centuries before the coming of the Christ. There wa..s Divine reason in this arrangement; and Paul saw this to be so, or he would not have put this forward in the forefront of this document. Observe these three evident intentions. L Thus the hopes of God's people were BUBtained. How needful must express promises have been to the godly who lived in the twilight of Judaism, surrounded by the dark night of heathenism I Often must their hearts have sunk within them, only to be revived by the gracious declarations of the universal Lord and King. 2. Thus were displayed the wisdom and the benevolence of God. He would be known, not only as the moral Ruler, but as the gracious Saviour, of mankind. The glowing lan.:,ITll&ge of inspired prophets depicted the attributes of the great Redeemer in 811Ch wlourB as to inspire the nation with a. lively and a blessed hope. 8. ThUB was pro- Yision made for e&tablishing the credibility and authority of the gospel, when revealed. Much that was written aforetime could not at that period be fully understood. These things were written, not for those who then lived, but for us. Looking upon the pro- 1,hecy, and then upon the fulfilmwt, recognizing the wonderful correspondence, we ace the presenCf. of the r;a.me God in the old covenant, and in that new covenant which is tD truth more ancient tl,o.u the old. .&l'l'LlCATION. 'l'he grc:a.t practical lesson conveyed in this passage is obvious enougb. oa,L 1-82.J THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 17

If the gospel wall tho matter of a Divine promise, repeated by prophet after proph~ through n long course of ages, and if the fulfilment of that proraille was tb'.l rrreateet event in the history of mo.nkind,-how immensely important must this gospel b; to ll81 A stranger to the Ohristian religion might naturally think it an unaccountable, even an unreasonable, thing, that o.n assembly of English people in the nineteenth century should spend an hour in solemnly meditating upon words spoken by religious teacherw who, thoueo.nde of years ago, lived in a remote strip of land in Asia, between the deserl and the sea. He might naturally ask-What possible bearing can such wordil have upon the principles which govern your life, the aims and hopes that inspire your heart? Our answer is plain. God, in the ancient days, gave to mankind a promise which their circumstances rendered unspeakably timely, welcome, and precious. A sinful race, in rebellion against the Divine authority, deserving and daring punishment, neroed nothing so sorely as an assurance of the King's compassion, as the revelation of a way of salvation, of reconciliation, of loyal obedience, of eternal life. Under the prophetic diapeneo.tion, this want was met; this declaration, this promise, was given. In the coming of Christ, in hiR life of benevolent ministry, his death of sacrifice and redemption, his victorious rising, hie spiritual reign, the ancient words of prediction and promise found an echo corresponding with, but stronger than, themselves. .And now the gospel is preached-that the counsel of God has been fulfilled, the grace of God has been displayed, the power of God has been put forth. We have not to tell of what God u,i1J do, but of what he has done. We have not now to raise men's hope, but to require their faith. To receive.this revelation is to come under a new principle, a new power, to become a new creation, to live a new life. Remember that the promise refern, not only to the facts which, in one sense, constitute the gospel, but to the blessings which the gospel secures to those who accept it. If the gospel of Christ has, as we believe and teach, Divine authority, then there is, by the Lord Jesus, forgiveness for sins, renewal for the heart, grace for all need, and immortal life and joys ; there is all that man can ask and God can give. In Christ provision is made for every want of sinful, ignorant, and helpless man. All the blessings of the gospel are offered of God's free mercy to the repenting and confiding applicant. What spiritual need is there which experienee does not show may be satisfied by the gospel of Christ, by Christ himself? None I All blessings are assured to his faithful people.

entries.title: ROM 1:5
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Th~ apostolic afrn. There was great dignity in the obaraoter, demee.nou~ nnd lllllgUage of the Apostle Paul. This was not inconsistent with the modesty e.nJ humility which were the ornament of his Christian character. Bnt whilst he feH his personal unworthiness, feebleness, and utter insufficiency for the vast nnd arduous work entrusted to him, his sense of the grandeur of the work raised his conception of his. own high vocation. It were well that all Christian ministers should cherish lowly views of self, and, at the same time, lofty views of the ministry they have received from God. I. OIISERVE THE QUALIFICATIONS BESTOWED UPON PAUL. He describes these in order both to justify himself in the tone of his Epistle, and to secure the respectful attention of his readers. 1. Whence were they derived? They were not the ordinary gifts which Pro,idence bestows upon men to fit them for the work of life. They were traced to Christ (" by whom"), the Gi,er of all blessings to his Church. It was the prerogative of tbe glorified Redeemer to confer gifts upon men. ~• He gave some, apostles," eto, Having redeemed his Church at a cost so great, he could not leave it without providing for the supply of all its needs. 2. In what did they consist? Paul uses two terms. One of these denotes the more general gift, "grace." By this may be understood, not onl~ the enlightening and quickening influences of tho Holy Spirit, which bring the soul into the enjoyment of the new and higher spiritual life, but all that distinguishes Christian character, a.nd fits for an effective and beneficent witness to the Saviour. The othf:I' term is "apostleship." The apostles occupied a place so prominent and so honourable among the servants of Christ, that we cannot be surprised that a. special word is here employed. Paul was "called to be an apostle ; " and he often refers to the memorable occasion when he was arrested upon his errand of persecution, converted to Chrut's faith a.nd service, and commissioned for the great and holy work of his llfe. He claims to be not behind the chiefest of the apostles, and glories in the grace of God which was manifested nnto and in him. . II. OBsi!:BVE THE END BOUGHT BY PAUL. " Spirits are not finely touched but to fine issues ; " and such endowments as were conferred upon Paul must have been iu preparation for no ordinary service. 1. The character of this end was moral, spiritual. It was to overcome the disobedience and rebellion of sinful men; to vanquish these by the grace of the cross of Christ, and. by the power of the Spirit of God. 'l'he obedience which our King and Father requires, he has resolved to secure by means devised by infinite wisdom and provided by infinite love. The gospel ofChrist, received by fl!-ith, is to be the means of reconciling man to God. 2. Faith, then, occupied a place of i:n.mense importance in the teaching of the apostle. '!'his Epistle to the Romans is, in itself, sufficient proof of this. Justification with God, and subjection and consecr~ tion to God, are secured by faith in the Mediator, Christ. Christian obedience is prompted, not by constraint or fear, but by this intelligent and lofty motive. 3. The sphere of this apostolic mission was unlimited, save by the boundaries of humanity, "All nations" were comprehended within the commission he received. A great modem preacher, John Wesley, is said to have claimed "the world as bis parish." .It was a sublime view of his ministry which Paul took; and it was taken, not under the influence of enthusiasm or self-importance, but upon the highest of all authority-that of the Saviour and the Lord of all. 4. '!'he ultimate i6sue of the apostleship of Puul IICemB to be implied in the expression," for his Name." It was the glory of the Son of God which his servant faithfully and consistently sought; there was nothiug personal or selfish, nothing petty or unworthy, in his aims. 'l'he Name of Christ ill m itself above every name, and at that Name every knee.shall bow, This assurance was enough tu animate and sustain the ar,ostJe in all his labcur aud in all his sulfering. entries.title: ROM 1:6
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content: -The Romam, Olvristians. In the great capital of the empire and of the world there was thus early constituted a congregation of Christian worshippers anti. disoiples. Amidst the grandeur, the opulence, the vice, that prevailed in this, as in every metropolis; amidst proud patricians, turbulent plebeians, and wretched slavLe,- there existed already nn obscure but, to us, notable society, composed of Jews, P.omans, and foreigners resident in the city, to whom Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles, wrote this letter. The members of this society were not characterized by any outward marks of distinction which would render them interesting to the inhabitants of Rome generaily. Yet, whilst the great and learned and wealthy, who either never heard of the Christian Church in their midst, or who, if they heard of it, despised it,-whilst they, for the most part, are forgotten, that Church is still remembered with deepest interest. Notice the marks by which it was distinguished to the view of the inspired apostle. He wrote' "to all that be in Rome," who were differenced from those around them in certain respects. I. 'l'HEY WEBE CALLED OF CHRIST. They had, for the most part, never seen the Lord Jesus; but their souls had heard his holy, gracious call. 1. They had been addressed by the audible voice of his uttered Word. The call of the gospel had reached their understanding. 2. They had experienced the inner call of his Spirit. To each one of them might the apostle say, "The Word is nigh thee, even in thy heart." 3. They had responded to the call by their faith and obedience; they had not received the grace of God in vain. II. THEY WEBE BELOVED OF Goo. 1. In common with all mankind, they were the objects of Divine pity. " God so loved the world," etc. 2. But there was a special sense in which they were partakers of the love of God. He had revealed his love to 'them, and they loved God, because he first loved them. He loved bis own image reflected in their character and life. 3. This love was especially manifested in their adoption. "Behold what manner of love the Father bath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the children ot God ! " III. THEY WERE SEPABATED UNTO HOLINESS. The word " saint" is now appropria tcd to personages of peculiar and distinguished piety. But it serves to remind us that Christians were intended to be pure amidst a sinful world and a sinful generation-I\ condition of the Divine favour, as well as a result of the privileges enjoyed by the people of God. 'l'he term may be thus unfolded. Saints are (I) distinguished from si!!ful society by which they are surrounded; (2) distingi.ilihed from their former selves; (3) filled with the Spirit of holiness; (4) and in character, aa well a.s by profession, witnesses unto a holy God and Saviour. Such "notes" of true, experimental Christianity were, indeed, not peculiar to the Roman Christians; but their conspicuous presence in the society addressed by the apostle was an earnest of the fruits of true religion which should a.bound wherever the gospel was proclaimed and received.

entries.title: ROM 1:13
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-A yearning heart. The ministry <'o( the gospel of Christ may he fulfilled in either of two ways-by personal visitation and oral teaching and preaching; or by written communications, in the form of letter or of treatise. Paul, like many since his time, adopted both methods, and it would be hard to say in which he was the more efTcctive. entries.title: ROM 1:21–24
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content: -Evil paulon. A more frightful exhibition of sin and its consequences than that gtveh by the apostle in the latter part of this chapter could not have been presented; yet to have eaid Ieee than this would have been to fall short of the f'acts of the caee, which needed to be stated in order to prepare the way for the publication of a. p;oApel of pnrdon and of purity. J. Tnm nooT 011' EVIL PA88ION, 0B LUB'l', IB IN THE WORBIIlP 011 THE CREATURE. The beginning of all evil is in departure from God, Hie works, and especially the most honourable and beautiful of all hie material constructions-the human body-are intended to lead the thoughts and aspirations of men to the great Creator himself, whose attributes they in some measure display. The symmetry and grace and beauty of the human form and features are the crown of the physical creation. And to the Christian the body of man has this higher interest-it was tenanted by the human mind, it was possessed by the Divine nature, of the Son of God himself. The attractiveness of the body is not only a fact indicative of the Divine delight in form; within lawful bounds it is intended to subserve the high purposes of social and especially of conjugal life. But when the interest centres upon what is corporeal, and does not pass beyond nnd above it, then the Divine intention is frustrated. Evidently the nobility, the enchanting loveliness characteristic of the human body in its grandest and fairest types, are designed to suggest the in.finite and eternal spiritual excellence. " Thus beauty here points up to that above, .And loveliness lea.de on to perfect love." But when this great and precious lesson is missed, what follows? Inevitable d8t,aradation. The creature is worshipped, and the Creator is forgotten or despised. The mind and heart seek to rest in what can never satisfy them. The emblem is mistaken for the reality, the shadow for the substance. II. 'l'HE FRUIT OF EVIL PASSION, on LUST, IS UNNATURAL AND DEBASil!iG VICE. Readers of the ancient literature of Greece and Rome, students of anthropology, travellers and residents in heathen lands in our own time, are well aware of the lengths to which sinful passion can lead those whom it masters. There is no need to go into detan,·and it is better for Christian people to remain ignorant of corruptions with which, happily, they are never· brought into contact. But it remains true that, with idolatry, the filthiest rites and orgies have often been, and still are, associated. Those abandoned to "fleshly lusts" appear to exhaust their ingenuity in inventing fo?Ilils of unlawful indulgence. III. TEE PUNlSHMENT OF EVIL PASSION, OR LUST, IS ASSURED BY THE BETBillUTITE ACTION OF GOD'S RIGHTEOUS GOVERNMENT. There is a natural belief in retribution. Nemesis is no mere invention of the human imagination j it springs from convictions and fears from which humanity can never free itself. Revelation confirms the natural utterances of human reason, assuring us that after death is the judgment, and that every man shall give account of himself to God, when evil deeds shall not go unpunished. The laws of nature to a large extent ensure some measure of retribution even here and now. Tribes and nations which have practised debasing and unnatunl vices have paid the pennlty in national deterioration, and individual sinners have reaped the bitter fruit proper to evil seed. And there is every reason to believe th11t the righteous judgment of God is not con.fined to this present earthly state. IV. THE REMEDY OF EVIL PASSION, OR LUST, IS PROVIDED IN THE GOSPEL OF OUB LoRD JEsus CHRlBT. It is the purpose of the apostle, in this Epistle to the Romans, to show that the mercy of God our Father hns abounded to sin(ul men, in the provision of (1) pardon for even heinous sin, upon the sinner's repentance and faith; IIIl.d (2) purity of heart and life suoh as the Spirit of Christ alone can create.

entries.content:
-PauZ's description of himsel,f; or, the story of a noble life. .An autobiography, the story of our own life, is a. dangerous thing for a man to write. We aro partisan judges of our own charo.cter. We conceal our own faults nud c:s:!\~ernte our own virtues. An autohiography, too. is often very dull nn•l very dry. But the THE EPISTLE o:r PAUL TO TRB ROIIANS. [on. L 1-89.

autobiography of St. Paul is at onoe Interesting and truthf'nl, As Pe.ley, In hl11 ' Horii! Paulinro,' he.e BO 0181\rly shown, Paul's 11.0COunt of hie own peraone.l history, II'! gi.yen in his writings, is borne out in the fu~lest me.nner by the account given of him in the Acts of the Apostle.q, written by a different person and at a different time. The irresistible truthfulness of the story of Paul's conversion and Apostleship is ao etrong, that the study of it led the celebrated Lord Lyttleton, who had been for me.ny years a sceptic, to embraoe the religion of Jesus Christ and become one of Its ablest advocates. In the.."8 opening verses of the Epistle to t,he Romans, St. Paul gives us, in brief but weighty words, the story of his life. L AN Al'OllTLE's TITLE. "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ" (ver. 1), St, Paul's titles a.re not numerous or high-sounding. He gloried in the title of "servant,,_ eervant of Jesus Christ. Oonsider what it meant for Pa'IJ), that 1uJ beca1M and lived a le'l"Vant qf Jesus Christ. It meant to him loss of worldly prospects. " For whom I have suffered the loss of all things." It meant to him bodily suffering. "I bear about with me in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus." It meant to him-a man of high ment.al endomnents, a ma.n of unblemished character-a life spent largely in the prison-cell, 'With the chains bound upon his wrists. It meant to him-and he knew it well-a life ended on the scaffold, or, like his Master's, on the cross. " I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand." But he had counted the cost, Three things sustained him as he trod that lonely path of service and suffering. He looked back to the cross of Jesus. He had the love of Jesus and the spirit of Jesus in his heart. And he looked forward to the crown of glory that awaited him. Therefore he was able to say, "But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry which I have received of the Lord Jesus." It means m11i,ch the same to be a servant of Jesus <Jlzrut in our own day. You may not meet with bodily suffering as a consequence of your faitclulness to Jesus. But there are other sufferings, perhaps just as bitter and as hard to bear, which must be endured by the faithful servant of Jesus Christ. Make up your mind to this-that you are not the servant of the world, and then what the world may say of you will affect you very little. ..4. servant of Jesus Christ. St, Paul was what he professed to be. The world has confirmed the description, Could the same be said of us? Could we look up to God, or look into the faces of our fellow-men, and say, "Yes, I am a servant of Jesus Christ"? II. .A:s APOSTL1!:'s woBX, AND now HE nm IT. " Called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God" (ver. 1). The word "apostl,i" means a messenger, or one who is sent. This was Paul's work, to be an apostle or messenger of Jesus Christ. Th.is was the form of service he rendered to his Master. His work, the great ambition of his life, was to win men to Christ. General Lew Wallace, in that beautiful story of his, 'Ben Hnr; a Tale of the Christ,' speaks of Jesus Christ as "the one Man whom the world con.Id not do without." That, too, was St. Paul's firm conviction. This was <me of the things that carried him on in his work. He realized the power of the gospel. He felt that it was something more than human. Heart and conscience and intellect told him it was Divine. He, who was so well instructed in the Jewish Scriptures, knew that the prophets EpOke of Christ. " Which he had promised afore by hie prophets in the holy Scriptures" (ver. 2). He knew that Jesus had come. He knew that he had died upon the cross. Ye.s, and he knew that he had risen again. Look at the fourth verse: "Declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holineSE, by the resurrection from the dead." Had he not seen him? Had he not heard his voice-that voice that spoke to him on the way to Damascus, nnd changed for ever the whole current of his life? Yes; Paul knew whom he had believed. He bad no doubt about it. He knt-w what Christ had done for him. And he knew what Christ could do for the world. He knew bow much the world needed Christ. And so he went forth on those great missionary journeys of hi,ll, burning with the one overwhelming, overmastering desire, to preach Christ crucified, and to persuade men In Christ's stead to be reconciled to God. This ia one of the great secrets of BucceBsjul tJJ<Jrk fur CM-iat ,till. We mUBt have a personal knowledge of Jesus as our own Saviour. "An educated ministcy is desirable," said the late Dr. Cooke, of Delfaet, "but a ror.verted ministry is indispensable." And we must then go forth in the conviction diat n,er, 11e;oo Christ, and that he will save them if thc1 come to him. mr. L 1-82,] THE EPIB'rLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMA.NB .

.. I love to tell the llt.ory, Beeanse I know it's truer It ee.tisfies my longings As nothing else can do. I love to tell the story, It did so mu<lh for me ; And that is jllBt the reason I tell it now to thee." Another great secret of Paul's success was this. He realized a Divim p'la,n and_purpose in his life. . He felt that he was "separated unto the gospel of God" (ver. I). Unknown to himself, the Divine hand had been moulding his character, drawincr out and developing his gifts, from his childhood up. How the various circumsta.n~ of his life fitted him for hie great life-work I Born and brought up in Tarsus, he there became a Roman citizen, thUB receiving civil rights and privileges which were of great service to him afterwards in his mission. There also he came in contact with Greek civilization and culture-an acquaintance useful to him afterwards at Athens and at Corinth. Then, coming to Jerusalem, and brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, he there received a training and a position which were of immense advantage to him in dealing with the Jewish people, his kinsmen according to the flesh. All this process of training and development culminated when one day that.Divine hand suddenly arrested his career on the way to Damascus. The light from heaven shone about him then, and shone into his heart. After those days of outward blindness, but inward questioning and growing spiritual vision, the scales fell from his eyes indeed. He saw it all then. Henceforth there was a new meaning and a new purpose in his life. He saw then that he was "called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God." He saw the unseen hand. He saw how it had led him. He saw that it was a hand of power-how foolish to resist it I He saw that it was a hand of love, moulding him for high and holy and eternal purposes. From that moment Paul was Christ's. Not as a slave, but as a. devoted servant. Not in any sense as a mere machine, but Christ's m.th all the persuasion and conviction of his mind, with all the love of his heart-separat&i by his own voluntary act, as he had already been separated by God's purpose, unto the gospel of God. In the seventh verse we see what the message was which Paul took with him wherever he carried the gospel. It is the message which the gospel brings still wherever it finds an entrance. "Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ." Grace-the favour or mercy of God. "Ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that yej through his poverty might be rich" (2 Cor. viii. 9). And where the gospel comes with its message of mercy and of love, the result is pe:ice-peace in the conscience, peace in the home, peace in the nation. Such was the character, such were the life and work of St. Paul. He was a. servant of Jesus Christ. He went forth as a. messenger for Christ, believing that he had been separated unto the gospel of God. And the message which he brought was the message of grace and peace. So may it be with every one of us, if we will only consecrate our lives to God.-0. H. I.

entries.title: ROM 1:16
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-" Noe ash<vmed of ehe gospel." When these words were written by St. Paul, Christianity did not occupy in the world the position that it does now. In the mind of the ordinary Roman, the Jew was regarded almost always with contempt. And when the Christian was at a.II distinguished from the Jew, it was only to be the subject of more reproachful terms. Some of the most eminent and well-informed of the Roman writers speak of the Christian religion as a pernicious and detestable superstition. The humble origin, too, of the early founders of Christianity was not calculated to impress favourably the worldly mind. If the gospel which told of Christ crucified was a stumbling-block to the Jew, it was indeed foolishness to the Greek and to the Roman too. Yet Paul had not been ashamed of this gospel at .Athens; he was not going to be ashamed of it at Rome. He had proclaimed the message of the Nazarene in the city of Plato and Socrates ; he would preach it also in the city of Cicero and Seneca. Paul is not afraid to teach where they have taught. He was right. The nam.e of Jesus is a greater name than Plato's. The religion which Jesus taught has moulded and purified the world. The apostle assigns two reasons why he is not ashamed of the gospel. These are- I. ITs PURPOSE. This is indicated by the words "unto salvation." The Greek preposition which is translated "unto" expresses purpose, or tendency, or aim. The purpose of the gospel is the salvation of all who will receive its message. To effect this purpose, the Son of God left the glory of the eternal, and descended into the misery and weariness of a life on earth. For this, he suffered the assaults of the tempter ; for this, he passed through the agony of Gethsemane; for this, he bore with patience the lingering torments of the cross. "The Son of man is come to seek and to sa,e that which was lost." The purpose of the gospel is salvation. Let us understand fully the meaning of that great word. Salvation is indeed deliverance from guilt, deliverance from condemnation. But the purpose of the gospel is something more than this. It is to save us also from the power of sin in our hearts and lives. Many professing Christians forget this. 'l'bey think that faith in Christ is simply to deliver them from punishment in the day of judgment, while they do not allow it to have present, practical influence upon their lives. Let us not deceive ourselves. There is no true sah·ation where there is not an evidence of present departure from sin and present following after holiness. "By their fruits ye shall know them." Faith, if it is real, will show itself. Salvation is a. present thing. "The blood of Jesus Christ, God's Son, cleanse/h us from all sin." The purpose of the gospel is to save us now There are many who long for some power that might save them from themselves, from some evil propensity or passion, from the influence of bad companionships. This salvation it is the purpose of the gospel to effect. "Thanks be unto God, who giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." IL ITs POWER, The gospel, sn.ys the apostle, is "the powor of God." Here is an encouragement for our faith. This is tho second reason why St. Paul wn.s not ashamed of the gospel. Its purpose, no doubt, seemed a very difficult one, but the apostle had no fear for its success. Its earliest messengers were humble meu. But the success of thoir message was in higher and mightier hands than theirs. That sin should be ovorcome, nnd men delivered from its power, was the purpose of the .Almighty God, n.nd his purpose nevor fails. In tho history of nations we see the gospel proving itself to be the power of God, The mornl miracles of Christianity, as Prebendary Row hM ahown, are the stron~est eviience of its Divine origin and power. It bas changed bnrba.rism to civilization. It has ernn.ncipated the slaves. It has put an end to the cruol sacrifices performed in honour of tho heathen gods. It hns accomplished moral and sooinl rovolutions thn.t to tho human eye seemed utterly impossible, So rueo In tho history of individuals. Mou who ha.Yo suuk so luw beneath tho power of degrading 98 'rHE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THl!: ROMANS. [cm. 1.1-311,

vioe that their frienda despaired of reacuing them, by the power of the gospel have been brought from death unto life. Jesusi and Jesus only, can oure men <Jf sin's power. If we but touch his garment, we shl\ 1 be made whole. No one haa any reason to lie ashamed of the gospel.. Its purpose is a high and noble one, the highest and noble1.1t mission ever undert.aken. Its power is not the power of a foeble or n puny arm. It is the poW8l' of the living God. These are thoughts to inspire, and not to make ashamed.-C. H. I. Vers. 1S-32.-Tlie i~knas of the heat1aen. In the twentieth verse the 11.postle speaks of the heathen as "without excuse." These words describe the condition of those who have wilfully rejected light. They do not, indeed, describe their condition from their own standpoint or from the st.&ndpoint of men generally. From their own standpoint men are reldom "without excuse." No matter how gross or glaring the offence is, the offender has usua.J\y some excuse to offer. Adam and Eve had their ex.cuses rea.dy when the Lord God said, "What is this that thou hast done?" Saul had his excuse ready when he returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites without having fully carried out the commandment of the Lord, when Samuel asked him, '' What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and this lowing of the oxen which I bear?" It might be taken as on the whole a fair description of the human race to say, "They all with one consent began to make excuse." However slow we are to excuse others, we are always remarkably ready to excuse ourselves. But these words describe the condition of those who reject light from the standpoint of him who is the great Searcher of hearts. He makes no mistakes. He makes no uncharitable judgments. In his sight those to whom he has given light, and who have chosen t.o reject it, are "without excuse." They are inexcusable. They have no Talid reason for their ignorance about the way of salvation and the path of duty if God has given them light about both. This is the condition described by Christ in that parable where he represents the king as coming to one of the guests at the marriage-feast, and saying to him.. "Friend, how earnest thou in hither, not having on a wedding-garment?" And the Saviour tells us, "And he was speechless." He knew that he was 'IDithw;t euwe. He knew the laws of the feast; be knew that the weddinggarment was provided, and he neglected t.o put it on. So shall it be in the great day, of judgment with all those who had the opportunity to know God's will, but who neglected to do it. May we be enabled, in considering the inexcusableness of the heathen, to think of this solemn subject with reverence and with fairness. • L LIGHT GRANTED. If God expects men to know him, we may be sure that he has given them the means of knowing him. God will judge every man according to the opportunities he has had. Paul's st.atement is definite and clear. They are without excuse, he says, "because that, when they lcnew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful" (ver. 21). They knew God, says the apostle. How, then, did they know him? And what did they know about him ? They knew him by means of his works, and they knew at least two things about his character-that he was a Being of power, and that his power was more than human. It is inferred a!J;o that they knew themselves to be dependent upon bis bountiful providence and care, else they could not have been accused of being ungrateful. " Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God bath showed it unto them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead ; so that they are without excuse" (vers. 19, 20). Here, then, it is clearly taught that it is possible to obtain a knowledge of God from bis works, and that such knowledge the ancient heathen bad. St. Paul knew very well what he was talking about when he said that the e.ncieot heathen had a knowlcd~e of God. He was well acquainted with the literature of ancient Greece. On Mars' Hill we fincl him quoting to the philosophers of Athens a statement from AratUl!, one of their own 1iocts. "As certain also of your own poeta have said, For we are also bis offspring." 'l.'l,e light of nature-this is the light which was granu,d to the ancient heathen. Two things that light of nnture taugbL them about G,.,d-biH power and his Godhead. '"l'hc heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament sboweth his handiwork." Beh;nd the stare and the Rea, there rnuat be some power that made and controls them •11. The order of tho seasona. au. r. 1-32.] Tim EPISTLE OF PA.UL TO THE ROMAN8. 29

the succoselon of dBy and night, the ebb and flow of the tides-all these thinzs require 11. controlling force, and that force must not only ha.ve a.lmighty power, but rnust ha.ve intelligence and reason nnd will, Buch a being mnst be a Person. Such a. Pernon is more thnn human-is Divine. Tho ea.me light of nature is granted to us all. But how much more ligllt has been granted to us/ We have the light of God's written Word. What mysteries that Word opens up to us, concerning which the voice of nature is silent I WhBt a light it gives ue about the mercy of God, and the Saviour's redeemincr love I What a light it gives us about immortality and heaven, a.ft.er which the best of the ancient heathen were groping and searching in darkneBB ! How thankful we should be, amid the darkness which sorrow brings, and as we look forward to the darkness of the grave, for the light which God in his Word has mercifully granted to us I But that great privilege, that unspeakable blessing, 'brings with it a solemn responsibility. We who have the Bible in our hands are without excuse if we live in godlessness or unbelief, if we reject the offer of salvation. II. LIGHT nEJEOTED, "They are without excuse, because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were t■ankful" (vers. 20, 21). And then, further on, the apostle says, "They did not like to retain God in their knowledge" (ver. 28). How often have nati()'ll,s acted thus-rejecting the light which was their best possession, their safety and their shield I The Jewish nation rejected the heavenly light, notwithstanding God's repeated warnings as to the consequences of doing so. !<'ranee rejected the light when it expelled the Huguenots, the God-fearing portion of its population. Spain did the same when, by its Inquisition and its autos-da,-fi, it exterminated all who dared to prefer the pure light of the Divine Word to the darkness and superstitions of Rome. Such nations were plainly without excuse, for they had the light, and deliberately rejected and quenched it when they could. & also u·e find rulers rejecting the light. That was the case with King Saul. He rejected the commandment of the Lord, and God rejected him from being king over Israel Belshazzar, King of Babylon, had plenty of light given him in the career of Nebuchadnezzar his father about the power and justice of God. But, as Daniel reminded him, he had disregarded the solemn lesson; though he knew all this, he had not bumbled himself, but had lifted himself up against the Lord of heaven (Dan. v. 21, 22). And so on that night of revelry the fingers of a man's hand came forth and wrote upon the wall, " Thou a.rt weighed in the balBnces, and art found wanting." He was without excuse. He had rejected the light which God had given him. Do we not see a similar infatuation in the case of the unhappy Mary Queen of Scots? Though she had faithful men of God in her ea.pita.I and often heard the truth from the lips of John Knox, she chose rather to be guided by her own ea.prices and by the influence of her frivolous courtiers. She, too, rejected the light which God had placed within her reach. We an not to think that it makes no difference whether we accept the Divine light or not. There is a danger that we may becomo too liberal as to the attitude men take up regarding God's Holy Word. It is well to be broad-broad as the mercy and the love of God. But, on the other hand, we ma.y be broader and more indulgent towards error than God's Word permits of. God des.ls with men as intelligent and rational and moral beings, with a free will, capable of free choice. He puts before them life and death. He tells them that "the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." He tells them that there is no other wa.y of salvation except through Jesus Christ alone. Upon them rests the responsibility and the guilt if they reject his salvation. It is worse than a matter of indifference; it is a sin in the sight of God. it is n sin against their own soul's destiny, for men to reject or neglect the mes.sage which the great Creator has mercifully sent them. It may be done in the name of science. It may be done in the name of advanced thought. But it is moral guilt nevertheless. " They are without excuse." III. WnATH REV:U.LED. "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven ~"'1Wl8i all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousnes.s" (ver. 18). And how could it be otherwise, If light bas been granted to beings of intelligence and reason and conscience, and they have deliberately chosen to reject it, is it not fair nnd just that thoy should take the consequences? It is in the very 1rnture of things that "wlmtsoovor II man soweth, that shall he also reap." A man c1mnot violnte a nntural law with imptwity. The most liberal-minded sci~ntilic lW\11 30 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [011. 1, 1-32

will eee no unraimess in a mnn suffering if he disregards or violates the well-known laws of nature. Fire will burn, water will drown, pitch will defile, bnd air will poison, If a man acts in defiance of these natural and elementary laws, he suffers tho coneo- quence. No one sees any unfairness in it. Why should there be any more tt,ifairne.,s in suffering a8 the result of disregarding and defying moral laws, On the contrary, is it not or more importance that a moral law should be vindicated, that men should learn t.o obey a moral law, than that even a natural law should be vindicated P Dut here, at any rate, is the fact, written clearly in God's Word, written over and over again on the page of hist.ory-light ,·e}~ted means wrath revealed. Was it not so with ancient Israel? Has it not been so with France and Spain? Was it not so with Saul and Belshazzar? It is a terrible thing when men so harden themselves against God's Word, so shut their eyes R,..01\inst the light of his commandments, yes, even against the light of the cross, that God says, "Ephraim is joined to idols : let him 11.lone." Let him alone I Light granted. Light rejected. Wrath revealed. "Without excuse." Such is St. Paul's description of the ancient heathen world. To a world in such a state Jesus came. He came to reveal the righteousness of God in contrast to the abominable deities of heathenism. He came also to reveal the mercy of God. The trumpet-note of judgment is loud and terrible. But the trumpet-note of mercy is equally loud. "There is therefore now no condemnation to them who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."-C. H. I.

And so the tru6 rai;:iister-a man first, one of the sinful. struggling mass of men, and saved with the common salvation. 2. And though the expression is to be applied very cautiously, lest the ba!1lber suggestions should mislead us, yet there are elements of meaning which are full of force. Absolute proprietorship on the one hand, and obligatoriness of service on the other; but the relationship transfused with blessedness, for the claims are claims of love, and the service is a service of love. All true Christians, like Paul. bear about with them the marks of the Lord Jesus (Gal. vi, 17 ; 2 Cor. iv. 10), and the brand-mark is this, "He died for me" (see 1 Cor. vi. 19, 20; vii. 22, 23). 3. The labourer in the field, and the hard worked· wife in household cares aa well a.s the man of letters, the statesman, or the prince, is "called or Goel." Such a one wa.s Paul Called to Christian service, in common with all his brethren; called to exclusive service, in common with many of his brethren; celled furthermore tu apostolic service, in common with a few selected ones, who led the van of the new faith, and tel!tified authoritatively of the crucified and risen Obrist. "By call an ar,.111tle." The distinctive call was made in conm,ction with one special crisis of his life-the Dama.scus journey, and the voice from hr•aven. Dut was this, with its ratification of Acts xiii. 2, the only "separation unto the gospel" of which Paul goes on to 6L,cak? Nay, we are rather led to think of tbE, phrase in Gal. i. 15, "separated ••• ea, 1.1-82.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMA:N'S. 81

from my mother's womb." For there is e. certain Divine fatalism which is in perfect he.rmony with moral freedom; every one born into this world is prc<l,ilstincd from the fil'st for some srecial work for God. The work may be marr~., or altwether left undone, by;man e perverseness; but the work is the Divine destiny of the ~an. .And the after-life is an equipment for the fulfilling of this destiny. 'l'he circumstances of our lot, and the events that ~befall us; our joys and our sorrows; and all our natural and moral education, combine with our original constitution and temperament at once to indicn.te God's purpose and to fit us for its fulfilment. .And was not Paul "a chosen vessel" ?-marked out from the first for the conspicuous part which he afterwards played in the world's history ; "separated unto the gospel of God." Buch wa.s the m&~ • II. TnE Cmrnon. And his apostleship was to "the nations;" the Gentile "world was his parish." Therefore the little Christian band at Rome, though not gathered, directly at least, by his labours, might well receive his message. They formed a Gentile Church, and as such he writes to them. They are threefoldly designated. 1. "Bel.oved of God." " God's love is the source of all his benefits, and the sure ground of our hope. Our consciousness of his love is the basis of the Christian life. Of this love all men are objects, but only believers are conscious objects. To them it is real and living. It moulds their thoughts and life" (Beet, in Zoe.). Yes; "we have known and believed the love that God bath to us" (1 John iv. 16): that is the inspiration of the new lifo. 2. "Called to oe Jesus Christ's ... called to be saints." Or, •~Jesus Christ's ... saints, by call." For the summons had been responded to; the love of God in Christ had changed their hearts. And now they were his people (see Titus ii.14), and for his Name's sake they were living consecrated lives. For this is our only sainthood: "Whether we live," etc. (eh. xiv. 8). 3. .And this by" obedience offaith." The spring of the new life, on the human side, even as God's love is the spring of life on the Divine side. --..ve yield to Christ's claim, and live to God as saints, only in so far as we receive Christ into our hearts by faith, and believe the love God hath to us. And in all the manifold departments of the Christian life, we "live by faith." We receive, or more actively we gra.i!p, the goodness of God and the life which is through Christ. And this "obedience uf faith" is the end of all apostleship and ministry (John vi. 29; 1 John iii. 23). : III. THE MESSAGE, 1. "Grace." God's favour, and all the saving help which he gives because he loves us. A continuous and increasing realization. 2. "Peace."' The abiding calmness of a conscience which has yielded to be justified by faith (eh. v. 1), accepting the grace of God's favour, rejoicing in the light; calmness of heart al.i;o, in view even of fierce conflict and trial, by reason of the voice which says, "My grace is sufficient for thee." "Grace and peace." So the old Gentile and Jewish sa.lutings were transfigured by the gospel of Christ. In conclusion, the keynote is the "call." God calls you, calls you through Christ, calls you to be Christ's, calls you in your own minor apostleship to be servants of Christ. And the true response to this call is by obedience of faith; for, from first to last of the Christian life, "by grace are ye saved, through faith" (Eph. ii. 8). Oh, be it ours to respond, "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth" !-1'. F. L.

entries.title: ROM 1:2–4
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Tlie characterization of" the gospel of God," to which Paul was separated. Tho awfulness of a commission of doom. Jonah. But to herald forth God's good tidings to a sorrowing world I This is the crown of all Christilm ministry. The angels might well siug nnd be glad whon ushering this gospel into the world (Luke ii. 9-H); and Paul is rejoiced that he can strike this note of gladness. Ther,i might well be proludes to this burst of joy: so the words, "which he promised afore," etc. F.:ir ~11 the indications of God's purposes of love, from Gen. iii. to Malachi, did but prepare thd way for the comploted announcement in "the fulness of the time." And so virtually they e.11 were Divine promises of a fuller gospel. The two main thoughts-God's gospel; its contents. I. GoD's GOSPEL, 1. A gospel carries the implication of e. wn.nt, and, it rr.ay be, of a sorrow and a loss. So do the good tidings of God to mon assume that msn blloS lost his Goel, and with God nll things good. (1) Man knew not, suroly. tho reality of his sin; WIMI decoivod by the tempter; but awoke from his dream to find that God was gc,no ! And this is the great loss of tb.o world, Tho voicos cry, " Whoro is thy God'?" ~ud 82 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [arr. L 1-82.

he? Tbe Gc,oo One-the light., the joy, the song of his crcntion. So man !ms blotted out his 0wn h('Rn'll", nnd the earth thereby has h)st its lustro nnd its grnco. (2) But the et1tmu;C'\i God is a condemning God. He may not abdicate his essential relntiouship t0 the world as God, and if the love be lost it is replaced by wrath I So me.n's con- i:cience testifies: stricken, 1,0ro, and bleeding. 2. A gospol c1uries the implication of a desire to have the want supplied, the sorrow and the loss removed. So man's sin has n0t hopelessly ruined him, else there could be no salvation. Room for God to work, imd God does work. (1) The historical preparation: God teaching the world to desire sal'l"'!ltion. The Jews by direct dealings, a positive discipline; the Gentiles by indirect, R ne~tive discipline. So, "the desire of all nations." (2) The individual preparation: G,_-,d's Spirit in the heart. Only the grace of God can bring us to God. And uow God's gospel means, in general, that the condemning God will pardon, and the estranged God be a Father and a Friend again; that the yearnings towards himself which he has called forth shall thus find their full satisfaction, which is nothicg other than the peace of forgiveness and the joy of adopting love. II. ITS oo~'"Tfil."TS. But this general message has special terms. God's love is mani- festoo, prove.cl., accomplished, in his Son. 1. "His Son." For it is God's own love, hia other self, which stoops to save us. Let us hold fast to this, for herein is the supreme pledge of our salvation. 2. His Son becomes "Jesus Christ our Lord." (1) By the assumption of human nature. "Born of the seed of David e.ccording to the flesh." That it may be one of ourselves who saves us. (a) A Man, making atonement to God for men; (b) a human High Priest and Captain of salvation, himself "perfect through sufferings," and therefore " touched with the feeling of our infirmities "-the onenesa with human-kind necessary for both the Godward and the manward aspects of the reieeming work. A Son of David, according to mere historical lineage and local appearance: "for salvation is of the Jews." But, grander and more royal than this, a Son of man-the Son of man, in his true human fashioning and for his world-wide work (Heb. iL 14). (2) By the glorification of human nature. "Declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection of the <lead." A Redeemer of men must assert their redemption in his own Person first. " We ree not yet all things pot under him [i.e. man]. But we see Jesus . . . crowned with glory and honour" (Heb. ii. 8, 9), the archetypal Man. His resurrection, which the apoi;tle here li.Dks on to its world-wide correlative and consequence," the resurrection af the dead," demonstrates the redemptive power of Jesus, who is therefore the Christ, our Lord, and therefore Son of God; for only he who has life in himself can give life t.o dying men-life from the death of sin, life from all death which sin has more indirectly wrought. Oh, let us hearken t.o soch a gospel I God's good news to a dyicg world, spoken forth with a.ll the power of One who waa God's very Son, and with all the tender sympathy of One who is our very Brother. And for a proper hearkening to this good news may God, in hia love, prepare our he.a.rte 1-T. F. L. Vera. ~15.-Ministerial sympathy. The apostolic commission has been presented; in thi8 section it is interfused with the sympathy and service of ·a brother. He is still prt,-~minently the preacher of the gospel (ver. 15), but he speaks as to those whose faith is one with his own, and who are therefore brethren in a most sacred brotherhood. We may con.sider, u in 10me sort distinct though mutually involved-his prayers, and hia purpose. L His PRAYEBII.. Does Paul for one moment here strike a happy comparison between his wurk and that of the priestly intercessor in the elder covenant? For the "service n of which he speaks now is the service as of a temple, and it is as though he said, "In tb.e gospel. ae under the Law, there is a holy of holies, and worshipful intercession there. 'l'he holy of holies is the shrine of the innermost spirit, where converse is b.eld with God, and the priiietly worship is the pleading for brethren in Obrist, o.nd concerning the things that touch the kingdom of God," Yes, he "serves" God "in bis spirit in the goapel of his Son." 1. .A th.vnlcsyivmg. "'l'bat your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world." It was fitting that be should use euoh langungo 8E tb.il!, hyperbolical though It wa1, t.o those who lived in the world's metropolis, Wherever he went he heard of their good name, and he thanlted God for it. He thaukod OB. 1. 1-32.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 88

God for H? Yee; for was he not spiritually identified with all who were identi fled with Ohrist his Lord? (1) Doubtless the fo.ith itself which was so eminent was the chief cause of graUtude. That there should be such a light Rhining in a dark place filled his. heart with joy. '!'hey were alive unto God I (2) That the faith of the gospel should have to.ken such hold on the world's central and imperial city was no lllllall caaB!l for joy. What visions of the future might not open up before his mind I (3) The wide proclama,- tion of their faith was gratifying, for if others were stimulated it would be for the furtherance of the gospel. 2. .A longing. "To see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift," etc. The grace of God that was in him was to be operative towards othera; he lived not unto himself. And was it not even so with them? A mutual duty, and a mutual blessing. (1) The interaction of their common faith: intensity by contact. (2) The special aspects of the common faith: "yours and mine;" "some spiritual gift." Thus their establishment. The fulfilment of what promised so well, and the supply of any lack. 8. .A request. "If by any means now at length,'' etc. ...ls Paul taught the Philippians afterwards (Phil. iv. 6), so he practised now. ...lnd doubtless, with all the wrestlings of that impetuous spirit, there was peace. For God's will was gO'll,vern,ant. "By any means." He learned in the issue (Acts x.xviii.) that his ways are not as our ways. But it would still be "prosperity" (see ver. 10), if it were God's doing; so eh. viii. 28. II. His PURPOSE, 1. The great constraint of the gospel,. "I am debtor." Nothing in the universe so free as the spirit of Christianity; nothing, on the other hand, which lays so commanding a grasp on love and life. A blessed yoke. (1) A.11 our possessions and powers are held in trust for the world; we all a.re "debtors," according to oar several capacities and circumstances. ~2) In an eminent degree are we stewards as being entrusted with the gospel of Gods grace. And the law-here, as in the former case-is, that being unused it ceases to be possessed. 2. The personal aim. "That I might have some fruit." Were the words of our Lord in mind, John xv. 8? Or was he rather regarding the world as a great field, and himself as a sower? (see John iv. 35-38; 1 Cor. iii 7-9). (1) The commission was to the Gentile world (..:\..cts ix. 15; xxii 21; so vers. 13, 14). (2) Must not the central purpose, then, be the evangelization of the great metropolis of the Gentile world? Doubtless this filled his mind, and hence his intense interest in these Roman Christians. What visions! Realized in history. How? and how may it yet be? Let us realize our stewardship (1 Pet. iv. 10); and that the fulfilment of our stewardship may become a freedom and gladness, let 118 realize our oneness with Christ, and with Christ's people.-'!'. F. L.

entries.title: ROM 1:16
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Not ashamed I Why should he be ashamed? The great metropolis of a world-empire, with Its wide-reaching power and permeating law; and he and his gospel I What a contrast it might seem I and how the supercilious Romans might overwhelm him with contempt I For they were not, as the Athenians, ever desirous to hear some new thing. And his gospel? it would be their laughing-stock. Nay, he shell not be ashamed. He will take his stand in the very centre of Rome's power, and at her fountain-bead of righteousness, and there present his gospel. For it power, ,ind in it was revealed a righteousness-the power of God, the righteousness af = a.

God. Let us regard these two aspects now. I. Gon's POWER. Man plumes himself with pride on the possession of might, but how impotent he is in the grasp of the great God I So, too, the "great powers" of the world's history: Daniel's interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's vision (D,m. ii. 31--!6). And " the powers that be ore ordaiue,l of God." God's power is manifold. The governance of nature, the control of the alfairs of men, the influence on the heart. And of thfa manifold power of God the gospel of Christ is a pre-eminent display. 1. Its aim. "Unto solvntion." No narrow restriction of this term; coexteusi,·o with tht110:is: the man, the life, tho world. Soo eh. viii. for this wide meanin~ of tht1 w0nl.. entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-TM revelation of wrath. "For." Note the transition. The introduction into a status of righteousness presupposes a status of unrighteollJlness, involving wrath. entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The gospel a, fulfilled prophecy. The apostle loved to dilate on the characteristics of the gospel, especially those which he "received by revelation.," and his aspect of truth became so essentially a part of bis being and preaching, that he speaks of it as "my" gospel. Sometimes be terms it the "gospel of Christ," whilst here the title is significantly the" gospel of God," since he is about to prove it a design purposed of God from the beginning of revelation. I. THE GOSPEL AS PBOMISED, 1. He alleges a,s proof of the promise the Scripture prophecies. Note the phrase, "the holy writings," emphasizing the quantity and quality of the literature of the Old Testament. 2. Such a, prurmse rebuts the charge of novelty. The Jews were conservative, and the only way to remove their prejudice against Christianity was by persuading them out of the Scriptures that it was no newfangled doctrine which the apostles preached. The difficulty in controversies is to find e. common court of appeal. The position of the Jews as custodians of the genuineness of the Old Testament has weight in argument to-day. 3. Shows the gospel to have been no a,fter0 thought in the mind of God. The Lamb was "slain from the fonndation of the world." The plan of Providence is gradually unfolded as the centuries pass. Looking back, we can see how the beautiful petals of the mature flower were foretold by the markillgs of the bud. 4. The predictions which animated the l,reastii of mm of old have their confirmatory value for modern faith. The patriarchs" died in faitb.D The prophets " searched diligently what time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify." And the fact that they were "heralds..,, proclaiming the advent of the King, prepares us to receive him with less fear of delusion. It is seemly that so grnnd a Monarch and kingdom should not be established without the pomp of previous notice. The battle of criticism rages most furiously at present around the Old Testament prefigurations of the new covenant, for men discern the impregnableness of Christianity unless the outworks of Jewish history and expectancy,,can first be stormed and demolished, II. THE PROMISE REDEEMED. 1. In th6 Man Christ Jesus. In answer to the inquiry of Herod, the scribes were able to give the place where the Messiah should be born, and the royal house of which he should be a direct descendant. 'l'b.e genealogies of Matthew and of Luke alike acoredit the olaims of Jesus to be of the stock of David. At the birth of Jesus wns there great "joy that a man was born into the world." entries.title: ROM 1:7
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-.An honor,rable clau. Describe Rome, and compare it with our modem cities. The metropolis of the world, with two millions of people in about sixteen square miles ; every trade, nationality, and religion represented there, The apostle knew the strategic importance of a Christian stronghold in Rome. What a mighty influence might radiate thence to every quarter of the globe I To energize the heart of the empire was to quicken with Christian life the whole world. L A SPECIAL CLASS SINGLED OUT. The "all" in Rome are restricted by the subsequent designa.tion.s. It is useless to ignore the New Testament line of distinction. Men are disti'flgUishm by their relationship to the gospel, not by their social standing or intellectual ability, but by their moral qualifications, as possessors of good hearts which have received the seed of the kingdom. To speak of Christiane is to mark them off from all besides, as a straight stick differentiates crooked ones. Would Christ send his messengers to our houses as to those "who are worthy" ? This distinction creates a bcmd of ur,iun. The snperficial diversities amongst the followers of Christ are merged in the one great feature of similarity. .All are "one" in Christ Jesus, whether they live in the East or the West End, in the great rooms of a palace or the attic of e. lodging-house. And in the primitive Church, as to-day, the uniting power of the gospel wa.s a striking proof of its Divine origin-that he who made the key to fit so many hearu was the same who first constructed those human wards. If Ohriet appeared tc,-day, it would be as when a magnet is introduced into a box of iron filings; the affinity of hi! people would be discovered by their instant attraction to him, and the closer they preesed to him the nearer they would draw to one anothor. Christianity is healthfni aocialism.. II. THEIB HAPPY OOliDITIOB'. "Beloved of God.., The Almighty is good to all his creatures ; he " is great, and despiseth not any; " his sunshine and rain benefit all indiscriminately. Jeaus weeping over Jerusalem exemplified God's infinite pity towards rebe!liuUA mbjf:Cte, 110JTowing over their distresses aud grieved at their sins. But the 1-'JVt: uf tl~ t.ezt iii that uf c<Ynpla«mcy, where God can rest in his love with satisfaction, rejoicing io the rentow•.:d nature and the evidences of reatored sonehip. Love must be 11tr01,gest and molli delightful when reciprocated by ite object, ae the mirror incrcasos light by reflection. It is cm CMW1M,Un(/ de,ignation ; for men need love as plants need sllDl!hioe and warmth. The loneliest heart may be cheered by tho assurance of Lhe Divwe paMinw &tfection. li ii an '1VMbUnv love. Many a man hu rben through ou, 1. 1-82,] THE EPISTLE OJ' PAUL TO 'l'RE BOHANB. 87

love to the height of hie capacity; hie power• baV'e been stimulated and developed. How strong for noble deeds must those be 'l'!ho think of the mighty heart of God pulsating to the rhythm of their feeble souls / Stunted lives may blos.-rom and grow fruitful under the "light of bis countenance," seeking to live worthy of bis wondrous love. It implies the weU-being of those laved. Not necessarily exemption from hardship and trial, not miraculous inter_POsition every day; but unfailing guidance and 811CCOW', and the certainty of a blessed issue to all events. Our God never intender] us to dwell all our lives in suspense concerning onr relationship to him, bnt to come ont inw the unclouded day by accepting hie declarations, and we honour him when we arm our breasts with these magnificent truths as with triple steel against all vexation, and flood our dwelling with the benignant splendour of hie promises. III. THEm DIGNIFIED VOOATION. "Called to be saints." The word "called" ha.a become so theological that to enter into its meaning with any freshness we must strip it of its technical clothing. A man's calliog is his occupation in life-that by which he earns his livelihood. The main bnsiness of the Christian is to cullioote hdine88. He is set apart, like the priest, with anointing oil for the service of God. This aim is in no wise incompatible with the fulfilment of his ordinary worldly avocation. Every situation is adapted to the pursuit of holiness, disciplining the soul, calling for endnrance or activity. The "saint" is "separate from sinners,'' not by reason of bodily absence, but through his consecrated thought and endeavour and behaviour. The same action may be performed from higher motives and with a regard to vaster issnes. The saints are furnished with all requisite aids to holiness. The written Word, the Spirit, the house of prayer,-these are all helps to a godly life. We are not set to make bricks without straw. The manner of our call enforces the obligation to sainthood. We have been called by Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, our Pattern and Power, who called the disciples by the sea-shore, and Matthew at the toll-bar; and his su=ons reaches ill! from his cross of anguish, and from his throne of victory on high. The title of" saints" is expressly assigned to the followers of Christ, and it behoves us to walk worthy of our high calling and of the name by which we are called. Mistrust disowns such high, grand titles; faith claims and justifies them. Will not some respond to Chri,,--t.'s call to-day? "Harden not your hearts, if ye should hear his voice."-S. R. A.

entries.title: ROM 1:9
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-.An appeal and a parenthesis. To the full and ardent mind the statement of one fact or thought calls up many associated ideas, and a parenthesis is the result. In the widespread recognition of the faith of the Roman Christians (ver. 8) Paul discerned an answer to his prayers. How constant those intercessions were only God could know, and to him the apostle appealed, justifying the appeal by a parenthetical reference to his life of faithful service, The text, therefore, suggests reflection on three topics. I. THE PROPRIETY OF INVOKING THE TESTIMONY OF Goo. Too frequently ha.,e publio utterances and conversation been interlarded with the mention of the Dinne Name, violating the third commandment and the Saviour's instructions. The tendency of modern legislation to restrict the occasions on which the taking of an oath is obligatory should be welcomed. It is allowable to call God to witness in solcrnr1 matters, befitting the dignity of the Most High. Especially in matters that lie tcithin God's cognizance only, as here respecting the frequency of the apostle's petitions at the mercy-seat. The invocation .of the Divine witness is seemliest from the lips of his servants. With what show of reason cau others demand his presence to cc,nlinu their statoments? Profane swearers convict themselves of inconsistency. Ewn ,\ rt'g",mi for others' feelings will sometimes lend men to o.bstain from trifiing with the s:,cn>J. Nam<J of our Fo.thor and Friend. II. Tmi: IMl'ORTANOE OF INTERCESSORY PRAYER. Largeness of heart contributes much to the enjoymont and prevnlenco of our prayers. When we seem dull in resp,:>Ct of our own uecds, the remombmnco of anot.her's want.s may "unlock the sealed fountain." We may gaugo our i11terest in our follows by ehe regularity Qj 0111· retiti,ms on thtlir bohalf. If wo pray uot oft on for t.hcru, how cun wo be ~id to caro tor their wt>lfsre? Speak of thorn whoro it sh1,ll ho of most avail. "For whl\t l\l'O tnen better than sheep or goata, 'l'ho.t nourish I\ blind life wiUiin the bnun, If, knowing God, they lift not h&nda of prayer Both for thamselvea and those who oall them friend P" The apostle evidently thinks of pmying a.s a real pirl of Christian. illlf"llice. Like the incenl!e which it was the honourable dnty of the priests to offer, so did Paul daily "lift up holy hands " as his continual sacrifice and ministration. It ie a l1Uv of God's paternal go.ernment that his children's requests should, though eo simple and feeble in themselve~, link them with Omnipotence, and achieve mightiest effects. Wha.t a.ils us that we &l"0 so slow to visit this "wishing-gate 11 ? God measures the co11,stancy and .ferwncy of our prayers. They a.re not a sma.11 performance soon forgotten. They constitute a revelation of our condition, a. spiritual thermometer whose readings are redstered. ~ill. THE QUALITIES THAT BEl....DER BEBVICE ACCEPTABLE TO GoD. It must be Bpiritutd, that is, not formal or ceremonial, but an expression of the inner life ; not rendered as a burdensome task, but a.coording to " the spirit that giveth life rather than the ietter -v;hich killeth." The apostle was constrained by love, for Christ had laid hold of his heart's affections and made him conscious of & new inward impulse, which transfigured obedience and made it liberty, a.nd altered wearisome duty into gladsome service. It was the difference between the mechanical elevation and motion of a kite by the wind, and the soaring flight of the bird joying in its vital powers. Spiritual service is not blind, unreasoning devotion, but a ministration approved of by the noblest faculties of the soul It is evangelical, a.rising from and moving in the sphere of the glorious revelation of the Son of God. Through Christ had the apostle "received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all nations, for his Name's sake" (ver. 5). The knowledge and reception of the gospel imply privilege and responsibility. The true Christian life is filled with gospel motives and aims, nor is any condition inapt for gospel service, its priesthood and sacri.fices.-S. R. A. Vers. n. 12.-Longing to meet. The vehement desire of the apostle cherished through many years was at l~uth gratified; but the manner of entering Rome how different from the anticipated voluntary visit I He was to arrive, after a tempestuous, perilous voyage, as a prisoner to plead for his life before the emperor. It is well that a veil hides the future, or our wishes for some event might die a.way in silence. I. LoVE IB KOT SATISFIED WITHOUT A MEETING. Augustine would have liked to see Christ in the :flesh, Paul in the pulpit, and Rome in its glory. The apostle thought little of the outward ma,,an.i.ficence of the metropolis; his heart turned to the company of Ch..ristians there. Some were his kinsmen, others had been his fellow-workers and pru!Oners, yet all who were knit in Christian fellowship were dear to him, and he longed t,o see them face to face. The ties of attachment in the early Church may have been cemented by the cold wind of opposition and persecution, which drove the members closer together for warmth and sympathy. Still Christianity proves itself able to banish worldly distinctions to-day, breaking down barriers of race and caste and language. The friends of the Saviour can feel no jealousy, since his love is large enough to embrace all, and a regard for his honour impels his friends to increase the number of his adherents. Love to Christ is the antithesis of narrowness of spirit. We may form an opinion of our discipleship from observing the degree of our longing to "885Cmble ourselves together." "We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.'' There is a. natural desire to look upon the face and form of fa.moue men. that names may become persons to us, and that our weak imaginations may henceforth be assisted in picturing their voice and gesture and appearance. And this yearning leaps np into a. sacred hope of the consummation of our bliss, when we shall be permitted to behold the Saviour and "see him as he is." Christ is " with us" now, but at death we depart to be "with Christ" for ever. Proximity and a.ffecticn are correlative ideas. ' II. THE )[EETING OP' CBll.lBTIAli'B HAS EDIFICATION AB ITS ODJEOT. Paul was Bnpremely anxious t< be the medium of spiritual benefit to the Christians at Rome. He believed that a BpiritWJJ, gift wa, the most valuable present he could bestow or they could receive. It ranked higher than scientific communications or almsgiving. -Glorying in the gospel. For many reasons the apostle might be supposed ashamed to preach the gospel at Rome. He had been long delayed from fulfilling his purpose to visit that city. The "good news" centred in the mission of a Jew, belonging to a race despised by their masterful conquerors. The story of the cross could not fail to excite ridicule wheu the Romans heard that this Messiah had O.."t'n njected by his own countrymen, and handed over to an ignominious death, and that his disciples seriously believed that he had risen again from the dead. A kingdom founded on humility and love would seem e. fanatical dream. Nor could the preachers point to many of the upper classes who had imbibed this new" superstition." Yet the apostle wavered not; he felt tho.t the gospel could bear strictest scrutiny and comparison, l\nd that it contained e. moral force worthy of recognition even by the most slavish worshippers of power. He gloried in the gospel- I. As OVERCOMmG HEN WITH MORE THAN HUllAN MIGHT. The desire of power is innl\te in the breast, and an exhibition of it is eagerly witnessed. The aposth1 had the intense conviction of tM power of the cross, which arose from its IDI\Stery over himself o.nd the ohan~os he had seen it effect in his conver~ everywhere, As the magicians snid of old, "This is the finger of God," and as the Samaritl\lls said of the sorcerer, "This m1m is the great power of God," so the apostle still more logicnlly discerned in the pea.co of mind, the spiritual liberty nnd gladness, the lofty llSpirations lllld ren<lwaJ f() THE EPISTLE OF PAUL ro THE ROMANS. nature which oame to Christians, the demonstration of a supeml\tural energy, • mlraoalom power wh09e l!Ol11'0e oould only be Divine. To spel\k and teaoh and live with this oonsoiousness of wielding a Divine power is to lose faint-hea.rtedneaa, and to let the ring of conviction in our tones bcget aoceptanoe in the listeners. The oure for many doubts is t-0 note historically what Christianity has achieved. Then the 't'llry' peouliarity of its introduction to the world, of its pl'inoiple of operation and of Um t.enets, will the more strongly evidence its origin from above. It is at every point anlike the workmanship of man. II. Al;, BEOURIKG AN EMINENTLY DESIRABLE RESULT-the salvation of men. We may be terrified and disp1sted at a force which threatens cruelty and oppression. But the might of the gospel of love is only beneficent in its design and effects. It aims at •ving men from the wrath to oome, at present deliverance from evil passions, e.t the development of all that is fairest and mostlovely. Its triumph means the healing of the Bin-sick soul, the entrance of light into the understanding, and holy joy into the heart. The Romans hated slavery, and proudly exulted in their freedom.
