IlL ~ OPEB.A.TJNG BY A Jm'l'HOD UNIVERSALLY AVAILABLE, viz. by faith. It is e&l!eDtial to a panacea intended to bring he]p and strength to our race, that it should touch the ~"'lle-spot of univenw disease and recognize the deepest need of man, howerer his customs, clothing, and language might di1fer. It ie equally necesse.ry that t.he remedy should assume such a form as to permit of its being received and e.pplied by all, whether learned or uneducated, wealthy or poor, old or young, civilized or barbarous. To hear of the Saviour's life and death and resurrection as the revelation of Dirine holiness seeking the reconciliation of man, to respond to the appeal by simple trost in the Redeemer,-tlrls requires no more than the use of the common faculties with "'hich all have been endowed. The news might be long in travelling from Jerusalem to Rome; pride, or gaiety, or intellectualism might stumble at the tidings; ba.t, the Spirit showing the thlngs of Christ to men, the responsibility rested with t.hemoelves if by unbelief they barred the heart against the truth. "To every one the.t believeth " does the gospel prove the spiritual "dynamite," not of destruction, but of alvation. Embrace it, own it, preach it 1-8. R. A. ,er. 20.-17ie revelation of God, in na,twre. To come into contact with the fearless writing of the Apostle Paul is like inhaling a breath of mountain air. He was not alarmed at the presence of any inquirer, though ancient as a Jew, learned :i,s_ a G:reek, or imperious as a Roman. He held UJ! the gospel as a lamp whose rays, shmm~ m all directions, search every system, refusmg to allow e1;or :-° pass for truth, vice f~r righteousness, or imperfection for completeness. He unplied that what the La~ did for the Jews, convincin~ them of sin, was effected for the Gentiles by the glones of creation, taking away all excuse for ungodly immorality, and thus shutting e.11 up equally to tLe sense of the need of such a righteousness, through faith unto salve.tion as the gospel of Christ proclaims. L A PABADOX-INVIBIBLE THD!iGB OLEA.BLY BEEN. The possibility of such a aeemmg contradiction is allo"'.ed, when w_e distinguish betwe~n t~e. outer vision_ of the body and the inner perception of the mind. Properly speakmg, 1t 1s only the mind that ever sees. The mind arranges and digests what is carried to it by the optic nerve. Like a chemist, the brain has its laboratory, into which the senses convey_ the ~oloure, aounds, impressions, facts, and figures of the world ~round us; e.nd. there m p~vn.te it a.nalyzes, synthetizes, manipulates, the pro~ucta till they seem mvested with new attributes. Tlew; they affect us fowerfully, and, though unseen by the bodily eyee, become clear to the eyes of the sou , II. THl!l PARADOX APPLIED TO THEOLOGY. 1. The work, of Mtwre =i/Mt a miglity Power. 'rhl.e world, eo wonderfully framed, exhibiting such unity in diversity, furniebes to the attentive mind abundant tracee of a Force which has been at work other than ourselves. The declarations of past investigators, such as Buddha, Plato, Oicero, are amply confirmed by scientists to-day, who confese themselves in the presence of a glorioue, awful Force, whose laws are to be ascertained and obeyed. 'l'he attempt is made to resolve demonstrably all phenomena into manifestations of the one indivisible force. Such thinkers we may claim as buttref!Sing the declaration of the text that the invisible power of God is clearly seen, being understood throu"h his works. Those regularities they call "laws" are hie habits; those numerous an~logiee indicate the one mind influencing similarly all realms. Note especially that epic of natural theology, the Book of Job. 2. This Power discermd. to be ,werlasting. There is the proper word in the text to denote "endless dmation "-that which is always existent. ~ The Power which originated the universe is needed to BUStain it. Evolution is perpetual creation, whereby "things that are seen were not made of things that do appear." Man has from of old contrasted his brief life with the everlasting mountains, the perpetual hills. Astronomy is making us familiar with the countless millenniums of God's lifetime, and geology reveals the measureless ages through which his power bas been working. The doctrine of the conservation of force, which Tyndall calls "the gift of science to the nineteenth century," echoes the same truth, that though the animals die, and even the bills crumble and decay, yet the Power 'l>hicb made them continues; they assume other shapes and do other work. Herbert Spencer writes of the "infinite and eternal energy whence all things proceed and by which they are sustained." 3. Such power r,weals Divinity. The "Divinity" of the Revised Version is preferable, since here the apostle is speaking, not of the incommunicable essence of God, as in Col. ii. 9, but of his nature as distinguished from our mortal humanity. The works of God show that he can originate life; man can only proJ>aocrate it. .And reflection proves that this power of God acts in favour of righteousness and in punishment of wickedness. He stands forth as the Holy One. We do not forget the dark problems of life nor the abysses of creation, but we must beware lest we underrate the clearness with which he has written his autograph on the laws of nature, and on his chief product-man. Froude says, " This is the one lesson of history-the moral law is written on the tablets of eternity••.. Justice and truth alone endure and live. Injustice and falsehood may be long-lived, but doomsday comes a.t last to them." Ill. THE INEVITABLE CONOLUSION, THAT, MD.-'B IBBELIGIOt;S, SD."'FtiL PRACTICES BEING INEXCUSABLE, THEY NEED JUST BUCH A GOSPEL AS ClmlsTIANITY PBOCLlil[S. Such a revelation ought to have prevented all ungodliness. A chief sin is to ignore God, as the greatest civil crime is treason a.,,crainst the ruler of the state. Not to worship and thank him is flat rebellion at court. How clearly the apostle implies that darkened views of the Creator, degrading his attributes, lead men first to b~e ingratitude, and then to indulge, unchecked and unashamed, the worst fleshly desires 1 .And these flames of ungodly passion, no longer subdued by the rains of he,wenly pity leap up into a fierce conflagration, by which the doomed are destroyed. Yet he whc formed the world and placed man upon it, has remembered man's frailty-has pro,ided an .Advocate for the defenceless criminal, 11. city of refuge for the despairing murderer. It cannot be an escape through our own merits, or justification by works; but by 11 transcendent exhibition of Divine power in its noblest garb of love, stooping to bear our sins, and to make his righteousness ours, through our contrite, humble, joyful acceptance of his mercy 11.nd help.-S. Abst.rnct ideas have little charm or power for men, and the 'IVClrship of fol'N! or humanity can never attract the multitudes. The yearning for a Yisible God = answered in the Shechinah, and in the many appearances of the angel C'f JehC'vah, and hl\8 received fullest recognition in the manifestation of God in Christ, The spirituality of Divine worship was to be preserved in Israel by the commandment not t-0 re.AI' graven images, and the ascension of Christ to heaven, withdrawing the Saviour from mortal eyes, is likewise intended to protect Christianity from the dangera liable to a system whose vot~ries should "walk by sight" rather than by faith. 'l'he Scriptures and universal hist.ory demonstrat.e the rapidity with which, as in the Roman Catholic Church to-day, men's homage and devotion are transferred from the Being represented, t.o the statue or figure which at first st.ood innocently enough as his symbol, There is a danger of modern literature seeking too much " to know Christ after the flesh," instead of relying upon the assistance furnished by the teaching of the Spirit, the invisible Christ dwelling in the heart. IT. THE TO"DEXCY OF mAGE-WORSHIP IS TO DEGRADE RELIGION, The argument of Xenophanes, ridiculing the Homeric theology that if sheep and oxen were to picture a god, the_r would im8<,"llle him like one of themselves, only showed that natural religion, in framing a notion of Deity, rightly attributes to him the highest attributes of personality and intelligence conceivable. And the Apostle Paul accused the Athenians of unreasonableness in fancying that the great Father could be supposed to be less powerful and intelligent than his children. But without supernatural aid man sinks lower and lower in his conceptions ; the direction of evolution in religion is J,;rwnv.ard, not upward, except where there is a manifest interposition of the Supreme I>eing. Note how strenuously the prophets bad to combat the desire of Israel to ally themselves in worship with the abominable idolatries of the nations around. Man, selected as God's representative, becomes man in his lowest moods and merely animal existence; the transition is easy to the wise-looking owl and soaring eagle, then to the cow and the dog, and fin.ally t.o the serpent and the fish. The unity of God is lost in the multiplicity of idols, and his power and righteousness swamped in bestial stupidity and depmvity. Religions rites became scenes of licentiousness. " The light that was in men has turned t.o darkness, and how great is that darkness I " ill TBl!: WOJISHIPPEB GRADUALLY ASSnnLATES BDIBELF TO THE OBJECT WOR- SHIPPED. Man does not rise higher in thought and life than the Deity before whom he bows and to whom he submits himself; but he may, and too generally does, adopt the worst features of the character and conduct of his gods. What we constantly meditate upon transforms us into its own lineaments. Where the lower animals are deified, there the passions of the brutes are rampant, and a merely animal existence is lived. The lie substituted for the truth shunts man's behaviour on to another line, and a descending plane lands him in moral ruin. " They that make the gods are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them." The revelation God gives of himself in his Word operates reversely on a similar principle, so that "we beholding as in a glass the true glory of the Lord, ~re changed into the sa!°e image;" and, the ima~e of God in man being restored, the likeness to God to which we are made to attain grows unto perfection, till" we shall be like him, when we shall see him as he is."- 8. R. A. Ver. L-~ author. Before appreciating any important work, we like to learn all we can of ite author. Hence the study of the Acts of the Apostles ie the beet possible p!"eparation for the study of this great Epistle to the Romans. The history given by Luke is like the portrait of _the apostle ~refixed to his Epistles; it is bett_er inde~d a. tbowiand times than any picture producible by art. Let us, ae a suggestive subject, begin with a 11ketch of the apostle's career, fitted as it is to help us in subsequent homilies. And- L PAtJL'II JllBTORY BEFORE BIS OO:NVEBBIOl'I. Gentiles," he WBB reo.dy to sink the Jewiah title and adopt what was nearest to it in the langue.go which we.a more largely used. As he said to the Pbilippians, he was" an Hebrew of the Hebrews" (iii. 5). Everything, therefore, which pure" breeding" implies would be his. The tribe of Benjamin had supplied the first king to Israel, and now it is supplying a more famous " king of men" in the person of this second Saul. His parents doubtless made him a" child of the Law" at the age of twelve, and later on provided for his education in the Jewish capital. 3. His training at the feet of Gamaliel. This meant the broadest culture of the capital, orthodoxy of the most prudential cast, as his master's conduct in the Sanhedrin seems to show (Acts v. 38). That Paul was an apt scholar his own testimony proves, not to speak of the testimony of his great career; for be speaks of " profiting in the Jews' religion above many my equals in mine own nation" (Gal. i., 14). 4. Bis enthusiasm as a man of action. It would appear that, setting aside the prudence of Gamaliel, he entered with all the ardour of youth into a crusade against the Christians. The Jewish authorities had perceived the vast capabilities of their instrument; and, from the subsidiary post of holding the clothes of those who stoned Stephen. be rose per saltum into the position of arch-persecutor, and the leader of the enterprise even unto strange cities. Not only was he, then, an orthodox, self-satisfied Pharisee, but also he became the chief man of action in connection with his party, the man of most abundant promise. II. P AUL's CONVERSION. Damascus was the goal to which he and his accomplices hastened, when lo! be is confronted, not far from the city, with an overpowering light, and hee.rs a voice demanding, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me ? " On asking the name of this brilliant and overpowering Person, he learns that it is Jesus, the risen and glorified Head of the people Saul is persecuting, who has thus appeared' to confoUDd and to convert him. Now, regarding this conversion let us notice: 1. The Lord's personal dealing with the sinner. The sinner feels himself in the hands of One whom !J,e has wronged in his own Person and in the person of his people. Conviction of sin is just a sense of injury done to an innocent and loving Saviour. Paul imagined that Jesus had passed out of the category of living factors in this world, and now he is confronted by him with the charge of persecution. 2. Paul dies immediately out of all self-confidence. As Adolphe Monod has beautifully said, "Saul is converted from the day, from the hour, from the moment that, recognizing that he is in himself wicked, unworthy, lost, and for ever deprived of all righteousness before God, he substitutes the Name of Jesus Christ for his own in all his hopes of eternal life, and throws himself without reserve at the foot of the cross, as a poor sinner who has no other resource in the world but the blood of the I,e.mb of God." 3 This is what we mean by his death out of self-confidence. He recognizes at once the hollowness of all his previous hopes, and puts Christ into the place once occupied by self. 3. Paul places Mmst:lf under the command of Jesus. He cries out," Lord, whe.t wilt thou have me to do?" Henceforth he is Christ's slave (lloiJ.\os), owned and ordered according to Christ's pleasure. This perfect surrender of self to the will of the Saviour is the practical outcome of conversion. It is a parallel to the surrender of Abraham, when he be= to be a pilgrim with God. Paul ha.s renounced the service of the chief priests and accepted service under the NI\Za.rcno they despised. And: 4. Paul receives from Jmis a new <)(fief!, When he goes blind into Damascus nnd waits, he is nt length told what he is to do. He is to be admitted by baptism into the Christian Church, and be filled with the Holy Ghost, and be apostle unto the Gentil111 (Acts ix. 16-18). His office is chll.D.ged from th,\t of Saul the persecutor to thnt of Pnul the apostle.' And whnt is it to be Wl a1-xistls? 1 or. It is to found the Church of God upon no other baele than that or the rlaen Jeeue. It is to be a witness of Christ's resurrection, and of all which this oardlnal fact and doctrine is to men. A mighty office, surely I And notice how singular and dlstlnot Paul ~tands. The Jews receive twelve apostles, but the Gentiles only one; yet Paul is wort.h all the others put t-0gether so far as the world's conversion is concerned. Like Darid, he WM worth ten thousand oommon soldiers. Ill. PAUL's 8UBSEQUE1'"T OAREBR. He began preaching Christ at once, just to try bis hand; but it was not intended he should pass at once from the publicity of persecution to the publicity of the apostolic office. He passes into the quiet of Arabia. and is for about seven years in an unobtrusive sphere of probation. It is not meant that he spent seven years in silence; doubt.less, wherever he was, he made his neighbours feel his presence and know his doctrine. But he was prepa1·ing, by earnest meditation and communion with his Master, for his tremendous mission. To all in haste to enter the ministerial office, Paul's patient preparation is surely a significant lesson I But next we find him spending fourteen years in missionary labours. Into the details of hie journeys we cannot here ent.er; but they were wise seizing of great centres, that from these the light of the gospel might go abroad. And lastly, Paul spent from five to seven years-we cannot be quite certain-in captivity at Cesarea and Rome, enjoying, perhaps, a short respite between the two Roman captivities, but ending his career by martyrdom. It is believed he was liom about the year 7 of our era; was converted when thirty years of age; and died when about si.xty.1 Now, it was as "apostle of the Gentiles " that he wrote this Epistle to the R-Omans. He wrote it, as is apparent from its contents, before be had visited the Church. He wrote it from Corinth, to lay before the Church occupying the metropolis of the world "the gospel of God." He was not ashamed of that gospel, notwithstanding the philosophy and culture of Greece or Rome. He knew the world's philosophy, and he felt that he had found in the gospel something finer far. Bnt we must not anticipate. Meanwhile let Paul's conversion and apostleship speak to tli! of personal dealing with the Lord Jesus, and of personal labour for him. It has been said that the apostolic race is like a lost species. Yet have we not bad, even in our own time, men of zeal who might even be named along with the apostles? David Livingstone, William Chalmers Burns, George Au,,austns Selwyn, John Patteson, and many others have exhibited the long-lost apostolic spirit. We want it to come again; and why should it not, in ourselves? Not that we would coun.sel one another to ambition, but, as Monod so well puts it, to fidelity.s Let tli! humble ourselves, as Paul did on the way to Damascus, through a sense of sin and shortcoming; let us accept of pardon through the Lamb's precious blood; and let our cry be, " Lord, what wilt thou have me to do ? " and the Saviour will give each of us a mission, as he gave Paul, and own us as true servants in the accomplishment of his gracions designs.-R. M. E.

This throws clear light upon the composition of the Church when Paal wrote his Epistle. The Jewish element was in a. minority, while the Gentile element abounded. Now, we can easily understand how populations gravitated from the provinces to Rome, and so converts would be going up from time to time from the Gentile Churches to the metropolis, and so swelling the Gentile element in the metropolitan Church. This seems indicated by salutations in eh. xvi. addressed to some fellowworkers with Paul, who do not seem to have come from Rome, like Aquila and Priscilla, but to have emigrated to it. A. third fact must be noted. III. 'l'HE JEWS WERE EXM!:LLED FROM RoME BY THE EHPEBOR CLAUDTI;S. Now, while this may not have affected in any great degree the numerical proportion in the little Christian Church, we know that it led to some Jewish Christians, e.g. Aquila and Priscilla (Acts xvili. 2), leaving the metropolis for other places. Upon this providence Paul's knowledge of the Church at Rome very largely depended. As he WTought with .Aquila. and Priscilla. at tent-making, they would have many a long talk about the Church they had been con1.,.ected with in Rome, and to which they subsequently returned. IV. THE JEWS, WHEN PAUL AT LENGTH CAME TO RoME, SEEM TO HAVE RAD LITTLE KNOWLEDGE 011' THE CHBISTIANB. This is evident from .Acts x.xviii 22. If we remember the population of ancient Rome, also that the Christian congregation had not, as far as we know, any church edifice giving notoriety ~ them, but were meeting apparently in the house of .Aquila (eh. xvi. 5), then we can understand the ignorance of Christianity the Jews possessed or pretended at Paul's advent. The little Christian. conventicle would be easily hid in the great city. The Church at Rome, then, from the foregoing facts, seems to have been a. congregation of believing Christians, cccupyi.ng no very commanding position in the eye of the public, isolated in a large measure from other Churches, yet very influential through its existence in the metropolis. Its major portion was Gentile; and on this account it received the special attention of Paul as "the apostle of the Gentiles." Some, who went up from provincial Churches to the capital, seem to have carried Paul's teaching with them, so that he had a. kind of spiritual fatherhood towards at least some of them, and a. brotherhood towards all How in the Epistle he fortifies them against the errors by which they should be beset, will appear a.s we proceed. It was a la.dy, Phcebe, who ca.rried up the precious document, She seems to have gone up on some business matters, and for her in these circumstances Paul seeks a.ssistance a.nd sympathy (eh. xvi. 1, 2). V. LET UB NOW NOTE THE SU11STANCE OF HIS OPENING ADDRESS TO TfilS CO'.S"GREOA- TION AT Ro:r.rn. (Vers. 2-7.) And here we notice: 1. His gospel is that of the risen SaviO'UT. This is God's "glad tidings" that his Son, who had been made of David's sced according to the flesh, and delivered in human nature unto death for us, had been declared to be his Son by the powerful, resistless demonstration of his resurrection from the dead. Paul and these Roma.n Christia.ns were, therefore, in the ha.nds of a living, holy Being, no less I\ Person than the Son of God, whom death and resurrection had denationalized nnd mnde Lord of all nations, who could a.nd would dispose of them, Gentiles as well as Jews, as he pleased. 2. Paul declares that he hnd received from this risen Jesus grace and apostleship. We saw in our previous homily how he wns first converted, and then wns called to the npostolio office. Now, this apostkship contemplated the subjection of all nations to the faith of Christ. It was a mi~hty trust which w&s thus committed to Paul. This Epistle shows how anxiously he tried to discharge it. 3. These Romnn Christinns are also the called of Jt1,-us Christ. J:.'or though there may not be such oclat connected with individua.l oonversion, as iu Paul's ,ase on the way to Da.m!lstus, there is yet as real o.n interview between the risen 46 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. Savfour and the sinner he would save. The words may not be audible 1\8 those addro..«sl'd t-0 Paul, but they are heard within and responded to. Like Abraham and like &ul of Tanru.s, we must listen to the call to come out and follow Jesus, if we ate t<' e>e Christians indeed. 4.. Thei'.r privilege is t°M enjoyment of God's love, their dtd¥, the proctitt ef holtfl&S. "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints.' This is what we mean by Church-membership; it is, when real, an experience of Divine love, and a practice of holiness. And, indeed, we have here the whole plan of salvation, God's love comes forth first to us, and then we walk in holineRs as hie gmteful people, It has been said somewhere by M. La Harpe that the doctrines of Christianity may be summed up in the words, "God has loved us," and its morals in the words, '' Let us love God." 1 Of course, God loves all men with the love of pity, and in consequence he sent his Son int-0 the world to save us (John iii. 16); but when we respond to his love, he proceeds to la"Vish on us a particular love-a love of complacency and of delight (John xi:v. 21). These Christians at Rome were, therefore, the objects of this special lo'"l; and thev manifested the benefit in holy lives. 5. Paul pronounces upon them 11 benedidicn. Now, when we analyze it, we find that "grace" is the favour of God, undeserved, and coming down in the shape of pardon. " Peace" is the precious effect produced in the heart which receives the grace. The Source from whom this benediction oomes down is "God our Father," nnd the Medium of communication is" Jesus Christ." In pronouncing this benediction, the apostle desires that they should have the supply of the grace a.s they daily need it. The idea. entertained by some, that we receive in con"Version all the pardon we shall ever need, is refuted by this benediction pronounced ewer the Roman "saints." The following practical lessons SiJXely suggest themselves : (1) .A risen and lifliflg Saviour has entered upon the government of the world. Paul's conversion a.nd apostleship, the conversion of these Roman Christians, the conversion @f men and women still, all go to prove this. We have not in Christianity a dead man's legacy, like Buddhism or Confucianism, or Islamism, but a living Saviour's wondrous work. (2) Its magnificent ambition is to bring all nations to the obedience of faith. ·It aims at world-wide empire; nothing less will content it. (3) Our sympathy should enlarge iu.elf aumdingly. The work for him will best advance when we have waited on him for his grace and peace.-R. :M. E. Vere. S-17.-The policy to be pursued in case Paul came to Rome. The good news is this, that God, though justly offended with us because of our sins, is yet prepared for Christ's sake to recei,e us into his favour and fellowship, as if the estrangement had never been. It comes about according to natural law, but it is not on that account any the less the sentence of the Lord who ordereth all. Sinners go from bad to worse. entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Judgment, human and Divina. This sudden and impassioned appeiu was made, in reality though not expressly, to the Jew. St. Paul imagined himself in the presence of a Hebrew fellow-countryme.n, whom he supposed to be listening to his burning denunciation of the vices nnd crimes of heathen society. Now, the distinctive characteristic of Christianity as e. moral system wa.s its insistence upon righteousness, purity, e.nd charity of heart, and not merely of conduct; and no one more thoroughly entered into this characteristic thau did the apostle himself. With quick perception, St. Pnul discerned, in the mind of the Jewish hearer or reader l'f his :first che.pter, indignation and disgust springing up e.t the picture of moral corruption which fairly represented the state of Gentile society. But the apostle wished to prove e.ll men under condemnation--Jew and Gentile alike; and upon the Christian principle that morality is of the heart, he was able to do this, 1U1d was justified in doing it. Hence the language of indignation with which ho turns upon the Pharisee, who recoils from Gentile iniquity, who pronounces upon those guilty of it the sentence of cc1 ndemnation. "Thou art inexcu~nblo; thou that judge~t doest the s,imt1 thing-, l" 'l.'ho appeal is instructive, as to judgment passed upon man's Cc)nduct by his l~llow-lllcn and by his God. I. 'l'mi: JUDOMENT OF MAN BY MAN, I. It is always fallible. For who has THE EPlSTLE OF PA.UL TO THE ROMANS. [on. 11. 1-29.

knowledge sufficient t-0 enable him to sit in judgment upon hie fellow-sinners ? 2. Ae a matter of fact, it is often unjust. For who is so parfoctly u}:lrigbt and. lm}:lartlnl u to ~ entrusted, not with judicinl authority over mou ns agents, but with mornl autbonty onr them as accountable beings? 3. He who judges his Mlow-man is liable to bRve his attention withdrawn from bis own sins, errors, aud ill deserts, He is troubled by the mote in bis brother's eye, and forgets the beam which is in bis own eye. 4. In t.he case of fallible and sinful men, the condemnation of others is alwe.ys condemnation of self. "'l'bou art the man I" is the response wbioh is suggested The form of wrong-ooing denounced. may not be the identical form by whioh the denouncer is chiefly t.empted; but the principle of sin is one, though the forms assun1od be many. . I~ ~ Jc:™?YE~"T ~F MAN BY ~OD. 1. 'l'his is always and exactly jmt; for Justice is a D1nne at-tnbute ; and it would be absurd to attribute to the infinitely perf~t Being, the Governor of the universe, either imperfection of knowledge or partiality and respect of persons. 2. It is not to b6 impugned. "The judgment of God is according to truth;" it needs no court of revision, no court of appeal ; its decisions are final and unquestionable. 3. It is inevitable. Foolish and ignorant must be the man into whose mind the thought can enter that the Divine judgment can be escaped. APPLICATION. Let a man judge, not his fellow-men, but himself, lest he incur the right.eous judgment of God.

entries.title: ROM 2:4
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
S.-Long-sujjeri11g. It is certain that we live under a moral government ad.ministeed by a holy and righteons Ruler, of infinite knowledii:e and irresistible power. Yet there are sinful men who, while admitting this to be the case, live as if they believed that government and retribution had no reference to themselves. The apostle, in this passage, appeals to such persons, expostulates with them, and shows them the gnilt and folly of disregarding the Di vine Law and authority, and of presuming too fac upon the Divine forbearance. L THE FACT OF GoD's LONG-SUFFERING. This may be traced: 1. In human history, which abounds with examples of Divine patience with the sins of nations. 2. In the Christian dispensation, which is certainly the crowning proof of the longsuffering of the Eternal. 3. In individual experience; for no man who will be candid with himself will question that such forbearance has been exercised towards him. II. THE Al!USE OF GoD"s LONG-SUFFERING. There are many who, instead of gratefully acknow~oing Divine forbearance, and using aright the opportunity of repentance and reformation which they owe to it, despise the riches of God's long-suffering and mercy. L The facts upon which this abuse is founded are these: God in his nature is kind and gracious, delighting in the exercise of clemency and compassion. God in his retributive action is slow and patient, often withholding the condemnation e.nd penalty threatened and deserved. 2. The false inferences drawn from these facts me.y be thus stated: Either, God will not fulfil the threats which be has made, will not enforce by the awful sanctions of hie justice the laws which he has promulgated ; or, we are for some reason exempt from the operations of God's judicial authority. 'fhis last eee:ns to have been the belief of many of the Jews, who, because theirs was the chosen and favonred nation, believed themselves secure from the penalties which would befall the w:.believing and impenitent sinners of the Gentiles. IIL 'IHE EnUUSTlON OF Goo's LONG-BUFFERING. 1. It must not be forgotten ' that what the apostle calls "wrath," and righteous retribution, are facts in the government of tbe Eternal. They do not cease to be facts, because God is forbearing and kind. He can have no compromise with sin. He cannot overlook the distinction between the rebel and the loyal subject. He cannot admit to hie favour e.nd fellowship those who detest hie laws and defy hie authority. 2. And it ls equally important to remember that the government of God is universal and impartial. It extends to all mankind.. There is not one code for the Jew and another for the Gen tile ; one for tb.t privileged and another ~or the unprivileged.. "Because sentence a~alnst an ev:n work ie not e1ecnt.ed speeclily, therefore the heart of the sons of men 1s fully set Ill them to do evil" But m thiH case it is vain for them to hope that they shall eecapo Gcid'M jllllt cewAll'e awl condem.ua.tion. All alike a.re guilty ; and all alike, If ae.ved 1 on. n. 1-20.] THE EPIB~.'LE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 69

must be saved upon the same terms-terms honoumblo to God, and beneficial to human nature nnd human society. IV. Tum PURPOSE AND USE Oll' Gon's LONG-BUFFERING. After all that has been said, it must yet be insisted upon that the attribute of Deity here referred to by the o.po~tle is o. glorious and blessed o.ttribute, and that we cannot be sufficiently grateful to God for its exercise towo.rds us, who stand so sorely in need of it. How ehall we so use it that it may be for our truest and eternal advantage? 1. Believe it, as o. truth harmonizing with Divine righteousness. 2. Submit to it, as an influence inducing to repentance. 8. Act upon it, as affording opportunity for practical reformation,

entries.title: ROM 2:11
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Divine impartiality. The apostle's immediate intention in thus stating the perfect equity of the Divine government, and the utter absence of partiality from his nature and from his administration, we.e to remove from the mind of any Jewish hearer or reader the belief that his descent from Abraham could be of any avail in God's sight if moral and spiritual qualifications were lacking. But, as is so ofren the case, especially in St. Paul's writings, local and temporary references gave occasion for the utterance of broad, general, and eternal principles. The simplicity and grandeur of this assertion must appeal to the moral nature of every reader of the Epistle. I. DIVINE IMPARTIALITY CONTRASTS WITH HUJUN PARTIALITY. However it mav be with God and his government, certain it is that, both in private and in public !if~, men's treatment of their fellow-men has usually been marked by personal farnuriti;im. No one can read those passages in the Old Testament referring to "gifts," i.e. bribes, and to "regarding the face" or the person of suitors, without perceiving how general was judicial corruption in the Oriental world. And there are allnsions in the New Testament which prove to us that even the great Roman officials were not free from this taint. The prevalence of the practice of bribery, corruption, and favouritism must have suggested to the minds of ordinary men the possibility that the Judge of all regarded men's persons. II. DrvnlE IMPARTIALITY JS SUPPORTED BY CONVINCING EVIDENCE. 1. There is the testimony of the unsophisticated conscience of man. Crime, no doubt, exists and flourishes in society ; and men's interests induce them to connive at its presence. But, explain it how we may, the fact is undeniable that the inner voice of reason :i.nd conscience bears witness to the justice and impartiality of God. Idolatry is indeed e.ssocie.ted with beliefs and expedients based upon the unfairness and corruptibility 6f the deities held in honour or in dread. But let the idea of one supreme God take possession of men's souls, and the moral nature with which they are endowed refuses to be satisfied except by a conviction that this Being is far above what :i.re felt to be human infirmities and faults. If there be a God, that God is just. 2. Revelation supports this conviction. There are passages of Scripture which may seem to conflict with it, but these he.ve been misunderstood e.nd misinterpreted, or they would have been seen to be in consistency with what is the general tenor e.nd the express teaching of the Word of God. How many a.re the passages in which the offerings of the insincere are indignantly rejected, in which we are taught that external circumstances nnd hypocritical pretences o.re valueless in the sight of him who "searcheth the heo.rt, and trieth the reins of the children of men" I 3. The ministry of Christ is especially emphatic upon this point. It is sufficient to refer to our Lord's rebuke of those who boasted that they were Abmhe.m's seed; he bade them reflect upon God's ability to raise up even from the very stones of the fields children unto Abraham. And be constro.ined the o.cknowledgment from his enemies that" he regarded not the person of man." Ill. DIVINE IMPARTlALITl!' IS EXHIBITED IN CERTAIN STRIKING PABTICl'LARS. 1. In judgment God is just to all. There is one law by which all are judged. In ths application of that standard a righteous regard is had to the opportunities of knowledgo and enlightenment afforded by circumstances; but no other consideration is allowed to onter. 2. 'rhe nlvation which is by Obrist Jesus is providcll for all alike. God is the " Saviour of o.ll men, specially of them that believe." Christ died, not for :,ny clnse, but for the ungodly, i.11. for nil mankind, who alike needed redemption and &\\vat.ion. And the heroJ.da of the crose prenched the Saviour to Jew auJ. Geutile aliku. Here is a rebuke addressed tu the proud the solfrigbtN,us, the self-confideut, to all who deem themselves the fuvourites of He~ven, and who indulge t.he persuasion that they are in possession of some speoial recommendation to the c,,nsiderati.on of the Lord aud Judge of all. 2. entries.title: ROM 2:13
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content: -Hearers a.nd doers. It is impossible to overlook the resemble.nee whioh this passage be&rs to words of the great Teacher uttered towa.rds the olose of the sermon on the mount. In this, aa in so many places, the apostle is evidently indebted for his thoughts, and almost his very words, to the Divine Fountain of all the streams of spiritual wisdom and life. L A PRINCIPLE OF C01'"DEMNATION. 1. It is possible to hear the Law, and yet not to obey it. 2. In the case of the disobedient, the continued hearing of the Law may be the occasion of continued and even increased insensibility, indifference, a.nd hostility. 3. Thus the very hearing and the familiarity resulting from it ma.y become the ground of condemnation, bee.a.use an aggravation of the offence. Thus the abuse of what is best leads t.o the worst results. The Law is holy, just, and good; but it is the severest condemnation of the rebellious and impa.tient. TI. A PRIXCIPLE OF LIFE. 1. In the case of those who perfectly fulfil the righteous Law of God, the consequence of their perfect obedience is justification by works. It is needless to say that no member of the human race has ever fulfilled this condition. There is none whom the Law thus justifies. One only among the sons of men has fulfilled all right.eousnes.s--even the Son of God himself, who came to fulfil the Law, not only by his teaching, but in his life. 2. Yet the very violation of the perfect Law of God is the means of calling men's attention to the need and the provision of sa.lvation by grace through faith in the Lord JCSUJ!. 3. And in the case of those who are saved by grace, the Law of God becomes the standard of conduct, to- attain which is the aim ol all who are led by the Spirit of God. The whole moral life of the true Christian is an endeavour to fulfil that Law which was formerly the principle of condemnation, but has now become a principle of life.

entries.title: ROM 2:17–27
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Tu quoque! Although himself a Jew, St, Paul shows no favow to his fellow-countrymen. No sooner has he characterized and condemned the sins of the heathen, than he turns upon the Israelites to include them in the same condemnation of sin and unbelief. In this passage, where close rea.soning is combined with vigorous irony, he presses home upon those Jews who censure the fiagitious crimes of heatheniBm the sentence which justice compels them to admit u their due. L PluvILEGE IS ADHITTED. 1. Hereditary advantages are undeniable. The Jew ent.ered at birth into a heritage of favourable circumstances, belonging, as he did, to the nation distinguished by privileges at that age of the world unpara.lleled. 2. Acquired familiarity with the Law of God was a natural result of national privileges. From childhood, the Jew was trained to reverence God's Name, to recite God's Law, to listen to the teaching of God's prophets. 3. There resulted a position of influence a.nd re.ponsibility in the discharge of the obvious duty of communicating and inculcating the Divine will The Jew was the "guide of the blind," the "instructor of the foolish," the "teacher of babes." He was the witness to the truth and to the commandments of the Eternal. Reflection may show us that we occupy, under the Christian diBpew;atio11, a similar position of privilege and responsibility. IL Ui.-YAITHYt;L1'"ESS IS DU'UTED. 1. The crimes condemned are committed by thoee who condemn them. The list is indeed appalling. Upon the religious Jew e.ro charged offences which it can hardly be supposed were all committed by one parson, in one human life. Yet there is no limit to the poBHibility of ma.n'H hypocrisy. 'l'hoft, adultery sacrilege, blllliphemy,-such are the awful crimes and sinH which are charged upon th; Jews, whc, professed so loudly their n1oral superiority to their Gentile neighbours. 2. The ungodly Jew not oDly commits tho crimes he condemns; he hinder, OR, u.1-29.J THE EPIKTJ,E OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 61

the cBuse it ie hie profeeeed busineee to further and to advocate. To him is committed, ne it were, the custody of monotheism; he ie called upon to witness to the Divine nnture Bnd charncter, as contrasting with the conceptions of their deities cherished by tbo heathen. And lo I he becomes, by his immorality, the occasion of God being dishonoured, of God'e Name being blasphemed among the Gentiles. The parallelism may be traced between the unfaithful Jew and the unfaithful Christian. III. CONDEMNATION IB PRONOUNOED. 1. Privilege avails not. It is in human nature to rely upon the enjoyment of great advantages. -But the truth is, that the possession of privileges heightens responsibility. No man can be saved because he pleads that the light shone brightly round about him; the question must be-Did be walk in the light while he ha.d the light? Circumcision did not save the Jew; similarly, mere outward participation in the sacraments of Baptism and Lord's Supper will not save the professing Christian. The possession of privileges is no proof of their due and proper use. 2. The less favoured may, in character and life, excel the more favoured. 'l'he uncircumcised may keep the Law which the circumcised allows himself to break. This fact was seen and stated by the Lord himself, who continually warned his fellow-countrymen that many should come from the ea.st and the west, and should sit down in the kingdom of God, whilst they should be thrust out. 3. The highly privileged who are unfaithful to their trust shall, it is foretold, be judged by those whose advantages have been fewer, but who have ma.de a good use of such as they enjoyed. It must have astonished the Jew of repute and standing to be told that be should be judged by those of the uncircumcision. Yet this was quite in harmony with the warning of the Divine Saviour that the men of 'l'yre and Sidon should rise up in the judgment against the unfaithful of his generation.

entries.title: ROM 2:28
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The religi011, of the.flesh exchanged/or the rel.igion of the spirit. It is difficult for us to understand all that was meant by this assertion. The apostle wa.s a Hebrew of the Hebrews, and we know, from the general tenor of his writings, how highly he valued the religion in which he had been trained, and how warmly he was attached to the race from which he sprang. That those who remained Jews in faith, who gloried in having Abraham as their father, and who prized as their own peculiar possession the covenant and the oracles of God,-that they would experience a shock of surprise and resentment upon reading such language a.s this, is evident. And even those who had accepted Jesus as the Messiah for the most part retained much of their hereditary confidence in the special privileges of their nationality ar..d their religion. Such teaching as this undoubtedly introduced a revolution into the heart uf reii::;iuus society-a revolution in thought, and a revolution in practice. I. A l'ROTEST. There is often no possibility of avoiding conflict and opposition in expounding and maintaining the trnth. Paul was certainly not the man to shrink from controversy; his was the nature of the warrior, and when he found himself face to fa.ea with error and sin, his nature was roused to its depths, his native combativ&- ness found a oongenial field of battle. And although Christianity was indeed the development and the fulfilment of Judaism, it could not but come into conflict mth much which human nature had connected with Judaism by bonds not easily to be broken. Spiritual as were the intuitions of the inspired psalmists and prophets in whose writings the Hebrew people gloried, it is clear that, at the time of our Lord's ministry, religious formalism was prevalent among the Jewish leaders ::m,l the Jewish people. Scribes and Pharisees we!'e too often hypocrites. Religion was too much an affair of rituBl and oeremonial observnuce. Even those who drew near unto God with their lips were deserving of censure, because their hearts were far from him. Now, the four Gospels make it pll\in to us that the ministry of Christ was a miuistry of protesi against a religiou of form. He would not have directed so much of his teaching against the religion of the letter, had he not seen and felt the necessity of such an attitude of opposition, such action of controversy. And, indeed, he was perfectly awan~for he know what was in man-that the evil wos one not simply of Jewish b:\bit, but of human nature. Where is the religion, however spiritual iu tho apprehensic,n c1f its truo expositor, which has not dcgenemtcd into formalism? Mau's nnture is bcxlily as well as spiritual; his religion must express itself, or it will die; words and outwaro 1'orehip, organization and official action, &ll seet11, if not essential, yet contributive to 62 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TIIE ROMANS. [oH. n.1-29,

religi(lus life and efficiency. And it is most n11tural that, iri the minds of the unthinking and the worldly, the symbol should t.ake the place of the truth It symbolizes, the letter should overgrow the spirit, and officfalism should substitute ministry. Certainly this is what happened in the case of Judaism. And against this the apostle of the Gentiles, in his Epistle to the Romans, raised the most vigorous protest which has pro• ceedoo from any disciple of Jesus. 'l'he seed of this protost was, indeed, sown in the teaching of the Master; but here we find that the seed was bearing fruit. The position which St. Paul occupied, the special work to which he was rnlled, threw tbe burden of the protest and the controversy upon him. His ministry was hindered by the religi0us proantry and. bigotry of those who had been trained in the same school with himself. His large hea1t resented with indignation the formality, the narrowness, the pettiness, which he encountered wherever he met his fellow-countrymen in their synagogues. His commission was one which admitted of no terms, of no truce, with a religion of "the flesh,"" the letter." If, a.s a worker, he was called upon to be the minister of Christ to the Gentiles, as a thinker it was his great vocation to exhibit the spiritual character of Christianity; and the identity of a. spiritual with a. uni versa~ religion must be obvious to every reflecting mind. The apostle's detestation of a. merely external religion is evident all through this Epistle, equally in the doctrinal and the practical sections. To no compromise upon this point would he for a moment consent. For a Jew who was a. Jew only outwardly, he had no consideration, and circumcision merely in the flesh he held in no esteem. Even in our own time there is need of a protest against a religion of forms and of custom; there is no Church which is free from the danger here intimated; for the temptation against which the inspired apostle puts us upon our guard is a. temptation which gathers strength from a. principle and habit deep-seated in human nature itself. IL A nocrnn..:. O,er against the protest contained in the twenty-eighth verse is the pJsitive assertion of the twenty-ninth. A man might be a. descendant of Israel, and yet might not be a Jew, in the deeper and spiritual significance which the apostle attached to the designation. There were many who boasted that they were" Abraham's seed." who had "Abraham to their father," according to natural descent, who yet lacked Abraham's faith, the true "note" of incorporation in the elect race. entries.title: ROM 2:1–4
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The goodness of God. The great object of St. Paul, in these opening chapters of Romans, is to show the world's need of a Saviour. In the first chapter he has shown the inexcusableness of the heathen, and their fallen and lost condition. But he remembers that he is writing to Jews and Jewish Christians at Rome as well as to Gentiles. He knows well the human heart. He can imagine some of hia Jewish readers saying to himself, "Yes, indeed; those heathen are certainly without excuse." But St. Paul does not allow him to cherish this complacent spirit of self-righteousness very long. He seeks to bring home the truth to himself. "Therefore thou art inexcusable, 0 me.n, whosoever thou art that judgest: tor wherein thou condemnest another, thou judgest also thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things" (ver. 1). As if he said, "It is quite true that the heathen are inexcusable. So are you. It is quite true that they have not lived up to the light they got. But have you lived up to the light you have got? Have you not come short of the Law of Moses just as much as they came short of the law of nature?" Thus the Divine Word ever seeks to turn us in upon ourselves. Thus it puts its searching questions, and lays down its searching tests. The Gentile is guilty; so is the Jew. The Jew needs repentance as well as the Gentile. It is this, as we have seen above, that makes the gospel a message for every man. It comes to our fallen humanity everywhere, and, with its message of the goodness and mercy of God, seeks to win us from the paths of sin and death to the way that leadeth to everlasting life. Hence St. Paul emphasizes here the goodness of God. I. THE GOODNESS OF Go», AND BOW IT IS SHOWN, The goodness of God is no new idea. It is as old as the rainbow, as old as the seasons, as old as the sunshine. So strong and deep is the conviction of the human heart about the goodness of the Supreme Being, that when our Anglo-Saxon forefathers were framing words to ~press their ideas, the word they chose to describe the Almighty was this very wurd "God," which simply means "The Good," "The Good One. n So even in that early 0.,,"'0 he was regarded as the personification of goodness. Let us consider how God's goodness is shown to us. Think of what temporal blessings he bestows upon us. Think of his good- ness to our souls. He has not left us, here on earth, to wander in the dark places of sin and sorrow, of uncertainty and despair. He has not le~ us, alone and helpless, to meet the king of terrors, and to step out from the darkness of R hopeless life into the darkness of an unavoidable eternity. If, on the one hand, he has given us the light of conscience and the moral law to show us our guilt, on the other hand he hM given us the light of the gospel, the light of the cross of Jesus, to reveal to us our hope of safety and pence, And, then, how much he has done for each of us personally! How very mercifully God has dealt with us I We are nsharued of m,my things in our own lives. 'l'he memory of them haunts us like an unbidden guest, like a ghost out of the guilty po.at. Yot God did not cast us away from his presonce, nor take his Holy Spirit from us. "Ho he.th not denlt with us nfter our sins, nor rewarded us according to our iniquities." Surely he must have an inexhaustible store of patience, of compassion, of mercy. Ah, yes I Paul was right when he spoke of "the riches of his 9oocl11eas atui forboaranoe and long-suffering," THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE HOMANS. [o~, n. 1-29,

• I know that blossings undesorved H11ve mnrkt,d my erring traok; ThRt. wheresO<''or 1i1y feet h1wo swerved, His chutening turned me baok. " That more e.nd more e. providence Of love is undersl;ood, Me.king the springs of time and sonae Sweet with eterne.l good. •The.t dee.th seems but a oovered way Whioh opens into light, Wherein no blinded ohild ae.n stray Beyond the Father's sight. " Tbe.t care e.nd trial seem at last, Through memory's sunset e.iJ: Like mountain-ranges overpast, In pnrple distance fair. "The.t all the jarring notes of life Seem blending in a psalm, .A.n,i all the angles of its strife Slow rounding into calm." Yas, • the good hand of God," as the old Hebrews loved to call it, is shown In every circumstance and event of life. "Oh taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." IL THE GOOD1'"ESS OF Goo, AND now IT IS RECEIVED. "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and long-suffering? " (ver. 4), There are few professing Christians who would admit that the goodness of .God is thus received by them. They would not like it to be said that they despise God's goodness, Yet must we not all admit that we do not think as much of God's goodness as we might? We take much of it as a matter of course. We forget that we have no claim on these bounties of God's providence and gifts of his grace, but rather the contrary. How little we praise him compared with what we might! How poor a. return we make for his goodness by any effort or service of our lives! How poor a.re the offerings we make of our wealth and substance for God's cause! What is all this but in a sense to despise God's goodness? It is treating God's goodness with indifference; it is making light of it; it is looking down upon it. How indi1ferent we e.re even to Jesus Christ, God's own Son I Wha.t an evidence of God's goodness was the coming of Christ into the world-his life, his sufferings, his death! "God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." Yet with what amazing indi1ference and coolness this message of Divine mercy, this message of redeeming love, is received! How cold and apathetic our hearts are to the love of Jesus! "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." From Jesus, the Crucified One, the King, who stands with outstretched hands waiting to receive and bless us, we turn away our hearts after the world and the things of it. Deaf to hie loviog voice, we tum our back upon our Saviour. We stretch forth our hands after money, and we say to it, "I will follow thee." We stretch out our hands after pleasure, and we sa.v to it, " I will follow thee." We stretch out our hands after popular applause a.iid the favour of men, and we say to them, "I will follow you." But, alas I how few have the gratitude and the courage to say, "Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goeEt " ! IIL THE oooni."ESS oF GoD, AlllD now IT IB MEANT. "The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance" (ver. 4). God's goodness is intended to lead us to repentance. And what more potent influence could he use than the influence of mercy and of love? What influence is so likely to make us repent of a wrong we have done to aoy pel'BOn than the kindn,si of that person toward us? If you have injured a neiahbour or a friend by woi,l or deed, and he meets you with angry words, this only tend!; to make you more stu\,bom, more hostile, than before. But if, on the contrary, you 11te him brsr with patience your att.acke, your unkind remarks, docs it not tend to make you sorry fur the: wrong you have done him? Or perhaps he heap11 co!llB of fire on. n.1-29.J THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS.

on your hee.d, and melts down, by deede of kindness and a forgivinu spirit the hardneaa of your heart. la it not a picture of how God deals with men? We 'have sinned. He has borne with us. We have stood condemned 68 guilty sinners in the presence of a broken Lo.w. He has sent his own Son to redeem, to justify, to eave our souls. All this God h11e done tho.t he might dro.w our hearts from ein, that by all hie overflowing goodness he might lead us to repentance. He puts before us the guilt of sin and the danger of it, the terrors of the jurlgment and the agony of the lost. But over and above o.11 he puts the message of mercy. " God commendeth his love toward WI, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." It is thie, the story of a heavenly Father's mercy; it is this, the story of a Saviour's love; it is this, the story of the cross,-that has touched the blunted conscience and melted the hardest heart, and won the most hardened sinners to repentance. "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts : and let him return unto the Lord, for he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon."-C. H. I.

entries.title: ROM 2:6–16
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-" The righteousjudgment of God." In the previous verses we saw how the goodness of God is too often received; how there are many who despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and long-suffering. It is especially to such persoll8 that St. Paul addresses his account of God's righteous jud.gment from the fifth ,erse to the sixteenth. Those who despise God's goodness have a great fact to face. Those who live as if there was no God, who evade his co=andments, who evade his offer of salvation, cannot evade his righteous judgment. As there is one event to all in the universal certainty of death, so we must all appear before the judgment-seat of Christ. It is good even for Christians to be reminded of the judgment to come. We live too little under its power. We realize too imperfectly that one day we shall have to give an account of our stewardship. We realize too imperfectly our responsibility toward those around us. How little we enter into Paul's views of the judgment, when he said, "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" (2 Cor. v. ll) ! The subject of God's righteous judgment is an important one both for Christian and for sinner. I. THE JUDGE. He is a righteous Judge. It is most important that, in thinking of the judgment, we should think of this aspect of God's character. "The righteous judgment of God" (ver. 5). We are not to think of the jud.gment as necessarily a. terror in itself. It is, what the laws of human society ought to be, a terror to the evil-doer, but a praise to them that do well. If we think of the judgment with terror, the fault lies, not with God, but in ourselves. God is a righteous Judge. His judgment is a righteous judgment. 'l'here are some who cherish hard thoughts of Goo. who think of him as a stern and relentless Judge. For such hard thoughts there is no foundation anywhere in God's dealings with men. His character is what we should call a character of perfect fairness. His judgment will be perfectly fair. There may be some one who will say, "I did not know that such a course of action wa.s wrong; I had not the Law of God to guide me." St. Paul meets just such a case: ".A..s many as have sinned without law shall also perish without law" (ver. 12). The judgment will be entirely according to our opportunities and privileges. If God condemns us or inflicts punishment upon us, it will only be because we deserve it. Every man will got a fair hearing. "There is no respect of persons with God" (ver. 11). Every man will get a fair chance. Those who have the Bible in their hands cannot say that they ho.vo not ho.d a fair chance. We have all got the offer of salvation. We have all heard of the love of Jesus. Wo have e.11 heard the invitations of the gospel What could God have done for us tho.t he has not done? He has done all he could do for our salvation, when " he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." Ho has done all he could, so long as man remains a free agont, to warn us to flee from the wrath to come, to win our hearts to himself. Ho is slow to anger, plenteous in mercy, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin; aud yet ho will by no means clear the guilty. Ho gives ns every chance, tlmt by his goodness he may lead us to repentance. It mo.y be obser.ed here that the idoo. of rightoouencss is so bound up in the idea of the jndgment ,,f Gtxl, that St. Paul uses uno wurd iu the original tu oxpross what we doscribo by two wuros-" right,x,ua,, Judgmunt." BOHANS. F 66 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [oH. n. 1-29,

II. Tm;; PER.."OKS JUDGED. That Judgment no one can escape. "Who will render to etwy man acrording to his deeds ' (ver. 6). Many escape here on earth the just reITT1.rd of their deeds. Gross crimes are perpetrated, and the murderer escapee the jnst sentence of the law; the defrauder and the betrayer and the slanderer occupy positions of respectability in life. But they go down to the grave with their sine upon their soul, to pass on into the presence of that tribunal from which earthly rank and earthly wealth can purchase no escape. As the apostle tells us in the eleveuth verse, "there is no respect of persons with God." God looks upon the heart; he looks upon the moti-ves; he looks upon the character. Thus regarding men, thus judging them, he sees but two classes. What are these? The rich and the poor? No. The learned and the unlearned? No. The Christian and the heathen? No. The Protestant and the Roman Catholic? No. In God's sight it is character and conduct-not country, or class, or creed-that dfride men. St. Paul speaks of the two classes thus: "Every soul of man that doetb eru" (ver. 9), and "Every man that worketh good" (ver. 10). Or, again, he describes them, "Those who by patient continuance in well-doing seek for glory and honour and immortality" (ver. 7), and "Those that are contentious [or, •self-seeking'], and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness" (ver. 8). To one or other of these classes every one of us belongs. ill. THE ETIDEKCE. Here again we see how righteous will be the judgmen t of God. There '\\ill be no circumstantial evidence needed, however strong its chain of many links may often be. There will be no need to depend on the testimony of others. There will be no danger of the Judge being led astray by the impassioned pleading or the fallible logic of a human advocate. Our own deeds will be there to speak for themselves. "Who will render to every man according to his deeds." .Ah, how solemn is the thought that we are now writing the evidence by which we shall be judged on the jud,,,"Illent-day ! In the red sandstone there are found, in some places, marks which are clearly the impressions of showers of rain, and these so perfect that it can even be determined in what direction the shower inclined, and from what quarter it proceeded -and this ages ago! So also scientific men have been able to trace out from the fossil remains, buried for ages in the earth, the shape and characteristics of animals whose species are long since extinct. So our deeds leave their record behind them, and that record in the judgment-day will testify to what our character was when we were here on earth. Thejudf[ment--day wul be a day of revelation (ver. 5). It will reveal the righteous judgment of God. It will unveil many mysteries in God's dealings which we did not understand before. It will reveal the true character of men. Then "God shall judge the secrets of men" (ver. 16). Then shall all hidden things be brought to light, all deceits discovered, all hypocrisies unmasked. Then, too, shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Their character, often here hidden under a cloud, often misunderstood, often misrepresented, shall then be -vindicat.ed for :ill eternity and before all the world. "The fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is." This also makes God's judgment a righteous judgment, that the evidence shall be the evidence of men's own deeds. IV. THE EESULT OF THE JUDGMENT. To aome wi1l be given eternal UftJ (ver, 7). That will be to those who have lived according to the light they had. No mere profession will save us. Neither will our own good works save us. But our works are the evidence whether or not we are believers on the Lord Jesus Christ. Those who have wasboo their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; those whom God's gc,c,dness baa led to repentance; those who have kept his commandments; those whc, have Dot been weary in well-doing, but "by patient continuance in well-doing seek for glory and honour and immortality;" those who have denied themselves, and ta.ken up their crC>lla ani followed Christ ;-they "shall have right to the tree of life, and shall enter through the gates into the city" (Rev. xxii. 14). To otMrB-Oh, what a dark Jutwre ! "Indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish" (vers. 8, 9). God's jucigmeot is a righteous judgment. "He that soweth to the flesh, shall of the flesh rear, cc,rruption." The apostle l!peaka of " treasuring up wrath against the day of wrath ' (ver. 5). That lil what every one is doing who g<.>eH on in the path ~f unbelief, impenitence, mc,bedienct, godleBSneas. What folly to lay up a treat1urc like that !-C. H. I. Vces. 17-29.-True religwn,. lloit men want to have a religion of sun,e sort, U orr. 11. 1-20.J THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 67

they do not want to have H while they live, yet, recognizing tbe importance of eternity o.nd the judgment, they wo.nt to have it before they die. Hence men who never think of religion in their hours of health and activity, will send for tbe minister when they o.re on a bed of sickness. Hence you have such cases as that of the great Emperor Oharlee V. of Germany, who had been a man of war and restless ambition almost all hie days, retiring into a convent for the closing years of hie life, and seeking within its cloistered walls that preparation for eternity which he had so long put off. But we want a religion not merely to die with, but to live by. After all, it ia but a poor religion which a man puts on as if it were to be bis shroud. What, then, is true religion? Where is it to be found? The answers are BO various and BO contradictory as to perplex the earnest seeker after truth. Old ecclesiastical systems contend that theirs, and theirs only, is the true religion, and in consequence of that belief, and in order to make others conform to it, they have persecuted, and imprisoned, and tortured, and burned those who differed from them. Then, in our own day, we have little companies of sincere and well-meaning people breaking away from all existing Churches, claiming for themselves that theirs only is the true religion, and excommunicating all others. But we come here as immortal souls, seeking after truth, and we turn from all human answers on the question of religion to the one infallible guide of faith and practice-the Word of God. That Word is the lamp to our feet, and the light to our path. entries.title: ROM 2:1–11
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content: -Without e'1:cuse. Hitherto Paul had carried his Jewish reader with him, for the Jews were glad to condemn the Gentiles. From the high tribunal of their Le.w they "judged" the misdeeds of the heathen. And, in the exercise of this censorious spirit of judgment, they would perhaps catch at the idea (eh. i. 20) that the bee.then were without excuse by reason of their possible knowledge of God. But how quickly does the relentless logic of the apostle tum back this truth upon themselves I "Without excuse," because they might have known God's will? "Wherefore thou art without excuse, 0 man that judgest I" For the very judging implied a knowledge of the wrong, and by that knowledge they were self-condemned. We have here-the false hope of the Jew; the just judgment of God. I. THE FALSE HOPE OF THE JEW. The Jew was greatly privileged, and God had shown him marvellous mercy. On either of these grounds, or both, he looked for exemption from judgment and wrath. 1. The chief hope of the Jew was founded upon the election of grace; he was called from among the nations to subserve a. special purpose of God, e.nd he fondly thought that he was called to security and bliss. He was singled out for service; he thought that he was singled out for inevitable salvation. He reckoned to escape altogether the judgment of God; he proudly deemed himself exempt by his very birth even from a.n inquiry into character. 2. But if perchance not quite so blind to spiritual claims, yet did not God's very goodness and forbearance and long-suffering, the wealth of which had been lavished upon the Jew, incline him to a careless ease, which was virtually presumptuous contempt? God had taught his wrath against unrighteousness, but he had also shown his mercy. Why not riot in the mercy. The old apology of God of the human heart," God is good; he will forgi,e.n II. THE JUST JUDGMENT OF Goo. But "let God be true, and every man a. liar! n Neither pride of birth, nor the affluence of God's love, shall be security a,,u:i.inst just judgment. 1. God's fudgment is true. (Ver. 2.) It proceeds upon the eternal principles of right; therefore an exemption on the ground of privilege, "respect of persons,n is impossible. "The righteous God trieth the hearts" (Ps.. vii. 9). 2. God's tnse judgment condemns the evil and i·ewards the good. (1) Now: "is a,,"llinst them that practise such things." (2) "The day shall declare it: n manifested judgment. There is an "end" towards which all things a.re tending-an end which shall also be a beginning. Reason and rovelation point to this. The law of future retribution is the same with the law of present judgment: "to every man according to his works." According to what a man is in himself shall he be regarded by God. And the deeds declare the man. So, then: (a) 'fo the good," eternal life,''" glory, honour, peace;" (b) to the evil, " wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish." 3. Goa's goodness, therefore, does but seek to prepare the way /or tha ea:ercise of fudgTMnl. He must condemn the evil, both now and then, and therefore he will seek to lead men from their evil that he may not condemn. The doctrine of justification is wrapped UJ.? in this ; for if God can but change a man's self, the obliteration of the past is provided for in Christ. The deep damnation of those who think to pervert such saving love; instead of a wealth of love, thera 1hall be a wel\lth of wrath for them I Let us learn the danger : of a blinded conscience-because we, forsooth, a.re " Christle.us," thorefore we are sl\ved I and of a hardened heart-God's very love, if we will not read its meaning, may be our deat.h. Eternally, and without any e.:s:ception, " the righteous Lorri loveth righteousness" (Ps. xi. 7).-T. F. L.

THE GEN'l'ILES AND THE JEWS IN TREI'R RESPEOTIVE RELATIONS TO LAW, The Gentile might have pleaded that his ignorance should Sl\ve him; the Jew certainly did 1111SU.me that his knowledge would save him. Paul will lay to their oharge "thnt they are all under Bin" (eh. iii. 9), and to this end he now shows that they are all under law before God. 1. Gentila. (1) The law of instinctive impulse: "by nature;" "e. law unto themselves." A correct and complete philosophy of the religions nature and relations of man seems almost impossible to us now; but doubtless we must recognize here the fact that man has still, more or less, the nRtive impulses of righteousness moving in the heart, which but for the Fall would have been perfect and all-containing in ua, and but for the redemption would have been altogether lost. This, then, is one part of man's primal oonstitution as a moral a.nd religious being ; he is moved to love and serve God, and t.o work righteousness, by an original instinct of his nature. Hence heroism. generosity, et.c., in ancient and modem world. God works in man, a.nd so far forth man does not suppress God's working. (2) The law of reflective consciousness: "their conscience bearing witness therewith;" "their thoughts one with another accusing or else excusing them." Man does not show his true moral nature till the instinct of the heart is obeyed with the intelligent approbation of the reflective consciousness. The instincts of the hea.rt, so far as they approach completeness, afford the essential contenai of the moral law; but it is for man to discern, embrace, and obey. And, till right.eousness is wrought thus of deliberate choice, it ma.y scarcely be called righteousness. For there are other impulses, which may lea.d to wrong; and, till the discerning jndgment has checked the native impulse, there is hardly moral worth in the one more than in the other. The "thoughts"muet excuse or accuse; then the will may act. 2. Jews. But man's heart is corrupt and man's mind is dark by reason of hereditary sin; therefore to the Jews God gave, in trust for the world, a Law, to correct and ccm1irm the law of the heart and mind. The coinciden·ce of the Law of Sinai with the true law of the heart and mind; the convincing authority of that Law, in its Divine power of a.wakening a.nd purifying the law within. Hence to the Jew there was added the Law of revela.tion. He was doubly taught his duty. II. Tm; SwPBEllE BIN OF THE JEWS. But to what end was the Law given, whether of natme or of revelation? To teach righteousness. And therefore the man who wrtrof:ht unright.eoUS11ess, according to his knowledge of the Law, whether Jew or Gentile, frustrat.ed the purpose of God, was under condemnation, and would "perish." Yet the Jew gloried in his enlightenment, oblivious of its purport and intent I 1. The Boast. (1) Personal. (a) His name--" a. Jew." Called by God, indeed, but for work rather than privilege. He perverted his call by a. narrow, selfish exclusion. (b) Resting upon the Law. Knowledge was safety, he thought; whereas knowledge was duty (see vers. 18, 20). (e) Glorying in God: a merely national God to him, and One who would merely" save." (2) Relative. (a) Guide of the blind. (b) Light of them that are in darkness. (e) Corrector of the foolish. (a) Teacher of babes. 2. The shame. (1) Inconsistency (vers. 21-23). (2) Crime (vers. 21-23). (3) Blasphemy (ver.24). T;,.ei,- God indeed; what must he be I . Our higher privilege, in the matt.er of la.w: Christ, and the Spirit. Our graver peril: orthodoxy, and the no.me of Christian. "Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the ihingB which I say?" (Luke vi 4-6).-T. F. L.

entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Symbolic religion. Closely involved in the Jew's boast of his name ad Law and God was his glorying in circumcision, the outward sign of the covenant of the Law. Thia leads the apostle to enunciate the law of symbolic religion, and to ~ t.he supreme value of a true spiritualism. L SYIIBOLIC RELrnroN. The law of all symbolism in religion is wrapped up in the worda, "Cirenmcisiun indeed profiteth, if thou be a door of the Law." That is, the sign ii of worth just in so far aa it leads to, and attests, tho thing signified. 1. Personal m.l,,ue. Man's naturr, is complex, and the spiritual and the sensuous react on each Mb.er. If the lesson is learnt, and the witnesa borne, the work is done; for "God is a Spirit, and they that worship him," etc. So the man of circumcised heart was the true Jew; the man of baptized spirit, and who feeds upon Christ by faith, is the true Christian.
