entries.title: ROM 2:6–11
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-.A righteous Judge. That the anticipation of e. judgment rises naturally in the mind is shown by the present testimony of conscience-a law recognized as in, yet above us, and by the utterances of heathen writers on morals. The Scriptures corroborate and clarify this conception. The apostle asserts of the future what Abraham felt of the present Pro'ridence, "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? Will he slay the righteous w:itb the wicked?" Note some particulars confirming the righteous- ness of God's judgment. L THE REOOKPENSE WILL BE PROPORTIONED TO MEN'S DEEDS. Not their professions, but their acu;, will determine their destiny. And the character and number of their acts will be reckoned. There is no conflict between this statement and other Scripture passages which speak of the reward as one of grace, not of merit, and as a gift bestowed on ali Christians. For the reward will be immensely greater than men's deeds deserve, an~ will not be earned by them, but conditioned by their conduct. The gospel comes not as a snbstitute for, but as a help to realizing, practical righteousness; and whilst every justified believer will be saved, each will have the praise that is his, according to his works of faith and labours of love. II. THE JUDGMENT WILL TAKE ACCOUNT OF MEN'S AIMS IN LIFE. The one class seek * glory, honour, and incorruption," and also "peace." Their choice does them credit; they selected what is fair and lovely and permanent, what is opposed to the rule of the :flesh, and is unaffected by the ravages of time. Their goal is not the "vain pomp and glory of the world;" not simply success, but to reach a position of pure, lasting excel- lence. And they shall receive in fullest measure what they desire, "Eternal life " oomprehendB all blessedness-<leliverance from the thraldom of sin; no need to gather up the skirts lest defilement ensne, for the very streets of their city shall be of pure gold; en wrapment with the Divine splendour; walking in the light of God; manifested w; his soD.B by the likeness they wear; elevated to princely employments and regal dignities. The objects for which the other class strive are not definitely stated, but may be gathered from antithesis and from the unrighteousness to which they yield themselves. They seek not "peace" and "truth," and their harvest likewise is the multiplied outcome of the seeds they have sown. No description of hell can transcend the awful picture of" wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish," resting upon the soul; that, clasping unrighteousness to its bosom as a prize on earth, finds it sting like a serpent and burn with :fiercest remorse when allowed full sway in its" own place." fil THE AWAED WILL BEAR RELATION TO TBE METHODS BY WBIOB THE OBJECTS Oil' &ABTBLY DDEAVOUB HAVE BEEN PUBBUED. A righteous aim can be permanently att&ined only in righteoUB ways. The recognition of this stamps the government of the univenie u moral The "patient continuance" of the one class could only be practised by the well-doing. It includes passive endurance and active perseverance; ~he trtationa,y p011ture of the caryatides, and the carrying of a burden in the face of wmd and storm. The other clase are described as " lactioUB," quarrelling with their lot, OO't'llting pleuan ad notoriety," working evil." Befu.sing to bow to the yoke of truth, ml, 11, 1-29,J 'l'HE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 73

they become the slaves of unrighteousneas; and a hard master and terrible paymaster doea unrlghteouenese prove. The judgment of God will proceed on easily intdligible principles, It le not difficult for men to decide whether they are working good or working evil, It ie not reaching a conclusion after abstract speculation, nor h,,Idini a creed with multitudinous details. Only an omniscient Judge, however, could brin" to 0 light the hidden deeds of darknese, the secret thing, good or bad. IV. THE JUDGE WILL OBSERVE RIGOROUS IMPARTIALITY. With him "is no respect of persons." Jew and Greek shall be tried with due regard to the presence or absence of religious light (cf. Acts x. 35 in the history of Cornelius). It is impossible to bribe the almighty Arbiter or to overawe his tribunal. T~e anticipation o~ a Divine j11dgment has been e. comfort to the oppressed, remembenng that "One higher than the hiah regardeth;" and it will be a terror to the worker of iniquity, and an incentive to all noble deeds. "Knowing the terror of the Lord, we persuade men." None can complain that their condition makes it impossible to be patient in well-doing. Christ, our Pattern and our Power, offers his "very present help" to all who find the stress and strain of life too severe for mortal strength.--S. R. A.

entries.title: ROM 2:21
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-.A serm011, to teachers. The apostle supposes a. Jew to have listened complacently to the long catalogue of crimes of which the heathen world has been guiltycrimes which blacken the lip to mention. And then the apostle turns strategically round upon the self-satisfied possessor of a Divine revelation to put the scathing inquiry, why he has not been freer from violations of the moral law. Advantage entails responsibility ; it was inconsistent to eagerly proselytize to a religion whlch the preacher observed more by precept than by example. A lesson here for all teachers of the Word: let their instructions mould their own lives I I. THE WORK OF TEACHING. 1. lts possi"bility. It presumes that some are able and willing to teach, and that others are equally in a position to learn. Knowledge begets the desire of communication to others; truth by its dissemination enriches all, leaves none the poorer. The possession of the Scriptures constitutes a. capacity in those who study to explain their meaning to others less happily situated for meditation. Besides the preachers of the gospel from the pulpit, we have a noble army of volunteers sacrificing their ease each Lord's day to impart to the young what they themselves have learned of Christ. And the youthful mind is plastic, its heart ea.sily impressed. 2. Its importance. Education is a work of beginnings, of seed-sowing, of filling the pockets with tree.sure in the shape of facts and principles to be afterwards used, applied, recognized, in fulness of meaning. The mind must be fed as well as the body, or we have dwarfed, stunted souls, miserable and corrupt. To neglect the garden is to fill it with weeds. We insufficiently value acquisitions whose worth cannot be tabulated in monetary figures. Of what priceless value is a new happy inspiring thought of God! To be led where we can get a better sight of Christ and his salvation, is surely a service for which we can in no wise adequately thank or pay our guide. 3. Its difficulty. Some hesitate to teach unless they can answer every objection which may be urged ll:,,"'ll.inst the truth they enforce. And on religious subjects there is no end to the queries which may be started. There are many adverse influences preventing the ready reception of the facts and doctrines of Christianity, or checking the subsequent advance in learning. Recall our Lord's parable of the sower, and its picture of the multiform ways in which sin works against the leaven of the truth. There is a roseate and there is a practical view of Sunday school work. Yet, whilst we would not forget the restlessness of the young, and the far aim of making them" wise unto salvation" so frequently hindered by unlovely homes, neither should any despair, but remember they are wielding the sword of the Spirit, and that to God e.11 hearts are open. Let preachers think of the Lord and his apostles as failing to conquer the opposition and win the assent of all their hearers, and, instead of renouncing toil, remember that they are not responsible for success, but only for effort. II. THE REFLEX INFLUENCE OF TEACHING ON TIDI TEACHERS. 1. I11citas to their oum culture. There is the felt necessity of bein" in advance of the le:\rners. The more we know !nd the more thoroughly and clearly ~e understand it, thti gM1ter the enjo:--- roent and the euooess of the work. We often take pains for the sake of others which we eho11ld reject for ,ureelves. How can we teach if we do not instruct ourselvc~? 74 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMAl'l"S. [oH, IL 1-29.

Tht>re Clught to be no Bild hiRtus between our declarations and our aplrltual conduct. We must not only be finger-posts, but guides-" lest, having preached to othera, we oUJ'Belves become 011Stawa.ys." • The lore of Obrist and hia apostles twelve He taught, but first he followed it himself." If we are the channels of good to our fellows, it behoves us to olear away all that might impede the ft.owing, and defile the purity of the stream of truth from God, 2. Necessarily promotes their own improvement. Earnest sincore teaching not only demands selr-culture and progress, but is oertain to result therein. All Christian service is aelf-rewarding. • Thou she.J.t be served thyself, by every senae Of service which thou renderest." Teaching clarifies our own views, enforces truth upon our own souls. Many a teacher has enjoyed prayer and realized the sweetness and significance of the Scriptures most -when preparing the lesson for bis scholars. The Divine plan for oblivion of our own sorrows is to become saviours to the helpless, physicians to the sick. The outrush of Christian benevolence protect.s against the in.flow of corroding cares or pleasures.-S. R. A.

And the people's query to John the Baptist, "What shall we do 1" like the jailor's request of Paul, " Wba.t must I d,o to be sa.ved?" shows this natural tendency, which begets in our day nominal Christianity; that contents itself with baptism and the Lord's Supper, reading the Bible, and subscribing to societies. Their religion ends there-mere formalism. Its causes may be found in the following circumstances. L v.r e are tlilder the governance of the senses. We like, and need to a certain extent, the visible signs and seals of religion, and thus run the risk of exaltin11: unduly their importance. Resting in the embodiment, we neglect the spiritual significance. 2. It Ba'l"es the tronble of investigating our spiritual condition. Definite rules please us, by relegating to codes or authorities the difficulty and weariness of understanding principles, and deciding as to times and degrees and dispositions of religious service. 3. The rites may be performed 'Without necessarily renouncing pleasurable vices. There is a ROrt of compromise effected. such and such duties condoning such other laxities. Even asceticism ;s easier than rigorous inward control and mortification. To depreciate internal religion is e,ridently wrong: (1) From the whole tenor of Scripture in many places. Even the Law of Moses affirmed the necessity of loving God with all the heart and BOul The prophets constantly denounced sacrifices which represented no moral feeling, no inward confession of sin or respect to the glory of God. (2) The intent of religio111 observances is as means to an end, and to stop at the means is to frustrate the aim of ceremonies, which are designed to purify our conceptions of righteousness, to strengthen our aspirations aft.er the noble and the good, and to leaven the whole life with godlineas. !L A WBOliO CONCLUBIOli OBVIATED: TlIAT EXTERNAL OBBEBVANOEB MAY J!l!I DIS• RF,<,ARDD>. It is ma11's habit, as Butler has remarked, when two thiuge are compared, tu fancy that the one adjudged less preferable may be whoHr, negleci.ed. "These ought ye to have done, and not to have left the other undone.' The practice of roligion dema.1:.1ds some outward rites. 1. ExpresMion iH helpful to our thoughts. Singing I.Der~ thankful1:.1eA; written vows stamp themselveB on the memory. And the ou. u. 1-29.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 75

eymbolio o.cte of o. religion thus lend impreesive definiteness to onr inward decisiom. 2. The union of Christians is assisted by participation in the same rites. Attending the eame gatherings, affixing the same badge to the breast, cements the convicti1m of brotherhood, and renders co-operation possible. 3, The honour of God is subserved by outward worehip o.nd confession, His glory ie in revelation, and by visible adoration the Ohurch reflects hie radiance e.nd becomes the light of the world. There ie a moral obligation reeting on the dieciples of Christ to respect the institutions he himself este.bliehed. III. THE TRUE RELATION OF EXTERNAL TO INTERNAL RELIGION, 1. TM external obse7"1Jance must be the outgrowth of the inward condition. The sign of a change of hee.rt or disposition. The profession is designed as an index to the soul, a dial-plate of the inner workings; otherwise it is false and worthless, a mockery and an injury. Hence the anxiety of the gospel method to reform and renew the heart, that from e. pure spring pellucid rills may flow. "Make the tree good, and its fruit will be good also." Even moral acts have no beauty in them if performed from unworthy motives. To give merely because we are importuned, or to head a subscription list, is not liberality. 2. When there is a conflict between moral duties and religious observances, then only can the latter be neglected. Whilst both are commanded, the moral obligations have the additional sanction of arising from the light of nature. Onr Saviour showed that it was better to rescue an ox or a sheep than to keep the sabbath. He declared the Pharisees not to understand the statement, "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice." '!'hey did not perceive that the general spirit of religion consists in piety and virtue, as distinguished from outward forms and regulations. "To obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." IV. THE DIVINE Al'PBOVAL WHICH CROWNS A TRULY RELIGIOUS LIFB. "Whose praise is not of men, but of God." The supreme object is to please him who alone can really see our thoughts and aims, and judge righteous judgment. Men praise where they should blame, and censure when they ought to approve. As Paul cried, "I appeal unto Cresar," so we may appeal unto God. His praise is worth having. The de:.;rees in his university mean merited honours. All our inward strivings against temptation and struggles to hold fast to faith in his Word he has witnessed. Human eyes can only discern our failures or our seeming successes, but Christ's "eyes of flame" te..«t the gold of our actions. And the commendation of the Lord implies blessed reward, to be publicly confQrred hereafter. With him is no inadequacy of testimonials to e3:press his sense of his people's services.-S. R. A.

entries.title: ROM 2:1–16
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The leading principles regulating the general judgment. Having stated so clearly the state of the Gentile world as under God's wrath, the apostle now introduces to us a critic who endorses the Divine dealings. He is e. severe critic, as guilty men will often be. His spirit towards the bee.then world, so manifestly under the Divine curse, is," Serve them right." He is evidently a Jew (cf. ver. 17). Criticizing the heathen world from the platform of superior privileges, the Jew concluded that they had got no more than they deserved. The apostle, however, ventures to tell him he is as "inexcusable" as his Gentile brother. If the Gentile had so misused" the light of nature" and of "conscience" as to bocome so degraded, why has the Jew so misused the additional light of God's Law as to become so self-righteous? God will not judge the secrets of men upon any narrow and partial grounds, but will dispense judgment fairly. The section now before us presents the lending principles of the Divine judgment in a most masterly foshion. I. Gon'e JUDGlllENT IB A.COORDING TO TRUTH. (Ver. 2.) The apostle declares to hi~ self-righteoue critio thnt he is sure-the Revised Version gives it "know "-that God's judgment in the ce.ses already reforred to is according to truth (itm A.\fjBe,u). By this we are to understand the.t it is according to the reality of the things in questic,n. That is to eay, the Divine judgment is not based on nppee.ranccs, it does not rest on superficinl grounds, but goes down to the very Dl\ture of things. And this is a genernl p11noiple characterizing God's jndgment alwnys. Men may judge according to the appearance, but God looketh on tho heart, and dispenses to each individual whnt he deserves. Now, wo could have confidence in no other judgment than this on,i which conforms to tho rol\lity nnd nature of things. If wo al'll able to analyze fairly God'a T6 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS, [orr, n. 1-29,

deal~ "«"ith sinful men, we shall find that his 86tlffl! fudgmmts have alwl\ye had ~ t r.-ascm. In the present inst&nce, the critic vindicates the Divine procedure. A~ h<.> declares the Gentiles to have suft"ered rightly, he really becomes the ohampion of Gcid, s.J.tbough in doing so he, 1LS the apostle 8hows, condemns himself. 11. Gon's JUDGME1'"TS MAY BE PRECEDED DY A DISPENSATION OF FORDB:ARANOE, (Vers. 3---5.) While God's judgments when executed are truthful and thorough, they may not be executed immediately. In the case of the Jew under review by the apostle, God hll.8 been exercising amazing forbearance. Although the recipient of superior prinleges, he bas been sinning just as really as his Gentile brother, and wholly misinterpreting the Divine forbearance. God, by his goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, bas been leading him to repentance, to a thorough change of character and heart (u"1booaa); but he will not be led, but insists on regarding l\ll this forbearance a.s merited on bis part. His heart still continues hard and impenitent (a.p.ET<W&71-ro11), so that be is really tre=ing up wrath for himself which shall be revealed at the day of jndgment. And this solemn warning should be heeded by many. There a.re many still who interpret forbearance as approval; who think highly of themselves because they have been exempt from suffering; who base upon their good health, good fortune, and general comfort the mistaken conclusion that God must contemplate such people wiih a large a.mount of complacency. Bnt it is forbearance be is exercising, and no justification could be extended to such self-righteous individuals. ffi REWARD il"D PtTh"ISHME1''"T Wil.L BE METED OUT EVENTUALLY AOOOBDING TO EACH J,L.,U.--'s DEEDS. (Vers. 6-10.) To the apostle's eye men resolved themselves int.o two classes: one class was seeking, by patient continuance in well-doing, glory and honour and immortality; the other class was contentious, not obeying the truth, but obeying unright.eousness (ill.,cui). Now, t.o the one, reward will be given in the form of all that is implied by " eternal life;" while to the other shall be meted out in strict proportion "indigna.tion and wrath, tribulation and anguish." Just as, in a well-ordered state, the doer of evil is pI!llished and the doer of good rewarded, so will it be, only with infallible accuracy, under the government of God.. Now, at first sight, it seems hard to reconcile a judgment according to works with a. justification by faith a.lone; bnt if we will only consider the fruits of justification, in those good works which God bath before ordained that his people should walk in them (cf. Eph. ii. 8-10), we can see that the scheme of grace can yet include a reward proportional to work. Let us grant at once that all the work got out of the believer is divinely prompted, that it is the outcome of grace, nevertheless it has its moral value in the universe of God and deserves reward. Besides, as the judgment-scene in Matt. xxv. shows, the servants that are welcomed and rewarded receive their reward with wonder. Just as magnanimous minds, when some acknowledgment of their valuable labours is offered, declare it t.o be beyond their deserts, and feel what they declare, so the rewarded well-doer at the Iaat will be the first to acknowledge that the reward rests, not on any absolute merit, but on abounding grace. On the other hand, the evil-doers will acknowledge that the" indignation and wrath, the tribulation and anguish," have been fully earned and richly deserved (cC. Jonathan Edwards's 'Works: Occasional Sermons,' Nos. vii., viii). And if we inquire how those who have died in infancy, and those who have been saved a.s by fire at life's last moments, like the dying robber at the side of Christ, are to fare a.t a judgment based upon works, we have only to reply that their history afi,er death ha.s doubtless attested the gracious Spirit which was given them, and will justify their reception into the joys of eternal life. IV. Goo's JUDGl[E]JT WILL BE WITHOUT RESPECT OF PERSONS. (Ver. 11.) In spe.aking of this reward and punishment according to works, the apostle is careful to note that each will be "to the Jew first, and also to the Greek ("EA'-11v1): for there is no respect of persons (,rpo11-0A.'l'/tla) with God." The reason why the Jew comes first in the order of judgwent is that he ha.s had all along such superior privileges as make hie judgment all the rnore serious matter. If he has not profited by these privileges hie jndgment shall be ol1 the more severe-he shall be beaten truly with many stripes; and ifhe profited., his reward shall be all the more glorioua. The Gentile, or Greek, on the other hand. with nothin" but natural light, sliall find himself judged fairly, although it mw;t r,eede be a. BV.,(Jndary matter under a. beneficent governmcut like God's. For he dooll 11ot accept tht peraons of men. He is not inftuenced in h1a Judgment by cB. 11. 1-29.J THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROM.ANS. 77

porsonal clnime. He puts away the idea of merit in individuals, becauRe all are guilty before him, and bases his judgrnent upon the one consideration of state, with its resultant outcome, either good works or bacl. Now, this was what a Jew found it hard to accept. He thought, as a thorough-bred Jew, he ought to be BCCepted. It muet have been a great humiliation to hnve to take up a position beside ordinary men, and have no store set by hie person nt all. V. GoD's JUDGMENT WILL BE ACCORDING TO THE LAW, WRITTEN OB UNWRITI'EN, WBIOH EA0H MAN HAS RECEIVED. (Vers. 12-15.) The Gentiles shall not be held accountable for an outward and written revelation which has never come into their hands, but only for that law of conscience which God has written on their hearts. For this law revealed in their nature, and the use they made of it, they shall be justly held responsible. Nor shall the tracing of the law of conscience to utilitarian or animal sources in the least degree diminish human responsibility. The question is no~How has this inward law '.and monitor come into existence? but-What use has each man made of it, come as it may? And so the heathen shall be beaten, thoagh with few stripes, for their neglect of the inward law. They shall in many cases perish, even though they had not the privilege of a written law. Conscience has had a Divine source, no matter how long it has taken to develop; and God will call all men into judgment for the use of it. On the other hand, those who have had the Law written and delivered shall be judged by it. For the Scriptures come to reinforce the conscience, and to reveal the mercy.of the Lord. In such circlllill!t&nces it is surely jnst that those who receive" the oracles of God" should be held responsible for the use and profit they have made of them. If they have been a dead letter to them, then God will justly punish their neglect of them. Such men shall be beaten with many stripes, because they might have known and ought to have done their Lord's will. VI. THE GENERAL JUDGMENT WILL BE CONDUCTED BY JEStJB CHR!sT. (Ver. 16.) God the Father will commit to his only begotten Son the duty of judgment. And here we see the wondrous equity of the Divine Being. This Second Person of the Trinity has added to his Divine knowledge a human experience. He has been in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin. He knows the human problem e:,;perimentally. He can consequently enter into our case more thoroughly than if he had never assumed our nature. And so he does not judge from above, or from outside, but from within, and can enter into the secrets of the human heart. Hence this general judgment is to be upon the most equitable principles, and by the most capable of judges. How important, then, that we cultivate the acquaintance of him who is to have us at his judgment-bar l Not that we may bribe him, but that he may prepare us for that thorough investigation which lies before us. If we make a "clean breast n of all to him, if we acknowledge our sin and shortcoming, if we ask him for a clean heart and a baptism of his Holy Ghost to enable us to live for his glory and our fello'W'S' good, then he will help us to a better life, and enable us, so far from dreading his judgment-bar, to "love his appearing." May the day of judgment break brightly on us all, for his own Name's sake l-R. M. E. ' Vere.17-29.-'.l7!e Jewiah world. In our last section we saw how the apostle takes the Jewish critic through the leading principles of the Divine judgment. In doing so, he had a practical end in view. He meant to bring home to the Jewish heart the fact of sin and danger, and thereby to lend the censorious, self-righteous Jew to humiliation and salvation through Christ alone. The present section contains the pointed application of the principles to the Jewish case. And here we have to notice-- I. THE POSITION ASSUMED BY THE JEWS AS THE DIVINELY E.,."{LIGHTENED LE.A.DEBS OF MANKIND. (Vera. 17-20.) 'l'he apostle states the Jewish assumption admirablf. 'l'hey were proud of their name: "Thou benrest the name of a Jew 11 (Revised Versiou). But this was because they hnd received the Law; and so they "rested iu" or "upon the Law; " they made their possession of the Law the be.fils of their confidence and tranquillity. Their notion was tbnt men entrusted with suoh a litemture had nothing in the world to fear, Moreover, it wns from God, and why should they not r8<,ua.rd themselves ns hie favourites, and "runke their boast" about him? And the book did not; remnin unread; they 8ought from it n" knowledge of his will; 11 were ,,bi~ ('l'US&l\l<:'utly, to 11xeroiee judgment " regtU'diug things that differed" (60,ci,u.d~"m .-a 61114>ipo,,.n); and THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [on. n.1-20,

~ived !I €'.6neral enlightenment through the Law . . Not only so, but they believed in their mission; they were t-0 be guides of the blind, lights· to those in darkness, correct-Ors (-•~•I/ff/>') of the foolish, teachers of babes, having at least the form (µ&p,po,rr,11) of knowledge and of truth in the Law. lu short, the Jews set themselves at the head of hum~nity as the qualified lMders and instructors of mnnkind. Now, it ie a great assumption for any men to make. Yet the Jews were not singular in their assumption. It is made daily by men with far less reason, perhaps, than they. The lenders of thought, "the men of light and leading," who profess to know how much is given us to master, and how much remains "unknowable and unknown," must accept of the l'e&'onable judgment of their less pretentious fellows, and, as superior persons, must be amenable to morals. By their fruits we shall know them. By their lives we shall be able to estimate the value of their principles. If they are benefactors of their species, if they promote the real welfare of mankind, well and good, If they are ~ndr:ances, then they cannot resist being condemned. It is this line the apostle adopts m this pa.."S&ge, II. 'l'HE PRETD.'"TIOUS TEACHERS WERE, AS A MATTER OF FACT, THE GREAT HIN- D&ANCE TO THE DISSEMINATION OF DIVINE KNOWLEDGE. (Vers. 21-24.) The first fact Paul dwells on is that these Jews preached too little to themselves. They fell into the error of teaching others what they did not feel inclined to practise themselves. And so he catalogues certain sins of which he knew them to be guilty. It would seem that they st.ole, committed adultery, were guilty in heathen temples of sacrilege, acd, in short, led such unworthy lives as t.o make God's Name a reproach and ground of blasphemy among the Gentiles. The morality of the teachers thus became the great hindrance t.o the acceptance of Divine truth. Now, there can be little doubt that the crimes of professed Christians constitute in heathen lands to-day a chief obstacle to the reception of the gospel ; missionaries meet this difficulty constantly. But we onght t.o apply tbe canon to the pretentious teachers of our time, and it will be found that their lives are morally defective when judged by the standard of the gospel they afiect to despise. The morality of a George Eliot, a G. H. Lewes, or a J. S. Mill, who afiected to be moral teachers of their time, will not bear any very close inspection; and e"en those of the same school, whose lives are outwardly blameless, fall far beneath the self-sacrificing enthusiasm which Christianity fosters, and in multitudes of cases secures. The test is snre and infallible. Men and women that are morally easy-going, that are practically selfish and indifferent iu large degree to the circumstances and suffering of their fellows, are unfit to be the teachers of their generation. .And their teaching is as sure to prove a failure in the end, as the teaching of Judaism was among the Gentiles. III. THE JEWS HAD A FALSE CONFIDENCE IN THE RITE OF OIRCUMCISION. (Ver. 25.) Their notion was that circumcision constituted something like the "hall-mark" on real silver, and distinguished them from all the mere electro-plating of the Gentiles, They thought that immoral conduct could not obliterate the value of the fleshly rite. This is the mistake made by all who lay undue emphasis upon rites and ceremonies, They fancy they have a value altogether independent of moral states and moral living. The apostle has consequently to draw attention to the fact that circumcision only profited one who kept the Law. It was then a sign of the covenant, and was taken along with the perfect obedience to the Law which had been rendered. But if a circumcised person turned out a Law-breaker, the circumcision really passed into uncircumcision. In other words, the Jew could break the covenant s~al by breaking the Law of the covenant. This is a very solemn and weighty truth. It has its applic11tion to the covenant signs of the Christian dispensation. It is perfectly possible for persons who have become members of the visible Church, by a course of reckless living to break their covenant sign, and to be in God's sight disfranchised. Let no undue value be assigned to ritai and ceremonies. They cannot be separated from moral states and conditions. IV. 'J.'BE JEWS IGNORED THE l'OS8r:BILITY AND EXI8TENOJII OF THE OIROUIIOISED lN BEA.KT. (Vers. 26-29.) If a. circumcised person may forfeit his position as in covenant with God by breaking the Divine Law, on the other hand, an uncircumcised ptrson, a Gentile, may so keep God's Law as U) be entitled to a position in covenant with him. His uncircumcision in such a Cl\llc, Paul maintains, should be counted or "r<:Ckonoo for circumci.iuu." Here the apo~tle is contending for the admlH8ion of (.it;nti.lt:a w the viMiblt; CJ:uirch without the 11ec1:ssity of circumcision, Many a Gentile, on. m.1-31.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 79

like Corneliue, or like the centurion in the Gospels, put to shame the Ieee earnest and Ieee devout Jews. The high morality of such men waa a standing condemnation (1tpwei) of the prctentioue Jew. Accordingly, Paul proceeds to affirm that the circumcision of the heart, not the mere circumcision of the flesh, is the all-important matter. There is o. circumcision of the heart which checks the unholy tendencies within and secures the reality, of which outward circumcision is but the type. Of it God the Searcher of hearts, is the true Judge. He rejoices in it, and regards those whohave submitted to it as his true people. The circumcised in flesh may secure praise from men, but the circumcised in heart look for approbation to God only. It is for us all to seek the inward and spiritual circumcision, the true sign of membership in Gorl's invisible kingdom.-R. M. E.

entries.title: ROM 3:19
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The purpose of Law. Although it is the main intention of the apostle, in speaking of the Law, to show its insufficiency for the purpose with which it.a introduction and publication were commonly credited, his teaching would be misunderstood were he supposed to disparage it; for St. Paul held the Law of God in the highest reverence, although he did not attribute to it all with which it was connected in the mind of the unchristian Jew. I. THE PBDIIABY PURPOSE OF THE LAW, This was unquestionably the revelation of the Divine chamcter, attributes, and will. God is not only the perfectly holy Being; he is also the perfectly righteous Ruler. Truth declares what he is; Law declares what be will have his subjects to be. Accordingly, revelation takes the form, not only of the indicative, but of the imperative. Law is the expression of God's justice, and of hie will that all the subjects of his moral government should partake of his holiness, l\nd, in their relations to one another and to him, should do those things that please him. His oommandments, statutes, ordinances, are the utterance of his judgment as to what is good, what is best, for bis intelligent creatures. II. THE BECONDABY PURPOSE OF THE LAW. It is upon this that the inspired apostle Jays stress in the passage now before us. 1. The Law reveals sin. It is a standard beside which the deficiencies and errors of men's conduct become plainly manifest. 2. The Law condemns the sinner. It is not simply a declamtion of what is right; it exposes and censures what is wrong. It speaks the sentence against the viols.tors of its rules. 3. The Law silences the sinner. It leaves him without justification, s.pology, or excuse. III. THE ULTIHATl!I PURPOS& OF THE L.Aw. This is unquestionably, in the c:u, of our humanity, to prepare the way for the gospel. The Law is the pedagogue, the slave who attends and conducts the pupil, and it leads unto Christ. "By the work! of the Law shall no flesh be justified in God's sight." Yet we cannot believe that a merciful God publishes the Law simply for the condemnation of men. It does reveal tht1 heinousness of eln, making it appear exceedingly sinful. It does reveal the helplessness of the sinner. But all this is preparl\tory to a remedial and redemptive intervention. What the Low could not do, God does by the gift of his Son, who obeyed and ma,,"Ilified the Law in hie own Person, and at the sl\Ine time ~eoured for sinful men, upon cam• THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. tos. m.1--at. pliancl' with the conditions of faith and repentance, their exemption from the Law's penalties, and their enjoyment of the Divine favour, participation in the Divine n11ture and life. and inherit&nce in the Divine and eterna.J. blessedness. Thus that which appeared the instrument of wrsth has been converted into the oooasion of salvation. ,er. 22.-Tlle cluli"".ti,rely C!hristian n"ghteom'MSS. The apostle ho.s clearly shown that rightoonsness by the Law is not possessed by men, and that in this way is no hope for the salntion of the human race. Such is the negative conclusion to which facts o.nd reason compel him. Yet it- is not his vocation to fre&eh a doctrine of despair. True, without righteousness there can be no salvation. 'Iherefore, if light is to be cast upon human darkness, it must come elsewhither than from the Law. So it is that St. P&ul preaches the ne"" and distinctively Christian righteousness, to be secured by conditions that may be fulfilled by men of every r&ee-iL righteousness that avails before God, &nd ensures the a.ccept.snce and the spiritual welfare and elevation of men. L THE CHARACTER A:!-'"D DESIG~ATION OF THIS RIGHTEOUSNESS: IT IS OF Gon, OB Drrn.--x. 1. It has its source in God. In this it is distinguished from the rectitude which is "by works; " that in a sense is of human origin. It is shown to be "of grace," i.e.. to be the provision of Divine favour, free and undeserved. And further, this expression, "of God," implies the perfection of this righteousness in comparison with all beside. 2. It is divinely adapted by God to man. There is presupposition of man's helplessness and dependence; it is presumed-which is indeed the fact-that man cannot work out a righteousness of his own. Hence there is a ground for this new ri!!hteowmess in a Divine provision of substitution. The apostle would be misunderatood were his teaching upon this point to be interpreted, as some have interpreted it, as representing God as indifferent to the person by whom suffering is endured and obedience rendered. Yet Christ, by his suffering the consequences of sin in this humanity and by his perfect obedience and holiness, has laid the foundation for the acquisition by man of the distinctively Christian righteousness. 3. It avails and is accep~able before God. According to the representations of the context, it consists in the remission of sins, and acquittal and accept&nce before the Divine tribunal, and in the manifestation of positive Divine approval; which may be regarded as the two parts of "justification." It is evident that such righteousness is imputed, and not inherent- & ~logical expression which mnst not, however, be interpreted to imply its unreality. Thus the Divinity of the Christian righteousness may be made apparent, as an object of ad.minltion and of aspiration. Il. THE lllE.AJ>S OF THE .A'I'l'.ilNXE:l."T OF THIS BIGHTEOUBNESB-THROUGH FAITH IN Jmms CmusT. In order to the fulfilment of this condition upon which the Christian right.eousness may be attained, there must be: 1. Belief in the Scripture testimony concerning Christ, that he is the Son of God and the appointed Saviour of mankind. This is indispensable; for faith is not a vague sentiment-it has an Object, and an Object which justifies and deserves it. Yet, though indispensable, this is not sufficient. There must be also: 2. Trust or confidence in Christ as a personal Saviour. Faith is not merely intellectual. assent; it is the consent of the heart and the will. It is capable of degree, and there is strong faith and weak faith. But the important point is that the soul, in the attitude and exercise of faith, is brought into personal relation with the buly Saviour. fil THE UNIVERSALITY OF THIB BIGHTEOUBNESS: IT IS UNTO .ALL, .AND UPON ALL, THEH THAT BELIEVE. The rectitude itself is a possession which men may share, whatever their natior:.ality, their condition in life, their individual history. And the condition. of its attainment is equally universal! there is nothing in faith w~ich li!Ili.ts ~te exercise to any special members, or any section of the human race. In this Chr1Bt1an1ty proves it.eel! to ~ n d thil is its glory, its Divinity-the universal religion,

Accordingly, revelation takes the form, not only of the indicative, but of the imperative. Law is the expression of God's justice, and of hie will that all the subjects of his moral government should partake of his holiness, l\nd, in their relations to one another and to him, should do those things that please him. His oommandments, statutes, ordinances, are the utterance of his judgment as to what is good, what is best, for bis intelligent creatures. II. THE BECONDABY PURPOSE OF THE LAW. It is upon this that the inspired apostle Jays stress in the passage now before us. 1. The Law reveals sin. It is a standard beside which the deficiencies and errors of men's conduct become plainly manifest. 2. The Law condemns the sinner. It is not simply a declamtion of what is right; it exposes and censures what is wrong. It speaks the sentence against the viols.tors of its rules. 3. The Law silences the sinner. It leaves him without justification, s.pology, or excuse. III. THE ULTIHATl!I PURPOS& OF THE L.Aw. This is unquestionably, in the c:u, of our humanity, to prepare the way for the gospel. The Law is the pedagogue, the slave who attends and conducts the pupil, and it leads unto Christ. "By the work! of the Law shall no flesh be justified in God's sight." Yet we cannot believe that a merciful God publishes the Law simply for the condemnation of men. It does reveal tht1 heinousness of eln, making it appear exceedingly sinful. It does reveal the helplessness of the sinner. But all this is preparl\tory to a remedial and redemptive intervention. What the Low could not do, God does by the gift of his Son, who obeyed and ma,,"Ilified the Law in hie own Person, and at the sl\Ine time ~eoured for sinful men, upon cam• THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. tos. m.1--at. pliancl' with the conditions of faith and repentance, their exemption from the Law's penalties, and their enjoyment of the Divine favour, participation in the Divine n11ture and life. and inherit&nce in the Divine and eterna.J. blessedness. Thus that which appeared the instrument of wrsth has been converted into the oooasion of salvation. ,er. 22.-Tlle cluli"".ti,rely C!hristian n"ghteom'MSS. The apostle ho.s clearly shown that rightoonsness by the Law is not possessed by men, and that in this way is no hope for the salntion of the human race. Such is the negative conclusion to which facts o.nd reason compel him. Yet it- is not his vocation to fre&eh a doctrine of despair. True, without righteousness there can be no salvation. 'Iherefore, if light is to be cast upon human darkness, it must come elsewhither than from the Law. So it is that St. P&ul preaches the ne"" and distinctively Christian righteousness, to be secured by conditions that may be fulfilled by men of every r&ee-iL righteousness that avails before God, &nd ensures the a.ccept.snce and the spiritual welfare and elevation of men. L THE CHARACTER A:!-'"D DESIG~ATION OF THIS RIGHTEOUSNESS: IT IS OF Gon, OB Drrn.--x. 1. It has its source in God. In this it is distinguished from the rectitude which is "by works; " that in a sense is of human origin. It is shown to be "of grace," i.e.. to be the provision of Divine favour, free and undeserved. And further, this expression, "of God," implies the perfection of this righteousness in comparison with all beside. 2. It is divinely adapted by God to man. There is presupposition of man's helplessness and dependence; it is presumed-which is indeed the fact-that man cannot work out a righteousness of his own. Hence there is a ground for this new ri!!hteowmess in a Divine provision of substitution. The apostle would be misunderatood were his teaching upon this point to be interpreted, as some have interpreted it, as representing God as indifferent to the person by whom suffering is endured and obedience rendered. Yet Christ, by his suffering the consequences of sin in this humanity and by his perfect obedience and holiness, has laid the foundation for the acquisition by man of the distinctively Christian righteousness. 3. It avails and is accep~able before God. According to the representations of the context, it consists in the remission of sins, and acquittal and accept&nce before the Divine tribunal, and in the manifestation of positive Divine approval; which may be regarded as the two parts of "justification." It is evident that such righteousness is imputed, and not inherent- & ~logical expression which mnst not, however, be interpreted to imply its unreality. Thus the Divinity of the Christian righteousness may be made apparent, as an object of ad.minltion and of aspiration. Il. THE lllE.AJ>S OF THE .A'I'l'.ilNXE:l."T OF THIS BIGHTEOUBNESB-THROUGH FAITH IN Jmms CmusT. In order to the fulfilment of this condition upon which the Christian right.eousness may be attained, there must be: 1. Belief in the Scripture testimony concerning Christ, that he is the Son of God and the appointed Saviour of mankind. This is indispensable; for faith is not a vague sentiment-it has an Object, and an Object which justifies and deserves it. Yet, though indispensable, this is not sufficient. There must be also: 2. Trust or confidence in Christ as a personal Saviour. Faith is not merely intellectual. assent; it is the consent of the heart and the will. It is capable of degree, and there is strong faith and weak faith. But the important point is that the soul, in the attitude and exercise of faith, is brought into personal relation with the buly Saviour. fil THE UNIVERSALITY OF THIB BIGHTEOUBNESS: IT IS UNTO .ALL, .AND UPON ALL, THEH THAT BELIEVE. The rectitude itself is a possession which men may share, whatever their natior:.ality, their condition in life, their individual history. And the condition. of its attainment is equally universal! there is nothing in faith w~ich li!Ili.ts ~te exercise to any special members, or any section of the human race. entries.content:
-Tlte dijfkulties of Dwim revelation, Jewish '1/A'/,belief, and Divine fastir,e, TLe apostle, in the twu preceding chapters, has now tihown that both Jews and Gentilot lltlwd er-' the &a.me platform 118 regards their need of a Saviour, Both are alike eiml.en

in God'e eight. The Gentile, who hae not the Law, if he does by nature the things contained in the Law, will be justified before God. " Shall not his uncircumcisir,n be oounted for circumcision?" (eh. ii. 14, 26). The Jew's circumcision will profit him If it be e. religion that affects the heart aud the spirit (eh. ii. 29). St. Paul, s,, quick to see the bearings of every etatemcnt, noticee at once that a difficulty naturaliy ari.BP,e hero, and he is prompt to meet it. "What advantage, then, bath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision?" I. Tmi: DIVINE REVELATION A GREAT PRIVILEGE. Notwithstanding all that had been said a.bout the sins and shortcomings of the Jews, the Jews were still a privileae<l people. Nothing could ever destroy the fa.et that th~y were the chosen people 0f G~, the people chosen to be the channel of God's revelation to the world by the patriarchs a.nd lawgivers and prophets, chosen also to be the channel through which the Divine Word become flesh and tabemacled among men-" of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came." The chief privilege which Paul mentiona here was that "unto them were committed the oracles of God" (ver. 2). It is an advantage to have a Divine revelation entrusted to us. The possession and knowledge of God's Word is a privilege not to be despised or lightly esw.med. There are degrees of nearness to the kingdom of God. While the gospel is" the power of God unto salvation t,o every one that believeth," while there are such events as sudden conversions, yet there are some who are in a more favourable condition for receiving the gospel than others. St. Paul, though he was suddenly converted, had a long and thorough training previously in the Word of God. The scribe who came to Christ, and whom the Saviour pronounced to be " not far from the kingdom of God," was one who had a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures, and who had been living a life of obedience to the Law of God. Such men were certainly more likely to be influenced by the personal power of Christ than those who had no previous knowledge of Divine truth. God works by miracles; but his ordinary method is to work by means. In these days of sensational evangelism it is well that we should not undervalue the importance of a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures. Paul wrote to Timothy, "From a child thou hast known the Holy Scri::,tures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus." They who are well instructw. in the Holy Scriptures are, as a rule, more likely to become true and permanent Christians than those who, under the influence of sudden excitement or emotion, without any previous religious knowledge, profess their readiness to follow the banner of Jesus. There are e:i::ceptions, but this would seem to be the rule. And those who ar" so highly privileged incur a serious and solemn responsibility. If unto us a.re committed the oracles of God, if we have the Bible in our he.ads and its truths treasured up in our minds, terrible indeed will be our guilt if we disobey its precepts, reject its invitations, and neglect its warnings. "To whom much is given, of them shall much be required." II. DIVINE FAITHFULNESS NOT AFFECTED BY HUllAN UNBELIEF. "For what if some did not believti? shaff their unbelief make the faith of God of none effect? God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar; e.s it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, u.nd mightest overcome when thou art judged" (vers. 3, 4). The promises of God will be fulfilled, even though there are some who do not believe on them. The Law of God will assert its claims, even though there are some who repudiate them. It will not save men from the punishment of their sin that they did not believe God's Word when it says, "Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also ree.p." Gorl'sfaiehfulness is not affected by the u11'belief of his ow11 peopl"-- Some persons a.rgue against the Bible because of the unbelief of those who proi"e$S to regard it as their guide. They nrgue against Christianity because of the inconsistencies of its professors. The argument is false. Christianity is to be judged by its own teachings and spirit, and not by the imperfect way iu which even its profo:,sors have received nnd prnctisccl them. Christianity is the !if~ and teachiu~ of Jesus Christ, combined with tho influence of his doi\th upon tho cross. No incousistt>ucy of profess- ing followers can over me.r the beauty aud sinlessness of that perfrct Eirnmple. No unbelief can ever do away with the inhereut power that is in the cross of Jesus to l!lwa ■inners. The preaching of the cross is to them tba.t perish foolishness; but to thtilll that are saved it is the power of God and the wisdom of God. III. DIVINm J'DBTIOE 1B NOT AFFEOTED BY THE CONSEQ'DENC&S OF H'DlUN illN. "Bu& 90 THE EPISTLE OF PAut TO THE ROMANS. [ort, rn. 1-81 '

if our unright.eommM! commend the rlghtoousness of God, what she.II we eo.y? Is God unri~hteous who ta.keth vengeo.nce? (I speak &Sa man.) God forbid: for then h0w ~h11.ll God judge the world?" (vers. 5, 6). 1. God judges not consequences, but c:harocler. He looks at the heart and at the motives. The Jews' unbelief we.a over- ruled by God for his own wise and gracious purposes. He brought good out of evil, But that did not ma'k:e their unbelief the less guilty. In the eyes of the lo.w, the guilt of ll fraudulent person is not always estimated by the consequenoes of his acts. A man may forge his employer's signature to cheques; but the employer may receive rmrh information as will enable him to stop the cheques in time, and prevent the loss which would otherwise ha'l""e resulted. But the forp:er's guilt is not diminished because the con11e4uences of his acts have been overruled. The law is not considered unfair or unrighteous if it punishes him, though his employer may not have suffered one penny of pecuniary loss. And even though the criminal's conduct served in some way to bring out more clearly the integrity or kindness of his employer, yet even this would not be regarded as any mitigating circumstance in his guilt. So it is right that I should still be judged as a sinner, even though the truth of God hath abounded through my lie unto his glory (ver. 7). 2. Man is not ;'u.stified in using sinful means to gain a good end. From the fact that God overrules sinful actions for his own glory and the good of humanity, it might appear to be a natural inference that it matters not what the morality of the action itself is so long as its object or result is good. "Let us do evil, that good may come" (ver. 8). Stated in this broad way, the immorality of the principle is apparent. And yet it is a principle which is too commonly acted upon. If you oppose some method of raising money for religions or charitable purposes, you will be constantly told, "Oh! it is for a good purpose." That is, simply, it does not matter 1ww you get the money so as you get it. It does not matter what the means are so long as the end is good. Now, it :is time that the Christian Church and Christian teachers should set themselves resolutely against such demoralizing ideas. How can the Christian Church rebuke the dishonest practices too common in the commercial world, money-making by unfair or questionable methods, so long as its own hands are not clean, so long as almost any method of making money is considered justifiable if it is in connection with a Church bazaar? The end does not justify the means. Let us not do evil, that good may come.-C. H. L

entries.title: ROM 3:9–18
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Total depra'IJity of kuman nature. Here we have a dark picture of human nature in its fallen and unregenerate state. (The Bible view of human nature is more fully enlarged on below, on vere. 21-26.) Here the apostle, as it were, calls up before him the different parts of human nature, and obtains from each of them an admission and an evidence of the moral corruption with which they are tainted. "My C01l8Cienoe bath a thousand several tongue&, And every tongue brings in a different tale, ; And every tale convicts me for a villain. All several sins, all UBed in each degree, Throng to the bar, crying all-Guilty I guilty I" L A DEPBAVED m:ABT. "There is no fea.r of God before their eyes" (ver. 18). There ill no motive-power to regulate the life. There is no reverence for God's Law within their Bpirit. There is no fear of offending the great Judge. There is no filial fear of grieving the heavenly Father. The conscience and heart have become seared and blunted. Remove the fear of God from heart and conscience, and what influence remains to check evil pusions and to reset the insidious allurements of temptation? " The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom ; and to depart from evil is understanding." II. A. DEPB.AVED trliDEBBTABDDTG. "There is none that understandeth" (ver. 11). It is fashionable in some circles to speak as if it was a sign of weak intellect to be a Christian, to believe in the Bible, or to regard with reverence the Law of God. Yet lllll!uredly it may be claimed without any presumption or prejudice that there has been at lc:a.st as much of the world's best intellect arrayed on the side of Ohristlanity u Oil die aide of ite opponeot.e. If there be credulity &Dywhere, there ia credulit7 dlapla7ecl C!J. ur.1-31.J TllE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TRE ROMANS 91

In o.ccopting o.s scientific truthR what very often are pure speculations. If there is weakness anywhere, it would seem to be in disregarding the ~idence in nature that points to o. greo.t persono.l and inte1ligent First Cause, or the evidence in history that point• to a wise nod overruling Providence. "The fool bath said in bit, heart, There is no God." It is sin, o.nd not godliness, that is the evidence of a weak and depraved unrlorstnnding. III. A DEPRAVED WILL, "There is none that eeeketh aftu God" (ver. 11). Nowhere is the depravity of human nature more painfully shown than in the exercise of the human will. How many deliberately choose evil rather than good I How many, with the experience of others to warn them, deliberately choose impurity rather than purity, intemperance rather than temperance I Life and death are put before them, yet they deliberately choose death. 'l'bey reject the highest ideal of character, and follow poor and weak and wicked examples. 'fhey reject the inspiring hope of heaven and immortality, and only live for worldly pleasure or for worldly gain. They reject the fountain of living water, and seek out for themselves broken cisterns that can hold no water. To all such God appeals, in mercy, to make a. right exercise of their wilL "Turn ye, turn ye; for why will ye die?" IV. DEPRAVED SPEECH. 1. Untruthfulness. "With their tongue. they have nsed deceit" (ver. 13). Truth is essential to the well-being and happiness of society, to the very existence of commercial dealings. Yet how many there are who "use deceit• as a means of obtaining advantage or profit in hasineSl!, as a means of obtaining some desirable object of their ambition! We have society deceitfulness, commercial deceitfulness, political deceitfulness. Against all such deceit the Bible sets itself. "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour; for we are members one of another." 2. Slander. "The poison of asps is under their lips" (ver.13). The sin of evil-speaking is a very widespread one, and it hardly receives sufficient discouragement from Christian people. Men and women who would shrink from doing their neighbour a bodily injury, who would be shocked at the idea of taking his property dishonestly, think it no harm to injure his character and reputation. "The poison of asps is under their lips." "0 my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united." 3. Profanity. "Whose mouth is full of cursing" (ver. 14). Here is a widespread evil of the present day. Everywhere one bee.re the profane use of the sacred Name. Just as the suicide act.a "As if the Everlasting had not fixed His oanon 'go.inst self-slaughter," the profane person nets as if it had not been written with the finger of God, "The Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his Name in vain." V. DEPRAVED LIFE. "Their feet are swi~ to shed blood: destruction and misery are in their ways: and the way of peace have they not known" (vers. 15-17). What a sad but true description of human life in its unregenerate and unchristianized condition I It is but the ordinary picture of what heathen nations were before the gospel entered into them. And where large communities throw off the restraints of religion, is it not what may be witnessed still, even in professedly Christian nations? Where there is no fear of the Law of God, there will be little fear of the law of man. Let the heart and conscience be godless ; let the reason and understanding fail to respond to the claims of the Divine Being and of his moral Law; let the will cease to be influenced by heavenly and upward motives; let men in their common speech be accustomed to speak lightly of sacred things and of their neighbour's character and reputation; and the step is but a short one to the disregard of human life and the disregard of human virtue. The nation that ceases to be influenced by the fear of God has entered on the broad way to its own corruption and decay.-O. H. I.

-" No difference." The Bible presents us with three pictures of man's condition and oharo.oter. They are very different, and yet they are all true pictures. There is the pioturo of man before the Fall, ll.'l he walked with God in primeval innocence of heart and sinless purity of life. There is the picture of man after the Fall, with the Divine imnge marred nnd stnined by sin. And then there is the picture of man renewed agnin-man o.n object of Divine mercy, man a subject of Divine grace, ma.n prepared 91 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [CH, m, 1-81.

for 11haring once more the Divine glory, Two of these views of huma.n na.turo concern man as he is now. The one humbles, the other exalts him. On the one hand, me.n is put before us as he is by nature-fallen, sinful, lost. On the oiher ha.nd, he is put before m: as ON w1U1ts him to be, and RB God has done all he can to make him- pa.rdoned sinner, a holy character, 11.Il heir of everlasting life. These two views are brought t('E---ether in these V8M!8. 'l'he apostle speaks of the righteousness of God whioh is by faith (\f Jesus Christ unto all ana upon all thl'm that believe (vers. 21, 22). And then he adds, as a 1'81L.'IOn for this broad, all-embracing statement, "1:t~or there is no differenoe: for all ha\""e sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (vers. 22, 23). 'l'here is no difference as t.o the fact of universal sin. Aud there is no difference as to the fact of univers&l mercy : " Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (ver. 24). There is no difference as to the need of salvation. There is no difference in the way of salation. Christ is the Saviour of all men who come to him in faith. L THERE IS NO DIFFERENCE IN THB FACT OF UNIVERSAL GUILT. .. All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." This is not a mere cynical statement. The Bible is not a cynie&l book. It does not look down with contempt upon human nature. But it deals with facts as they are. And yet, if it speaks of human nature as sinful, it is in t.enns of pity and compassion and desire to save. You will often meet with cynical viewl! of human nature. You will meet some who will tell you that all men are equally bad, or that one man is as good as another. You will meet some who will sneer at the idea of virtue, or unselfishness, or honesty being found in any one. They will tell you that no such thing exists. They will tell you that selfishness is the ruling principle of human nature, and that, if men or women are honest, or virtuous, or charitable, it is because it is their interest to be so. Now, it will generally be found that those who speak thus of hnman nature have not a very high moral character of their own. They judge others from their own standpoint. They look at everything from a selfish point of view, and they think that every one else does the same. But this is not the way in which the Bible speaks of hnman nature. It paints it very black, it is true-because it paintE it in it.s true colours. But it speaks of human nature as it is, not to depreciate it, but to elevate it. :Moreover, it allows for the good that is in human nature. It meetB human nature half-way. It recognizes that there is sometimes even in the most fallen nature a d.emre for bett.er things. It represents the f,OOr prodigal e.s coming to himself and saying, "I will arise, and go to my Father.' Jesus says," Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." The Bible is no cynical book. And yet it ays tha.t .. all have sinned." This does not mean that all are equally bad, that all have committed sins of the deepest dye. But it does mean just what is said, that all haf1tl sinned-that there is sin in some degree in all, sin enough to condemn, to destroy. How humbling this is to human pride I And this was just how the apostle meant it. His whole desire in these opening chapters of Romans is to show the need of a. Saviour, of a perfect righteousness. He first of all showed that the heathen needed a righteousness. Then, tnrning to the Jews, whom he knew so well, he saw at once their selfrighteons spirit. They made their boast in the Law, and yet all the while they were transgressors of the Law. And so he proves that both Jews and Gentiles are all under sin (ver. 9). "For there is no difference: for all have sinned." It is amazing to see how one professing Christian can look down upon another, just because the other is of a humbler class in society or wears a poorer dress, when, if they were true Christians, they would remember that they are all sinners saved by grace. Yes; the Bible is a. very democratic book. It teaches that God hath made of one blood all nations of men to dwell upon the face of the earth. It teaches that the rich and poor meet together, and that God is the M.aker of them all But it does not, like many democratic leaders, give the people a false idea of themselves. It does not say, as I once beard a poP,ular speaker say in Gwgow, that" the democracy is always wise and true and just.' It plaets all men upon a common platform, as sinners in the sight of God. It says, "'17.ere i6 r.o dijferenC£: for all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." IL 'fHEllE 18 NO lJlfl'EllESCE IN THE OFFE!l OF UNIVEnBAL MEl!OY. "Deing justified fr1xly by Lis grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." It is when wo corr.1: iv look at the cr06s of Jesus that we can see how God looks at human nature. lt WIIB certainly no depreciation of human nature that call80d the Son of God to como oe. m, 1-31.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO 'fllE ROMANS. 93

nnd dio upon the oroBB. It we.e no deeire to depreciate hume.n natnre that caured God to give "hie only begotten Son, that whoeoever believeth on him 11hould not perish, but hove everlasting life." Ah no I When we speak of the depravity of human nature, of the fnll of man, of universe.I guilt and sinfulness, some persons would char"e us with taldng low viewe of hume.n nature. They are Bible views, at any rate; and the cross of Jesus shows ue the.t, if God looke upon human nature as fallen, he dr,es not loDk upon it with contempt. No I He looks upon it with infinite compassion. He looks npon it with redeeming love. He looks upon it, helpless, sinful, fallen; and as he ]r,c,ks, he stretches down the hand of mercy to save, to save for ever! On the porch of an old house in England is this inscription cut in stone, "De:;r;tram Cl.ldenti p;rr¾Jo" (" I stretch out my right hand to him that is falling"). That is just what God does. He stretchee out the strong he.nd of mercy, and not only to him that is falling, but to him the.t is fallen. He does not exclude the proflige.te, or there would have been no place in the kingdom of heaven for St. Augustine or John Newton. He does not offer salvation only to his friends, or where would the Apostle Paul have been? There is no difference. "Whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely." How, then, is this, the.t the guilty sinner is an object of Divine mercy? He is guilty, and yet God not merely pardons, but justifies him, declares him just. "Being justified freely by hi.3 grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (ver. 24). It is on account of what Jesus did and suffered that the sinner is accepted in God's sight. This is to be remembered, that Jesus not only bore our punishment (which one human being might do for another), but he bore our gui1t. "The Lord bath laid on him the iniquity of us all." It is thus that the sinner is looked upon as jnstified in God's sight. Thus God's righteousness is shown: "That he might be just, and the Justifier of him which believeth in Jesus" (ver. 26) . .And hence there is no difference. It i:! no merit in man, no penances, no good works of his own, that obtain his justification, his aalvation. It is free grace. It is the righteousness that is in Jesus Christ. What large-hearted charity, what universe.I brotherhood of Christians, this large view of God's universal mercy ought to teach us I "The same Lord over e.11 is rich unto e.11 that call upon him." How this view of the universal mercy, the universal love of God, should break down all narrow views of creed and party and class ! The day is long in coming, but surely, under the influence of this Christian gospel, it will come at last- "When man to man, the world o'er, She.11 brithers be for a' that." Yet it is to be observed that there is a grw.l differe:na in man's treatment of thia universal offer of mercy. Some accept the mesa&ge. The goodne.ss of God leads them to repentance. The love of Christ melts their hearts. Some reject this m~ae. They put it away from them. They neglect it. They are too much occupied with other things-with pleasure, money-making, and the like. Now, this difference in the Wll.Y ln which men receive the offer of salvation will make a vast difference in their condition throughout eternity. How could it be otherwise? If Christ died to save those who take him as their Saviour, it must be a sad but stern reality that those who do not believe on him must perish. There is no difference in the universal guilt. There is no difference in God's universal offer of bis mercy. But there is a difference in man's treatment of this offer. And there will be an awful difference throughout eternity. -0.H. I. Vere. 27-31 (with Jas. ii. 24).-Faith and works. One of the most fruitful sources of disoussion and strife among Christians has· been the selection of particular p&.SS&,,<>'88 of Scripture 11nd building doctrines upon them, without at all considering what other pe.ssages of Scripture ml\y h11ve to say on the same subject. Truth is many-sided. 'fwo views, which o.ppelU' contrndictory, may both be right. 'l'here may be an element of truth in both; 11nd they may both be different sides of the same truth. The statements of Po.ul and James on the subject of justification are an instance of this. They appear at first sight contmdictory, but they o.re in reality two sides of the same great truth. This great truth is justification by J1JSus Ohrist. One side of this truth is found in the words of St. Pl\ul, " A man is justified by- faith without the deeds of the La.w" (vor. 28); that is to say, faith in Jesus Christ is 1ufficient to justify a man in 94c THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. God'f!. sight. That ie very true, says James, but let us be sure that we have a real faith. '!'here is no real faith except works go along with it. Thus James brings out 1w side of the truth: "Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only." It is the exa~eration of this latter truth that mainly divides the Roman Catholic Church from the t'rotest:.ant Church as a whole. This exaggeration was the immediate origin of the Reformation. Instead of teaching men to put their faith in Christ, the Church of Rome taught them to place their confidence in their own good works. By the performance of certain penances and mortifications merit wae laid up for them in heaven. By the payment of certain sums of money absolution was obtained for past sins. Clearly this was very far from being the teaching of Scripture. Then Martin Luther arose, and, in words that soon rang throughout all Europe, proclaimed the doctrine of justification by faith. It was time that a check should be placed on the progress of error; that men should be taught to rest their hopes of salvation no longer on a prieet, on works of merit, or on sums of money, but on the Lord Jesus Christ. On the other hand, the doctrine of justification by faith bas been so much insisted on that there has sometimes been a neglect of good works. This error has not been committed by any Protestant Church a.s a whole, in its formal teaching at any rate, for all the reformed Churches have insisted on the neoessity of good works and a holy life as the elidence and fruit of true faith. But there has been sometimes an undue attention to beliefs combined with an undue neglect of practice. It is a well-known fact that very often the persons who are most dogmatic in their assertion of certain doctrines, and most fierce in their denunciation of those who differ from them, are among the most irreligious and most godless persons in their parish. With them the belief is everything; the practice is nothing. But this is not Christianity. To believe certain doctrines is not true faith. If the life is not changed, it matters little what we believe. When a man says that he believes in Christ, meaning that he believes certain doctrines about him, and is confident that therefore he is justified and safe for ever, while at the same time he lives in the practice of sin, that man's justification is very doubtful. It is important to keep before us the twofold meaning and influence of the doctrine of justification. L TBB TEACHING OF Sr. PAUL. "A man is justified by faith without the deeds of the Law." We are to remember that Paul, in this Epistle, was writiug to a Church largely composed of Christians of a Jewish origin. Ju the Christian Church at Rome there was, consequently, a considerable tendency to magnify the importance of good work:&--& tendency which was fostered by Judaizing teachers. It is easy to see, from many expressions in the Epistle, that Paul has Jewish Christians largely in his mind. He speaks, for instance, of" Abraham our father;" he deals with positions which were peculia.rly Jewish-as, for instance, the necessity of circumcision, and the exclusion of the Gentiles from the Church of God. "Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not al.so of the Gentiles?" (ver. 29). It was natural, therefore, for the apostle to lay t,peeial emphasis on the necessity for faith in Christ. He wants to show that something more than good works was needed for jnstifica.tion. Abraham, it is true, was a good man ; but the works he did would not have saved him, were it not for the faith that he exhibited. " Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousnesa.., We cannot be jwitified by our own deeds, says Paul, because our best deeds come far short of the standard of righteousness which the Law le.ye down. Our own deeds are powerless to justify us. We need the righteousness of Christ. If we take hold of that righteousness believingly, and trust in it, we are justified. We a.re ju11tified by faith is the clear teaching of the apostle. But does he therefore do away with good wo;b? Certainly not. Most forcibly he himself repudiates such an idea. " Do we then make void the Law through faith?" he asks (ver. 81). "God forbid: yeo, we establish the Law." That is to say, the necessity for good works, for holy life, is Btill &B great. as ever. So, also, in the sixth chapter he protests against the idea that any one who professed faith in Christ should continue in sin. If we are made free from the guilt of sin, because we have believed on Christ, then we have become the servants of righteoUBneu (eh. vL 18). In the eighth chapter he brings out ev<ln more fully the duty of holy life. We are not to res~ con!,cnt in the ~su~an~o ihat there i~ no cun- demw.tion to 111. There mWlt be active life. 'l'he spmt 1s hfo because of righLeous- .Qell• &lid through the Spirit we Ill.Wit mortify the deeds of tho body, Henco we see on. m.1-81,] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROM.ANS. 95

that, by the faith which leads to jW1titication, the apostle plainly means only such faitl! as directly results in good works. True jWltification implies sanctification. II. Tm1 TEACHING OJI' BT, JAMES, "Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only." From what we have seen of Paul's teaching, it is clear that this statement, which at first sight appeared to contradict it, is really in harmony with it. 'l'he teaching of James ie, in fact, the complement of the teach- ing of Paul. Wha~ St. Paul brings out in the ~ixth and eigh~h chapters of Romans, namely, the necessity of good works as the evidence and fruit of faith, that is the purport of the whole Epistle of St. Jamee. James, noticing the inconsistency which prevailed in his time, and which still prevails in the Christian Chnrch, between the profession of many Christians and their daily conduct., especially in regard to other 3 , in very clear and forcible language calls attention to the necessary connection of faith with practice. A faith which does not influence practice is useless. It is dead. Such faith cannot save a man. It may be so.id that Abraham was justified by faith. That ie true, But was his faith a mere belief in a particular doctrine, such as the mere belief in the existence of a God? No. Even the devils believe that; but it brings them no confidence, but rather fear. Something more than that is necessary, if we a.re to be sure that we have true faith, and that we are therefore justified. We must act, And so Abraham's faith was a faith that included action. He offered Isaac his son upon the altar. Thus by works was faith made perfect. In this sense it is evident that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only (Jas. ii. 14-26). To sum up: Paul shows the uselessness ef works without faith; Jama shows tM uselessness of faith without works. Both are agreed that Christ alone can deliver; us from the condemnation which our sins deserve. Both a.re agreed that he who is truly conscious of this salvation will stri7e against sin; that he who believes that Christ. can save him from the guilt of sin must believe also that Christ can save him from its power in his heart. Both are equally strong in insisting upon tee uselessness of profession without practice. The two sides of this great truth both need to be strongly emphasized in our own day. On the one hand, the necessity for a living, personal faith in Jesus Christ alone, needs to be emphasized in opposition to the substitution of forms and ceremonies for the gospel. And, on the other hand, the necessity for a life of practical godliness needs to be emphasized where there is so much of barren profession-orthodox belief, but fruitless and sometimes careless life.--C. -Redemption working rightelYl/,BneBB. A whole system of theology is corn pacted into these few words. The keystone of the arch. We have here-redemption. righteousness, ' L REDEMPTION, The redemption centres in Christ; it touches on either side God e.nd man. Originating in the purposes of God, and actualized in the work of Christ., it is approprie.ted in the consciousness of man. These verses deal with one e.spect of Christ's work and of man's salvation-justification through Christ's atoning sacrifice. Hence we have-God's grace, Christ's se.crifice, man's faith. 1. Uod', graa. (Ver. 24.) This is the fountain-head, whence all salvation issues. Importance of holding forth this truth ; not that God loves us because Christ died, but that Christ died because God loved us. So John iii. 16. And yet the error has some element of truth. It was God's compassionate love which prompted the bestowal of the gift, and the " setting forth" of the Propitiation (ver. 25); but only when the girt has been received, and the propitiation me.de ours through faith, does God, can God, love with an intimate, complacent love. First the pitying Father, then the forgiving Father, and then the reconciled, rejoicing Father. 2. Christ's sacrifice, (Ver. 25.) We are in the presence of a mystery, which we may not analyze too closely. In Christ, God and man are one, and therefore the ee.crifice of Christ represents a sacrifice of God and a sacrifice of man. In him, man expiates his own sin; in him, the Infinite Love stoops and suffers and dies. It wae a real atonement of the race; it was a real atonement for the race; and what God hath joined we may not put asunder. 3. Man's faith. (Vers. 22, 25, 26.) To reduce it to its simplest, ultimate form, it is but the acceptance of what God gives, of what can only come to us from without, ape.rt from any efforts of our own (ver. 21), "freely" (ver. 24). And such faith is virtually included in true penitence-the penitence of the "poor in spirit;" and, we doubt not, such true penitence is therefore virtually in possession of the pardon which hovers round every repentant heart. But, for a. consciousness of pardon, there is required a conscious faith, i.e. an intelligent, glad acceptance of the gift of God in Christ. And the more vivid and realistic the conscionsness of faith-or, may we say, the more strong e.nd energetic the laying hold of life?- the stronger and more joyous will be the experience of salvation, and the resultant love for God through Christ. II. RIGHTEOUSNESS. Redemption e.nd righteousness are not at variance, but rather redemption is the great instrumentality whereby the righteousness of God works the righteousness of man. 1. Man's righteOU$MSS. Man's righteousness is wronght by the redemption of Christ, and therefore it is all Divine (vers. 21, 22). And yet it is truly man's, The righteousness which is expressly spoken of here is a relative, not e.n actual, righteousness; i.e. a condition of acquittal in presence of Le.w and ju~"'I!lent.
