entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Vi.e joy of tribulation. Paul has taught us that peace, nay glorying, may be ours, though this be a world of trial. He now teaches that we may glory in the very trials themselves. And this teaching he enforces by a chain of arguments. In other words, he taught in the previous verses that we are conquerors; now he teaches that we are "more than conquerors." L TRIBULATION WOBXETH PATIENCE. No character can be truly formed without the opportunity of endurance; we must learn to resist. Tribulation affords this opportunity ; it calls us to resist. II. PATIENCE WOBKETII PROBATION. Or, as the word means literally, "triedness." We must be as the genuine metal, which rings true. This can only be, in the case of character, as we have become true, III. PROBATION WOBKBTII HOPE, Triedness works hope in a double sense: the tested strength we have warrants confidence; and past triumphs are pledges of future. So a veteran soldier, by reason of victories that he has won, and because he is a veteran, looks forward to future victory. IV. HOPE PUTTETII NOT TO SIIAME, The hope of victories to come is merged in the great hope of the crowning victory, the standing approved in God's presence at last. But shall this be? Axe we not most unfit for such a presence? And may we not, therefore, when we confront him at last, confront his wrath? So would our hopes belie themselves, and by them we should be put to shame I Nay, but this =not be. For is not all the spiritual education, upon which partly we build our hope, an education of God? Does not he mercifully suffer tribulation to befall us, that we may endure? and that, enduring, we may be approved ? and that, being approved, we may have hope? This hope is of him. But, beyond all this, does not he himself now a._ssure us of his love? Is it not shown to us by the Spirit, which searcheth all thin,,,~ yea, the deep things of God? Nay, is it not transfused through all our nature, "shed abroad" by th«r Spirit given to us? Yes, truly, all our consciousness pulsates with the assurance of the tender mercy of our God ; all the voices of our experience say to us," God loves you." And Cl\n such a hope be put to shame? Never, while God's Word lasts I God is eduoo.ting us ; but in and through ell, and above all, God loves us ! Let us hold fo.st to this blossed fact. While yielding to the discipline, let us at the same time hold his hand, and be strong in hie mighty love.-'1'. F. L. Vora. ~.-The gr«JI love. entries.content: -T/u, reign of death. The summing up of this first divi~;on of the Epistle: Christ has undone what sin bas done, as regards our objective relation tQ God. In these three verses-Sin through one works death to all. I. Sm WORKING DEATH. "Death" a word with many meanings in Serii,t,,re. Dissolution of complex nature; corruption of spiritual nature; and final abandonment by God, Here the first. An objective punishment of an objective trans~e55ion; a manifest sentence of condemnation. Hence symbolic of condemnation itself, showing forth God's wrath. May well lead thoughts to death that mUBt reign in the inner man, through the withdrawal of God's favour-a spiritual paralysis. Also might well be premonitory of the total casting-off. Such, then, the triple death-condemnation, helplessness, and the culmination of both in the hereafter. .And thi., the dea.tb which "entered into the world" through sin. IL DEATH REIGNING OVER ALL. Bat this sin the sin of one. How, then, the universal death? Look around-death, death, death I Yes, might answer, because sin, sin, sin I True ; but carry thought back to time anterior to Law. Death still ! And no sin then such as Adam's was, such as yours is--so conscious, so deliberate. There was the presence and working of sin, indeed, but the working was the spontaneous working of a corrupt nature. Ko law, and therefore, strictly, no transgression. Argument might be reinforced by similar consideration of heathen now, and infants : death reigns I So, then, the death even of those who have the Law is not on account of their individual transgressions of the Law, but most be traced to the same canse as operates in the case of those who have "not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression.n III. THE SIN OF ONE THE BIN OF ALL, Therefore, if death be an objective pWJishment for an objective offence, it can be for none other's than his offence who first trallilgressed God's manifested will. .And therefore, if the condemnation be imputed to all, the sin was imputed to all. Or, in other words, in him "all sinned n (ver. 12). The marvellous solidarity of all things-species, genus, world, system, universe. So in respect of mankind, and the spiritual history of mankind: the act of one, the act of all. So, then, all rest under a shadow-the shadow cast by Aaam's sin! All bear a. brand -the brand of his punishment I Where is the path from darkness into light? Justification through Christ I Can this be coextensive in its range with the results of sin? Is there a. solidarity here also? Yes:; for Adam was "a figure of him that was io come." We have another Head, a second Adaml-T. F. L.

He saw the needs of hie creatures, pitied their forlorn wretchednees, woul,l shelter them from the storm, and lavish on them proofs of kindness. Peace reigns there a sense of blissful security, Every article of furniture, every picture on the walls,'every robe worn, every meal provided, speaks of Divine mercy, of a changed attitude towards those received within the sacred precincts. It i, a permanent home, which we enter to go out no more for ever, Grace alters not, is not fickle ; therefore "we stand " (abide) therein without fear of one day losing our situation from the arbitrariness of the Master. Il, THE GATE OF ENTRANCE. "Through onr Lord Jesus Christ." He is " the Door of the sheep," a living Way to the holiest of all. He is our in trod action(" acce.~s ") to the court of the King. His work of mercy and righteousness has availed to procure free entry into the inheritance. The cherubim and flaming sword no longer bar the way to the Paradise of God. Man's own moral power availed naught to force a way into the temple. He could make no breach in the walls of governmental justice. III. 'l'HE ONLY PASSPORT REQUIRED. "By faith" we enter into this state of grace. The inquiry at the gate is, "Dost thou believe on the Son of God?" To trust in Christ is to feel the longing for a renewed heart, for Divine forgiveness, and to recognize in him" the Way, the Truth, and the Life." Scepticism may keep men at a distance, unbelief may tum the back upon the mansion, timid doubt may remain gazing wistfully at the portico, but the believer is impelled to march humbly yet fearlessly through the appointed entrance into the halls of light and song, IV. THE JOY OF THE INMATES. They are filled with exultation because of their present condition; they are already encompassed with so many marks of Divine favour. They are constantly finding new beauties in the construction of the rooms, and new evidences of Divine skill, forethought, and love. But they know that this ii! but the foretaste of further bliss; they triumph in the expectatfon of roming glory. They have the promise and many a sign of a fuller revealing of the character and purpose of God. He comes nearer to his guests, till at last the veil of sense shall be removed, and e,ery occupant of the palace be e..iwrapped in the radiance of his throne. All the dust of the journey to the home, every vestige of defilement, vanishes from the pilgrims crowned with the brightness of God's heavenly presence.-S. R. A.

entries.title: ROM 5:3–5
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-THlndation made subsidiary to hope. Trouble is usually considered antagonistic to joy. A ready objection might occur, therefore, to the apostle's declaration of Christian rejoicing. How was this possible, seeing the many hardships to which the profession of Christianity exposed its votaries? The text refutes such an objection. I. THE CHRISTIAN FACTORY, Tribulation is God's method of disciplining his people. Sin having entered the world, bringing sorrow in its train, the very afflictions of life are forced by Divine grace to contribute to the improvement of those who undergo it religiously. This was evident in Old Testament times, but is still more visible under tho dispensation of the Spirit, where chief stress is laid upon graces of character. The faith of the Christian is the material on which the machinery of trouble operates. spinning out of it the thread of patience. In the school of trouble are the meaning and the mercy of pain leo.rnt; only those who ho.ve experienced opposition have been taught true resigno.tion to God's will, content not to hurry events or to quarrel with them, but confidently to awo.it his time and issue. With the threads of patience is wo,en the cloth of probation. He who continues steadfast in the will of God proves for himself the truth of the promises, the accuracy of the Divine forecasts, and the success of the Divine methods. The long succession of days nnd nights produces its gl:\d ho.r,est, when the fruits of patience attest that not in vain did the sower sow. .And the mill of God's training ceo.ses not its work, till out of probation is constructed thd beaut[f11l garment of liope, in which the Christian is gloriously arrnyed. \\'hnt can ho do who ho.s tested tho faithfulness of God, but entertain unshaken confidt•nce respecting all that yet awaits him? we look through the things seen t.o the unseen and eternal can we welcome trouble as working out a weight of glory, and it loses its fearsome aspect, 2. 'l'hen tribulation must have the Christian spirit to work upon, or its results may be disastrous. Not every substance will pass unlrnrmed through the wheels and rollers, the spindles and l'hutt-ll's. It. may be t-0rn in the proces,,, or reduced to pulp, '!'rouble does not necessarily improve the world~v minded. Instead of softening, it may harden the heart l the man may become peevish and morose, soured by disappointment. a. And the Christian may dread the allurement of prosperity more than the endurance of hardship, '!'he chilling blast causes the traveller to wrap his cloak the closer around him; it is the hc~t which leads to throwing off his !(&Xment. '!'roubles drive us to the appointed Refuge; in our joys we are like Hannibal's soldiers at Cannre, relaxing the bonds of vigilance and soberness. Times of persecution have often proved an invigorating, l>rscing season t-0 the Church. Perhaps the hope of future glory appears more lustrous and enviable when in contrast with present danger. IL THE VALUE OF 'IRE PRODUCT. Hope is cheerful, like the light wherewith God decks himself and adorns the landscape. Hope is the eye of the soul; its clearness and brightness tell of good heslth. But the point on which the apostle here insists is the reliabk cAaracJer of Christian hope. It is a robe of which the wearer will never have cause to be ashamed. It suits the wearer. There hn.s been an inward preparation for the outward adornment. God's love has been diffused through his breast. Assured that he is a beloved child, the anticipation of bliss and perfection is an appropriate vesture for his peaceful, happy spirit. The man excluded from the wedding-feast because of an unsuitable dress showed thereby that his heart was not right; pride or obstinacy had rejected the garment freely offered. The w<>rlcmanship of the robe displays the same graci.ous <iesi,gn that has filled the heart already with assurances of reconciling, redeemi'Tl.g love. The Spirit showing to the believer the things of Christ reveals· the character and purpose of God, and the hope of glory is recognized as corresponding in every particular to this experience of the wondrous love of God. • It is a durable garment, not flimsy iD texture, looking well for a season, then suddenly giving way. The hope of IDAny is like a palace of ice, glittering, but yielding to the rays of increasing light, or like a torch extinguished by the wind of death. But this hope, amid every change of circumstance, shall subsist in undecaying, yea, growing, splendour. -S. R.A.

entries.title: ROM 5:19
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Ruin and redemption. By itself the first clanse expresses a fact of deepest gloom. It calls attention to the prevalence of sin and death. The history of the world is traced in darkest colours. We see the race from Adam till now marching to the grave, with the taint of corruption upon all. We are confronted by that profound mystery, the existence of moral evil, with its widespread, deep-seated effects. The possibility of man made upright and free yielding to temptation does not em.au..st the explanation of the actual Fall. And when the Scriptures point to the influence of an external agent, the serpent, employed to bring a.bout the downfall of the first pair, the pall of mystery is not removed; its comer is lifted a little that we may see how our difficulties relate to questionings concerning the origin and continuance of evil in beings superior to man. This appears to be God's mode of dealing with us. Enongh is said to allow faith a foothold, not enough to place the whole territory at our fuposnl. Instead of unlocking the house of previous being and inviting us to its darkened halls, to explore for ourselves the tragedy with which our own world-tragedy is connocted, the Scriptures point to a Sun that has risen to shine upon our moral firmament, and bid us note its blissful tendencies, kindling fresh life and beauty, arresting decay, reviving hope, attesting the interest of the Almighty in his creatures, 11nd showing that the permission of evil is not to be ascribed to any lack of Divine love. The subject of sin c11nnot be beneficinlly studied unless combined with the antidote which the wisdom and affection of the Most High have provided. Fllith may wa.er as it contemplates the inroads made by sin upon the intelligence and happines..<: of the human family, and faith must be strengthened by meditation on the remedinl work of Christ. Do you wonder at the transmission of contagion from generation to generation, at the long-drawn-out penalty of the race? and does the law seem inequitable that lays many of the nets of the guilty as a burden on the shoulders of the innocent? 'l'hen notice the operntion of the same law in redemption, where the Son of God sheds his blood to save sinners, and observe how from him is perpetu.'\ted tb~ blossing of pence and godliness. Separate the two hemispheres, and the mind l'<it:Lm1es 11, proy to chilling doubts and oppressive fears; unite them, and hope asserts its bc~e~cent vivifying power. Whilst we declare in am!IZemont, "How unsc:uclmb!,, aro his Judgments, and his w11ys p11st finding ontl" we can udd, "'l'o whom be glory for over;" "Just 11nd truo 1iro thy w11ys, thou King of saints." The npostlc assumes the truth of the story in Genesis. He proves the universality of sin hy a reference t-0 the fact that all have died, showing that even the ancients prior to 1.foses must have tranS!!ressed some Jaw, and so incurred the penalty for disobedience. The principle of heredity confirms the truth of the doctrine that our progenitors have transmitted a Titiated nature t-0 their descendants. Jesus, the second Adam, is the Head or a new race, to whom he imparts a new ,birth, with its issue sanctification. By the m<Xiil of his flawless obedience, and by the grace which flows into us from that spring of obedience, the curse is removed from believers, and righteousness is imputed and imparted. III. THE COMPARISON OF THE :t,."'Ul,{])ERS INFLUENCED. Thie passage should enlarge our estimate of the kingdom of the saved. In each case it is "the many" who are affected. The obedience of Christ is sufficient as a meritorious cause to justify the whole world, though only those who " receive the Word" are consciously gladdened and sanctified the.reby. No man is condemned on account of Adam's transgression; it is his O'Wll disobedience t.o the written or innate law which determines his sentence. The millions -who have died in infancy are redeemed by Christ; multitudes in the Jewish and heathen world were saved by virtue of his atonement, though not explicitly revealed to them, and the Apostle John saw in heaven a number beyond the arithmetic of earth to calcnlate.-S. We saw in last chapter how Abraham was JUStified by faith alone, and how his case really covers olll"B, The promise of blessing througe a seed. which Abraham believed so implicitly, has been fulfilled in Christ. We accordingly believe in the faithful Promiser who raised up Jesus from the dead, 11Dd we regard his death and resurrection as being a deliverance to death for our offences, and a deliverance from death for our justification. Faith enables us to draw the assnrance of our justification from the resurrection or our Saviour. But now we pass under the guidance of the apostle to the consideration of the delightful state into which the justified come. And here we notice- L THE .A.SS'D'B.ANCE THAT WE ABE THE OBJEOTS OF THE DIVINE LOVE. (Vere. 1-5.) By nature and by reason of our sin we are the objects of God's righteous wrath; but when we are enabled t.o believe in a Saviour who died for us and rose again we find ourselve11 passing out of the condemned condition into an assurance of God'; love. And the apostle here gives us the stages in the blessed process. 1. We pass into a state of peace with God,. We prefer the indicative (lxoµu,) adopted in the Authorized Version to the subjunctive (tx"'µ.,,) adopted by the Revised Version after W eetcott and Hort. For the state of peace is not some uncertainty into which we may come, but it is a et.ate which results from justification if it has really taken pla.ce. ,ve cease from war, we are no longer enemies, we have entered into a state of peace. The believer as he calmly meditates on the atoning work of Jesus Christ, sees that he Las bt,en Jed' thereby out of the storm into the calm, out of war into peace. Enmity is over and peace ie proclaimed. 2. We realize that (Jhrist conducts us into a ,tanding in grace. By hie gracioue mediation we pass into a new relation to God ; we realize that we are justified, as believers, from all things from which we could not be justified hy the Law of Mosee. We can now stand before God, and realize our pardon and acceptance in the Beloved. 3. We are cnauled to rejoice in hope of God's heavenly 9lory. For the justified condition into which we have come through Christ is intended tu reach through the present life and issue in the glory of the life to come. It ia no men: temporary frame of mind, but a permanent Htate, into which our Saviour he.a Lrou"ht us. 4. We are enabled to profit by life's tribulations. So much is thi~ the cai;e "'that we are enabled to congratulaw our11elvcH upon (1t1iux~µ,81i) our tribulatioue; ou. v.1-21,] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMAN8. 158

for through these we reach the power of patient endurance (r,,,.oµwf,), and through the power of patient endurance we reach experience (5o,uµ.~, which means the rmdt af the probation, as well as tbe "probation" itself, and the former gives here, notwithetandin.,. the Revisers, the better sense); land through experience we reach hope-the hope of heavenly glory, since as its earnest there ie shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost a consciousness that we are the objects of the Divine love. The hope can never be disappointed. We have a " present heaven" in our happy assurance of God's love. We have passed out of the gloom into the gladness, and beyond us and awaiting ns there lies the glory. Thus our tribulations conduct us to assurances of Divine love such ae we could not otherwise enjoy. II. THE NATURAL mBTOBY OJ!' TB& DIVINE LOVE. (Vere. 6-10.) The apostle, to confirm believers in the assurance of God's love, proceeds to exhibit its history. 1. And he shows its sovereign character. That is to say, it was when we were without strength, when we were helpless and hopeless in our guilt, that God gave love's greatest proof in Christ dying for the ungodly. It was, therefore, no reason in us, bnt solely the exercise of God's sovereign love, which led to the death of Jesus for the ungodly. 2. The death of Jesus is the great dem<>nstratiM of Gorl's me. Men have occasionally sacrificed their lives for good men, never for a merely just one; but God in Christ sacrificed his life for those who are yet sinners. No mightier demonstration of Divine love can be imagined than this dying of God's Son for sinners. And it is well here to notice that as a" trinitarian transaction," as Shedd has happily put it, God in Christ's death exhibits "hie own love" (Revised Version). Through the unity of Father and Son in the Divine essence, the death of Jesns is really the self-sacrifice of God. It is, therefore, the most marvellous of all exhibitions of love. 3. The re.mrredi<m-life of Jesus is the great guarantee of our salvation from Divine 'IDTaih. Jesus died to secure our justification. We are justified by his blood. In this God ha.s reconciled us to himself. The resurrection of Jesus is accordingly the proof that God is satisfied with his own self-sacrifice in Jesus Christ, and so his wrath is turned a.way from us through the spectacle of a risen Saviour. "The highest form of love," says Shedd. "that, namely, of self-sacrifice, prompts the triune God to satisfy his own justice, in the room and place of the sinner who has incurred the penalty of jnstice. In the work of vicarious e.tonemeut, God himself is both the offended and the propitiating party. Thie i~ taught in 2 Cor. v. 18, 'God hath reconciled ns to himself;' CoL i. 20, 'To reconcile all things to himself.' God, in the Person of Jesus Christ, is Judge, Priest, e.nd Sacrifice, all in one Being. The common objections to the doctrine of the propitiation of the Divine anger rest upon the unitarinn idea. of the Deity. According to this view, which denies personal distinctions in the essence, God, if propitiated, most be propitillted by another being than God. Christ is merely a creature. The influence of the atonement upon God is, therefore, a foreign influence from the sphere of the finite. But, according to the trinitarian idea of the Supreme Being, it is God who propitiates God. Both the oiigin e.nd the influence of the atonement are persona.I, and not foreign, to the Deity. The transaction is wholly in the Divine Essence. The satisfaction of justice, or the propitiation of anger (whichever terms be employed, and both a.re employed in Scripture) is required by God, and made by God." It is a risen Saviour, living and reigning, who saves us from fear of Divine wrath and assures us of acceptance. III. Joy TIIROUGB RECEIVING TB& RECONCILIATION. (Ver. 11.) Now, when we appreciate God's wondrous love in providing n reconcilintiou, then we receive it by faith, and find ourselves constrained to rejoice in God who could so provide for us. Moreover, it is clear from the term "received" ( llt..dfJoµ..,,) that the "reconciliation" (itcz'Talt..lt..a-r¾,) ie not something paid by the sinner, but something divinely provided which he.a to be ncoepted. It is an additional obligation imposed, not a price pa.id. God is so regal ns to "reconcile himself," nnd then ask us to receive the benefit thereot: We ought to rejoice in such n God. Verily his thoughts are not our thoughts, nor his ways our wnys. The justified hM·e every reason to be joyful in their King.-R. M. E. Vore. 12-21.-R';llresentative responsibility. In ll\st section we saw the blesse.i ate.to into whioh the JUstified boliovor comes-I\ state of pence, of gmcious acceptance. See Shedd, ,n loo. 154 TIIE EPIBTLE OF PA.UL TO 'l'HE ROM.ic\.NB. or glorious hope, of joy in God. 'l'he apostle in the present section expounds the relation in which mankind stands to the two grel\t representatives, A.dBm and Christ. We CRI1not do better than com1ider these two roprcsontl\tives in the order named, and bow they are related to the race. I. Tm:_ Fms! ADAM AS REPRESEl>'"TATIVE OJ.I'_ 'l'1IE RAOE. Now, the Bpostle distinctly declares m this p&..-.sage that death entered into our world through one man's sin. The one man in his sin must, therefore, have been acting for the race; and it is for us to get a clear view of his representative position. Now, the usual mistake made in this subjeot is in supposing that representatives· must be voluntarily selected by those they represent. This is not always the case. A representative may occupy his position of wecessity. This was t-he ca.."8 with our first pa.rent. The human race is not made up of a number of independent un.its, but of a series of dependent generations. Conse- quently, as first parent, Adam was in the very nature of the case representative of the race. "The unrea.«oning :flippancy," says an able writer, "with which some object to their responsibility for the act of Adam, because they had no part in choosing him as their representative, shows singular want of thought and of discriminating observation of the settled order of God's providence. It is evident that when God himself directly institutes a social organization, he always appoints, either by special act or by an invariable natural order, the ruling and representative head . . . . The unity of the human race is his own immediate institution, and be appointed Adam its ancestor to be its representative and federal head. And in this case also he rendered an elective appointment by man impossible, by the constitution which brought man into being in successive generations. Not having from the beginning contemporaneous existence, consenta.neous action was impossible. Their unity, therefore, was made to depend upon a common head and upon his representative action. . . . The constitution of nature and the course of providence render it a matter of social justice that one generation sh.a.l.1 bind the succeeding, however remote, for good or evil. All legislation and all government proceeds upon this principle, and cannot avoid it. The evil entailed upon the race has come upon us by the selfsame principle, and its repudiation is impossible without the violation of the moral order upon which the stability of society depends. Our responsible relation to the first sin of Adam in no way depends upon our consent to his appointment-as our covenant bead, any more than our responsible relation to the D&tional debt of Great Britain is affected by the fact that it was contracted without our personal consent, and before we were born." 1 It will be found also that Adam's parental authority carries with it the idea of kingship; he was in a regal as well as representative position; be had dominion not only over the creatures, but also over his own post.erity. His acts were consequently of a regal and representative character, Carrying these necesrary principles with us, we can see how his sin in eating the for- bidden fni,it W(]Jl II representative act. In this the race was represented, by it the race was bound; he was actini: in his representative capacity, and there is no good gained by repudiating it. But, further, we can understand in some measure how a sin like Adam's affected his constitution, so that he became with his wife tainted, and so transmitkd the sin to succeeding generations. The death of infants is the positive proof that the race has been treated as a.n organic unity, and that the taint of ein has been transmitt.t:d by ordinary generation. The whole subject of "heredity," as now scier,tifically treated., bears upon this relation of Adam to his posterity. It is evident that the generations have been linked ea.eh to each. Representative responsibility has been in operation from the first. Instead of quarrelling with the arrangement, our duty ia to recognize it, and to see how out of the same principle we may receive bl-ing u a glorious set-off to the curse which has been transmitted to us. IL THE sWOND A.DAM .A8 REPBESENTATIVJ~ OF THE JUSTIFIED. We have seon how the first Adam was COWltituted the representative of the race, and by his sin involved tbe whole race in tre,pase and condemnation. Death passed unto all men, for that all i11 him have eim-.ed. But now the apoBtle showa ue the glorious set-off to this inheritance of guilt and death. God has given a new Representative to the raoe, even .TesW! Chriat his Son. By bis obedience the representative principle ie transmuted into an organ of 6,ra.ce ir,st<:ad of an organ of condemnation. But let us carefully note tltu i.ature of t1e relati,,n S<,t up between us and Christ. And here let u1 observe: 1. ' C!. Wallace'•• Ilepreaentative Re1ponlibility,' pp. 40-42. clt. \It, 1-23.] 'fHE EPISTLE O:F PAUL TO TRE ROMANS.

While Wll arll united to the first Adam by ordinary gemraUon, we get united, tlJ the second Adam by regeneration. Tho first union is iuvoluntary; we cannot determir.e who our parents shall be. But union to Christ partakes or a voluntary character. When tho Spirit is received and regenerates us, he makes WI willing in the day of his power. Freedom of the will he.s its place in the relation into which we enter towards the second Adam. We rne.y reject the union or close with it. Hence the whole race Is not necessarily embraced in Christ's vicarious work, simply because the whole race will not be. All will not come to Jesus that they mav have life (,John v. 40). 2. Jesus proposes to quench the fire, not only qf original sin, but also of actual sin, in tho~ who receive Ms grace. This is the apostolic idea in this passage. The arran"'ement might have been to checkmate merely the original sin; that is, to put the ra~ upon e.s good e. platform as our first parent occupied before the Fall. Christ's obedience might thus he.ve been the mere equivalent for Adam's disobedience. But the free gift of justification through Christ embraces our actual sins as well as our original sin. Grace is thWI seen to abound. All sin in which we have been involved get3 cancelled and put away through the obedience of our Representative. And: 3. Jesus propose8 not only to counteract the sin, but also to secure a reign of grace unto eternal, life. The abounding grace of the second Adam rai8es its recipients into an eternal life in the favour and society of God. Thua is it that the representative principle provides the most magnificent compensation for all that it entails through onr first parent's fall. If we by faith are united to the second Adam, then we get the benefit of his obedience; his endure.nee of the penalty we deserved is accepted as ours; his perfect obedience to the requirements of the Divine Law is imputed to us; and his gracious Spirit come:; to abide within us. 'l'he result is the.t the grace so a.bounds as to overmaster the sin and to raise us into that fellowship with God which is life eternal The second Adam thus more the.n redeems us from our relation to the first Adam. IIL THE ADMINISTRATION OF GRACE THROUGH JESUS CBJIJ.ST llliKES Alll'LE COll- PENBATION FOR ALL APPARENT ANOMALIES IN THE PREVIOUS COVENANT. Now, one of t)le facts referred to by the apostle in this passage is, on the admission of almost all the commentators, the death of infants in consequence of their relation to Adam. It may, of course, be said that these infants were in the loins of Adam when he sinned, as Levi was in the loins of Abraham when he paid tithes to Melchizedek. Still, the fe.te of infants would seem an anomaly in the government of Gud. if they are to receive no compensation through relation to the second Adam. But if it is scriptural to believe the.t all infants who die because of their relation to the first Adam inherit everlasting life because of their relation to the second Adam, then all harshness disappears and the anomaly is overborne. Now, this is, as we believe, the proper doctrine. .All who dio iu infancy are, through the all-a.bounding grace of the second Adam, saved. We need he.ve no fears for them, wherever they have passed a.way. Their suffering unto death is a cheap price to pay for exemption from the temptations of the present world; aud each of them in the glory will accept the painful passa~e to it as, after all, a. merciful arrangement, seeing that glory lay beyond it.-R. M. E.

entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The meaning of (Jhrist's 'l'esurredion. The prominent position occupied by the resurrection of our Lord in the apostolic wri~as and preaching need occasion no surprise ; an event in itself so wonderful, and in its consequences so momentous, could not but be constantly in the minds and upon the lips of those to whom it was the supreme revelation of God. It may be well to gather up in a. few sentences the import and significance of this central fact of Christianity. J. .As A FA.OT, THE BESORBECTION OF ClmIST RAS A GENERAL ..U.--0 WO&LD-WIDB INTEREST. The historian of humanity, the philosopher reflecting upon the most impol'tant factors in huma.n life, is constrained to acknowledge the central and universal interest of our Lord's rising from the dead. 1. It was a fulfilment of predictions, and a realization of hopes sometimes dim and sometimes bright. 2. It starting-point of the Christian religion. The existence of the Church of Christ is the = Jnly to be explained by remembering how firmly the first promulgators of the new faith held the belief that their Lord had risen from the dead. 3. It was, in the view of the Christian community, the pledge of the general resurrection of &11 men to another life; it gave definiteness and power to the belief in persoMI immortality. !I. .As A DOCTRINE, THE RESUIUIEOTION 011' CHRIST HAS A SPECIAL CimlsTI.L.'I' INTEREST. 1. It is the chief external evidence of the Messiahship and Divinity of Jesus of Nazareth. It WIIS in fulfilment of his own e::i:press declarations that, aft-er enduring a death of violence, he rose victorious from the gro.ve. His resurrection is in hnrmony with his claim to a nature and character altogether unique. 2. !t is the seal of the efficacy of his mediatorial sufferings. However the humiliation and sacrifice of the Redeemer were related to the forgiveness and justification of men, it is certain that Christ's rising from the dead was the completio.n of his redemptive undel'taking on man's behalf. JU. As A POWER, TBE RESURRECTION OF CHRIST HAS A PEBSONAL AND SPIRITUAL INTEREST. This is the aspect of this great fact which is insisted upon mosi strenuously in this passage, and its praoticl\l import.a.nee to every individual Christian is manifest. The true believer in Christ shares in his Lord's resurrection. 1. Our sins were crucified in Christ's death upon tho oross, and in his resurrection we were delivered from their power. 2. Our past sinful life became dead to us as Christ died; and our newness of life began in his rising from the tomb. We have the sign of this, the apostle teaches us, in baptism, with its teaching regarding renewal and consecration. 3. By our faith in the rt•surrection of our Saviour, we are raised above trial, doubt, tempt.'1.tion, darknoss, and fear. '!'he cross tells us tlmt it mo.y consist with the wisdom aud the goodnoss of God tho.t for a season we should endure trouble, disappoiutruent, and lltleming faibre. But tho empty tolllb as~ures us that for e,;exy good w:1u aud fo, 164- THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [err. vt.1-28.

e'l"ery good ~-ork there is a resurrection appointed. Death is for I\ senson ; God's people csunot be "holden of it." The corn of wheat dies, but it dies to live, and to bring forth much fruit. 4-. In Christ's resurrection the Ohristinu is begotten to a living hope of an immortal inheritance. His people are appointed to share his triumph and his glory. , er. 4-.-" Nt1V1MSS qf l(fe:" a Neu, Year', sermon. Things new and old make up ~e sum of human experiences. All that is new becomes old, and the old disappears to come before us a,,,aa.in in new combinations, in new shapes. The mind of man seems to have a natural leaning in both directions; we like the old because it is old, and the new because it is new. This is one of the contradictions inseparable from human nature. There is some truth in the common saying that the young prefor novelty and the aged cling to "use and wont." It is easy to see how, to the youthful, change should be welcome, for their knowledge is yet very limited, and new experiences are the appoint.ad means of furnishing and equipping the mind. It is less easy to explain the conserratism of age and its dread of innovation, for experience must have taught the old how imperfect is e'l"erything that concerns man's culture and condition ; this trait of character may be largely owing to the increasing feebleness which indisposes to the unwanted exertion of the faculties, or to accommodation to new circumstances. True religion takes advantage of both these tendencies of human nature. It appeals to the natural att.achment we feel to what is ancient and sanctioned by prolonged existence ; and it appeals also to the yearning for progress and for fresh experiences, which we all either have felt in the past or feel to-day. But observe in what way revelation makes use of these natural tendencies, and remark the harmony there is between the moral necessities of man and the Divine communications of Scripture. Broadly speaking, whatever concerns God is commended by its antiquity and unchangea.bleness; whilst that which refeni to man approaches us with the cha.rm and the allurement of no'l"elty. A moment's reflection will show us why this should be so with true religion. Man, in his brief life, with his feeble purposes and his petty achievements, looks away from himself for the et.ernal and the unchanging. Thie he knows is not in himself or in his race ; and he seeks it in the unseen God. And herein he is right. He does not seek these attributes in vain. For, knowing God, he knows that in him there is absolute being, unaffected by the changes to which all creation is subject. Man can find his true stability and his true peace only when he rest5 in the care and love of "the Father of lights, who is without variableness and shadow of turning." But, on the other hand, man, when he knows himself, is aware that his past has been a past unsatisfactory to himself, and blamable by his Creator and Judge. His changes have often been from evil to evil; and he looks forward, mther than behind him, for relief. His only hope is in hie future. The old he can regard only with pain, with regret, with distress. If there is improvement, it must bt: in what is new-in a new condition, new impulses, new principles of the soul, in new associations and new help. Accordingly, Christianity comes to man with gifts of heavenly newness in her hand. Christianity establishes with man a "new covenant," and gives to him a "new commandment;" makes of him a "new cre11tion," traDSfoI'IDJ! him into a "new man." It opens up to him a" new way" unto the Father by the Mediator of a" new testament," gives him a "new name,'' and teaches him a "new song," and inspires him with the hope of a "new heaven and a new earth." In short, it enables him to serve in "newness of spirit," and to walk in "newness of life." "Life" is, in the New Testament, used as equivalent to the history of the spiritual nature. The Lord J eeua professed to be " the Life," " the Life of men ; " he came that "we might have life, and that more abundantly," and the acceptance of him as the Divin.e Saviour is deeignat.ed the "passing from death unto life." Thle being understood, it will not be auppaied that by "newness of life " the Apostle Paul refers to the life of the body, or to the outward circumstances ln which physical life may be passed. And yet the context ahowe that he is not treating of the future and blessed life in the nearer presence of God. Accordingly, we understand by "newness of life" that which contrasts with the spiritual deadnese which hung as a cloud of darkness over heathen humanity, and which contrasts also with the earlier and imperfect developments of spiritual vitality. It is a newness of life which is peculiar to the Ohristian diupensa- till. VI. 1-23,] 'l'llE EPIS'l'LE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS.

tion, but is yet found wherever Christ is known, trusted, and loved. We greet the new Y?ar _with gladness and with hope, becallll? it seems_ to offer us the opportrmity to begm hfe anew. We are thankful for the relief of leavmg the past behind and we oheri~h the hope that ea.eh new year will ~e .one o! greater spiritual pro~ess and happmees than the years that are past. Chnstians wish to forget the thinus that are behmd, and to reaoh forth to those things that are before. Some who have been u!ldec~de~ as to their course ba~e resolved wjth the new year to make a. fres~ beginwng m bfe, and henceforth to live by the faith of the Son of God, and to his service and glory. The subject ought, therefore, to be appropriate and welcome to such as are hopefully and prayerfully aspiring unto "newness of life." I. The newness of the Christian life will appear from the consideration that it is A LIFE IN CHRIST, This very language must be at first unintelligible to a. person unacquainted with the gospel. That life should be in a person seems monstroUB and meaningless. Yet Christ himself has said," Abide in me, and I in yon;" and bis Apostle Paul has taught us that "if any man be in Ohri.st, he is a new creation." Christ is the Basis upon which the Christian builds, the Foundation of the edifice of his new and higher life. Christ is the Vine-stem into which the Christian is grafted, and from which he draws all his vitality, his vigour, and his fruitfulness. Christ is the Head, in dependence upon whom the Christian is a living, active, and obedient member. The signs and evidences of this life are these : 1. The renewed man learns who Christ is, and what Christ has done and suffered for him. 2. The renewed man admits the claim Christ has upon his gratitude, his faith, his love ; and trusts in him. 3. The renewed man consciously accepts life as the gift of God in Christ. 4. The renewed man, by maintaining fellowship with Christ, advances in the new and higher life. IL The newness of the Christian life is manifest from THE AGENCY DY WHICH rr D EFFECTED, 1. A spiritual agency. 2. A Divine agency. 3. A / reely acting and gracious agency, 4. • A transforming agency. 5. A ceaseless and progressiue agency. IIL The newness of the Christian life is displayed in THE MOTIVES AND l'lllNCIPLES BY WHICH IT IS GOVERNED. 1. 'fhe love of Christ revealed and responded to is the motive power of this life. 2. The law of Christ becomes a law of friendship. 3. The approval of Christ is an animating and cheering power in the heart. 4. Thus self and the world, the common motives to action, fall into their proper place, or are banished from the Christian's soul. IV. NEW ASSOCIATIONS are a feature of the Christian's new life. V. The Christian life tends and points to A FURTHER AND HIGHER REGE!iERATIOB m THE FUTURE. Al'PLIOATION, Newness of life depends comparatively little upon outward circumstances. There is nothing in the colour of a man's skin, the climate of a man's birthplace, the nature of a man's occupation, his condition whether of poverty or wealth, hie education whether scanty or liberal, his age or his station,-there is nothing in rul these things which can interfere with or hinder him from becoming a new = Christ. Does it seem to any one that for him this is an impossibility, because of the in unfavourable circumstances in which he finds himself? Disabuse yourself of this illusion, for illusion it is. It may not be within your power to become a learned man, or an eloquent mnn, a rich man, or a powerful man ; but the circumstances which may prevent you from becoming learned or wealthy, mighty or persuasive, have no furce to hinder you from becoming "a new man." 'l'he obstacles to this renewal a.re to be sought within, not without; they are to be found in the will, which is often resolved to resist the authority, to reject the truth, and to ignore the love of God. If you take a eavnge from his native woods, olothe him in civilized attire, place him in n lordly palace, surround him with books nnd with music, with paintings and with flowers. does he cease to be a sl\vl\ge? Not until the mind is chl\Dged, The nrnn himself may remain the same, whilst all his surroundin~s are altered. These external ch:rnges do not ml\ko of him a now man, l\nd his lifo hM not in virtue of them becl>tue a new life. So is it with man in relntion to tho kino-dom of Christ. Deprivo a hmn,m being of the liborty which he h~s abused, ~move him from his evil c?ru~iouships, s~ut _out !rom him the temptations to wh1oh ho hns been wont to yield, mtroduco h,.n mto 166 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL 'l'O THE ROMANS. [on. vr.1-23.

ChriMian eociety, constrain him to frequent the means of religious instruction; yet his life ha!! not thereby become a new Jifo. The old nature is still there, 'l'he Ethiopian has not changed his skin, nor the leopard his spots. The man's true life lies in the bent of his thoughts, the affections of hie heart, the bias of his will; and whilst all these are toward evil, the old nature is supreme, and the new life is not yet. Love is the one only potentate at whose master-bidding old things will pass away. Before's Love's wizard wand alone, tha ancient shadows will depart from the gloomy cave of the unregenerated soul, and that cave will become a temple peopled with the forms of the holy, and echoing with the songs of heaven. Divine love can make the wilderness a paradise, can change each thorn into a flower, and all the thistles into fruits. When Love smites the rock, the spring of health and of refreshing will gush forth. He who hears Love's voice shall forget the weakness and the weariness of the pilgrimage; and his footst.ep, erst so heavy and so dull, shall bound elastic onwards.

-1?ie ~fronchisement by ~ The Law, by exhibiting the heinousness of sin and its awful consequences, was the occasion of the introduction of the gospel and of the nctories of God's grace. If, then, where sin abounds, grace much more abounds., some sophistical reasoner may propose to continue in sin. It is against this wret.ched argument that the apostle appeals in the language of the text. '' Sin •shall not have dominion over you; for ye are not under law, but under grace." The very fact which was adduced by some as an excuse for sin is shown to be the chief reason for freedom from sin. L Sm HAS HAD, .U."D BAS, :MASTERY OVER :MEN, Sinners are under the rule and bondage of a tynmnical and wicked lord. 'l'urning away in a rebellious spirit from their rightfnl King and Ruler, they have submitted themselves to the usurper's sway. Sin takes possession of their affections, their judgment, and their will. Il. Ul!IDER TEE LA.w, MEN WERE COMMONLY AND HABITUALLY UNDER THE MASTERY OF SIN. By the Law, the apostle means chiefly the Jewish Law; yet not this exclusively; for it appears that the unwritten law generally is intended in the argument of the Epistle. 'l'hey were "under the Law" who lived under legal ordinances and sanctions, and who, in theory at all events, acknowledged its claim. Sin to them was transgression, and the motive for avoiding transgression was the fear of penalty to be inflicted by the Lawgiver end Judge. Now, it is urged that those tmder the Law were in very many cases the slaves of sin; for the Law entered that the offence might abound. History, sacred and profane, bears out these assertions. The stB.ndard of morality by which men judged themselves was low, and even to this they did not generally approiwh, much less attain. This was so with the Jews, and more conspicnowtly with the Gentiles. ill JT IB TBE EFFECT OF TEE DISPENSATION OF GRAOE TO BET :MEN FREE FROM '1'IIE llA.6TEBY oF sm. L What is it to be " under grace"? It is voluntarily and consciously to receive the free favour of God bestowed through Jesus Christ upon all who believe. It is to participate in the new and distinctively Christian righteousness. It iB in the exercise of faith to be brought into harmony with God's government and purposes. It is to come under the influence of a new, Divine, and powerful motive, furnished by the infinite love and clemency of God. 2. How does being "under grace" Bet and keep a man free from sin ? The apostle explains the process by employing three figures. According to the first, by baptism, the initiative act of faith and consecration, the Chrilltian is joined to his Saviour in his death upon the cross, ar,d, thW! being united to an almighty Saviour, must consequently rlee in the likeness of his resurrection to a new and holy life. Acoording to the second, the Christian, fol'l!ak.ing the service of sin, yields himself by faith to the service of Christ, and la therefore bound to fulfil the obligations which he has undertaken. The third figure repreaentl hie atate under the Law ae abolished by fa.Ith In Christ, just as a woman ie releaaed from her hW!band by his death; fidelity to Christ's service and law are o.s binding upon the Chri.Btlan as 1B fidelity to her second husband ~n ~he part o~ tho newly married woman. Duty and love combine to render the obhge.t10n to hohue~s ltringent and effective. IV. 'IBE POWER OF GB.ACE EXCEEDS THE POWER OF THE LAW. In explaining how ibis is we may obee"e: 1. 'l'he principles appealed to are hlgher; love and gratitudo OIL vr. 1-23.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 167

are high~r. than fear and interest. 2. The aid afforded i~ ~ea~; it is the aid of the Holy Bpmt of God, 3. 'l'he example set before the Chnstum lB more stimulating and inspiring, 4. The prospects presented are more alluring and glorioua.

entries.title: ROM 6:17
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content: -The mould of (Jhristi(1111, doctri'M. The Christian, in remembering what he wo.s, deepens his impression of Divine grace, to which he owes it that the change has been eftected in which he now rejoices. St. Paul took a peculiar satisfaction in reviewing his own experience, and acknowledging his indebtedness to that Divine grace which had fashioned his character a.new. And if the Christian will consider the state in which he would have been apart from the supernatural doctrine and influences of Christianity, he will see reason for gratitude in the provision made for the transformation and renewal of his character. In this verse the change is attributed, instrumentally, to the power of Christian doctrine, which is, as it were, a pattern by which be is reconstructed, or a mould into which the metal of his nature has been cast, in order to its taking a new and divinely ordered shape and form. J. THE CHRISTIAN DOCTRINE 18 .AS A. MOULD PREP.A.BED IN OBDEB TO GIVE A :l.-ZW SHAPE A.ND FORM TO THE HUM.AN CHABACTEB. When iron is "cast," it is run, in a liquid state, into a shape or mould of earth or sand of the desired form ; and thus the artificer produces a bolt or a cannon. Thus, in the intellectual and spiritual realm, ideas govern men ; and the character and life are largely owing to the thoughts wbich are familiar and congenial. And Christian doctrine is not an end, but a means; the righteousness and love of God, revealed in Christ, having power to reconstruct the character and to renew the life. The doctrine is alive with the power of the Holy Spirit of God. II. THE CHRISTIAN DISOIPLE IS CAST INTO THIS BPIBITUA.L MOULD, TH.AT HE MAY TAKE ITS NEW SHA.PE A.ND FOBM. The old elements of human nature, old errors and _old sins, are dissolved and melted down when brought into contact with the gospel of .Jesus Christ. Old things pass away, in order that all things may become new. We may fancy tbe.t the doctrine is delivered unto us, to do what we like with it; bnt tbe reverse is the case. We are delivered unto it, in order that it may do its work upon us. So it is with the Christian education of the young, and with the evangelization of the heathen. The mould of Christian doctrine imparts to him who is brought into living contact with it a new motive to holiness, in the redeeming and sacrificial love of the Saviour; a new rule of holiness, in his law and life ; and new help tow:i.rds holiness, in the provision of the Spirit's help and grace. A moral transfiguration is _effected, e.s the natural result of intelligent acceptance and voluntary allegiance. For if faith is the soul of obedience, obedience is the body of faith. There is no change so wonderful and so admirable as the.t which is wrought in human character by Uie .moulding power of Christian doctrine.

entries.title: ROM 6:1–14
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The practical power of the Rssurrection. Here the apostle enlarges still more fully upon the truth that the Christian's foit.h lends not merely to the pardon of sin, but also to deliverance from its power. Beco.use grace has abounded over sin, o.nd our unrighteousness has commended the righteousness of God, it does not therefore ,follow that we nre to continue in sin. If we he.ve a real union with Obrist, we have been baptized into his denth. We are buried with him by baptism into death ; " that .like as Ohrist wo.s rnieod from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so wo also 11honld wo.lk in newness of life" (ver. 4). I. THE FA.or OF THE RESURREOTION. Tbnt the rosurrection of Christ is surrounded with mystery, no one will deny. But the evidence by which the great central fact itself is established is so strong, Bo olenr, BO decisive, that even sccpticislll has some- times to ndmit itseH convinced. 'l'he effect of the most able an,l ad,·en,o criticislll hns only I.icon to ostnblish moro nud more ocrtaiuly the fact of tho Hesurrectiou, and , thus to co11finn rnoro strongly the Chrislit\li's faith. It is remarkable tb:\t two of the, greatest rntionnlists of tho prcsont century, who doubted nllllost every fact of tho New _l'estt1ment history, admitted thnt tho Hesurrectivu wn.. o. fact whidi they could u,-1 168 THE EPISTLE 011' PAUL TO TllE ItOAIANS. [oit. vt.1-23,

doubt.. Ewald, who dMl.s destructively with most of the gospel inoidents, "regarding 110me III mythic&l, some 11.S admitting of a rationalistic interpretation, e.nd some 11.8 combining the elements of both," is unable to destroy or explain away tho Resurreotion. "Rejecting all attempts to explain it, he accepts the great fact of the Resurrection on the e'l"idence of history, and declares that DOthilllg am be more historical." The testimony of De Wette is even more remarkable. He was more sceptical than Ewald; so much so that he was called "The Univel'l&l Doubter." Nevertheless, such is the force of the evidence, that this great rationalistic critic, in his last work, published in 1848, said that the fact of the Resurrection, although a darkness which cannot be dissipated rests on the way and manner of it, cannot itself be called in question any more than the historical certainty of the &SS&SSination of Julius Cmsar. 1. The/act of CM ~ is attest.ea by the four evangelists. The four Gospels were written by men widely separated both in time and place. Their very variations are a proof of their substantial truth. They give varying accounts of the Resurrection, as would naturally be expected from men whom so great an event impressed in different ways, but they all agree in testifying that the event occurred. 2. The narrative of the Besurrecti,on was accepted by the e.arly Christians who lived at the time when the event took place. It is spoken of constantly in the Epistles to the various Churches as an event with which they were all familiar, and about which there was not the slightest doubt. When Peter is proposing the appointment of a successor to Judas, he speaks of the Resurrection as one of the great subjects of apostolic preaching. Indeed, it would appear that he regarded the preaching of the Resurrection as the great subject for which the apostle should be chosen. His words were, " Wherefor-e of these men who have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out amon,,"'St us, mnst one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection." 3. The cunflerS'ion of St. Patd, and his subsequent advocacy of the doctrine of the Resurrection, are perhaps ,he strongest proofs of its truth. Paul was a persecutor and a bigoted Pharisee. He suddenly became a member of the sect that was so hated and despised. The explanation that he himself gave of this change was that Jesus Christ had appeared unto him. It was not likely that Paul, a clear-headed man, accustomed to weigh evidence, would be deceived as to Christ's appearance. He could not be lightly led to take a step of such immense importance to his whole life. Something more than a mere dream or hallucination must be found to account for his whole subsequent career. He was not likely to undertake those missionary journeys through Asia Minor, through llacedonia., and through Greece, and to persevere in them, in the face of much opposition, ridicule, persecution, and many hardships and dangers, for the sake of a mere fancy. He was not a mere visionary or fanatic. His Epistles show him to have been a man of robust mind, great reasoning power, and soberness of judgm.ent. And yet, in every instance in which a public speech of his is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles; in his address at Antioch in Pisidia, in hie address at Athens, in his address to the multitude when he w-as ta.ken prisoner at Jerusalem; whether he is in the presence of the high priest, of Ft:l.i.x, or of Festus and .Agrippa, he most distinctly proclaims the fact of the resurrection of Christ. 4-. .AB the life of the Apostle Paul was changed, so the lives of all the apostles were changed from the moment that the risen Ghrist appe.ared to them. Before that they were timid and frightened. The boldest of them became so cowardly as to deny that he knew Christ at all. They had all forsaken him and fled when the time of crucifixion drew near. Christ has brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. He bas satisfied the yearning of the human heart for a life beyond the present-a yearning so strong that one of the greatest thinkers of our own time, though the logical conclusion of his system is universal death, nevertheless tries to avoid or overcome this dreary prospect by the suggestion that out of this death another life may spring. Our poet-laureate has expressed that yearning thus. Speaking of love, he says- " He seeks at last Upon the last and sharpest height Before the spirits fade away, Some landing-place, to clasp and say, 'Farewell I We lose ourselves in light I'" Yes, it is when the grave is near, it is when our loved ones are ruddenly taken from us by death, that we learn what a precieus truth the resurrection of Jesus is to rest on. -The two services and their rewards. In the closing part of the fifth chapter, and throughout this chapter, the apostle is contrasting the operation of two great principles. The one is tbe principle of sin; the other is the principle of righteousness. He compares them to two kings reigning in the world, controlling men's lives, and influencing men in certain directions and to certain actions. Sin reigns unto death. That has been its operation all through hum3,n history. But 3, new power has entered to dispute its influence. That power is the free grace of God, exhibited in Christ, God's Son. That power operates in righteousness. It provides a righteousness/or men by the blood of Christ. It produces a righteousness in men. "Where sin abounded, grace did much more abour..d: that as sin bath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord." And now in these immediate verses St. Paul is making an appeal to his readers. He has set beforo them the two great principles. He has contrasted them in their opero.tion and their results. Now he makes th4 matter persrmal. He enforces his appeal by the question of the sixteenth verse," Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey ; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?" And then be says, "As ye he1ve yielded your members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity; even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness" (ver, 19). I. EvEnY LIFK IS A SERVIOE OP' SOME SORT, 1, 8oTM are Slll'Va11ts of the love of money. Of money and how to make it they are always thinking; for the sake of it they will go through many risks and toils and hardships. Their first question about everything is, "Will it pay?" and all their money-gl'l\8ping does not pay them in the end. They may have much goods lnid up for m!\Ily years; they may have g,,od 1ecuritios for their investments; but they have made no provision for tht'ir imm,,rtal souls; thoy ho.ve laid up no tronsure that will be of use to them beyoud the grnve. God. 2. Som~ are servants of tM «we <if dress. Even in our Lord's t.ime, he found· It l1ecesAAry to wa.rn his hearers against thinking too much about their dress. Even Cliristi~n people, who profess t.o be the servants of Christ, are too frequently the servants of fashion. There is sometimes more attention given to the dress of our neighbours or of ourselves in the house of God than there is t.o the voice of our Creator and our Saviour, or than there is to the quest.ion whether we have the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, or the spotless robe of Christ's righteousness. It is said thnt St. Bernard of Cla.ir.-aux, who rebuked princes, and fired all Europe with a ne1v crusade, all the while living himself in utter poverty, used t.o ask himself every day the stern question, "Bernarda, ad quid venisti? "-" Berna,-d, wMt'ifore art thou here 1" So it would be well if we would ask ourselves more frequently what is the purpose of our lives. 3. Others, again, are tM servant.s of ambitwn. To be higher than their fellow-men, to be fawned upon and flattered, to receive the homage of the poor and the favour of the rich, to be talked about in the gossip of society,-that is the object for which many persons live. Yet, when attained, it brings no lasting peace or contentment to the mind. The praise of men, moreover, is a very fickle and uncertain thing. The hero of to-day will be forgotten to-morrow. Earthly fame has ever been- " Like a snow-flake on the river, A moment seen, then lost for ever." Such are some of the services to which men devote their thoughts, their time, their energies. How vain and profitless are they all ! Wben the hour of death draws nigh, let any one who has spent his life in the service of any of these masters ask them to help him in the death-struggle, to give him hope for the future: will they be able to give him any assistance? They cannot even keep his poor mortal body from the dust; much less can they give life to the soul They have already helped to produce death in the soul They have dragged him downwards to the earth. And eo it is that, when the soul must go from this world into the unseen, it is earthly still. There is no fitness for heaven in it at all The pleasures and possessions of the world, innocent in themselves, become positively harmful to many. 'l'hey become sinful to them, because they keep the soul away from God. II. THE SERVICE OF SIN AND ITS RESULTS. Even what we call the more innocent service of the world results in death at last. The death of the body is accompanied by the death of the soul Much more is this true of all kinds of positive sin. The apostle seeks to point out here the result of being the servant of sin. " His servants ye are to whom ye obey, whether of Bin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness" (ver, 16); "The end of those things is death" (ver. 21); "The wages of sin is death" (ver. 23). Even in this life there is a clear connection between sin and death. The Eervice of sin is a fatal service. Take, for instance, those who are the servants of the craving for intoxicating drink. A special committee of the British Medical Association brought in a report at the meeting of 1887 on the relation of alcohol to disease, which stated that, after careful and prolonged examination of the subject from a scientific point of view, they came to the conclusion that every man who indulged in alcohol beyond the most moderate a.mounts shortened his life by at least ten years. The President of the United States, General Harrison, has testified that of a class of sixteen young men who graduated with him, almost all had gone to early graves through intemperate ha.bits. Even in this world the sin of intemperance leads to death. But it brings a more lasting and more terrible death than this. The besotted mind, the darkened intellect, is but a beginniDg of blackness of darkness in the future. •• No drunkard shall enter into the kingdom of heaven." When drink becomes the master, how terrible are the results for time and for eternity I In like manner it is true of all other linful service8, that they lead to death. "He that soweth to the flesh, shall of.the flesh reap co1TUption;" "The wages of sin is death." IIL T.u SERVICE OF CBRIBT. "Being then made free from sin, ye beoame the 5enantB of righteowmea" (ver. 18); "But now, being made free from sin, and become i;ervants to God, ye have your fruit unto holineHe, o.nd the end everlasting life" (ver. 2~)- Thia is the only service that leads to enrla.'iting lifo. It is the cuJy 11erviee which can be called an unmixed good, tLe only service tl.t.at brings perfect oil. vi.1-23,] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 171

peace to heart and mind and coneclence. It is an easy 118l'Vice, for it is a service of love. Instead of growing weaker by our efforts in the eervice of Christ, ae we do by our efforts to serve sin, we grow stronger; for the true C,'hristian is a better man, a stronger man spiritually, every day _he lives. It fB ~he o:n-Zy 11ervir.JJ that has a ~ beyond the grave. It was because Christ saw us penshmg m the service of Bin, guilty, lost, and helpless, that he came to eave us. He calls us now to believe on him to follow him, and he promises to all who do so the gift of everlasting life. "The gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." " How long t.o streams of false delight Will ye in crowds repair? How long yonr strength and substance waste On trifles light as air?" Over the triple doorways or the Cathedral of Milan there are three inscriptions spanning the beautiful arches. Over one is carved a beautiful wreath of roses, and underneath is the legend, "All that which pleases is but for a momer,t." Over the other is sculptured a cross, and there are the words, "All that which troubles us is but for a. moment." But undernea.th the grea.t central entrance to the main aisle is the inscription, " That only is importa.nt which is eternal." If we would only realize these three truths, we should not let the world or its pleasures keep us from Christ, we should not let trifles trouble us, we should not hesitate long about making our choice. The relation of the death of <Jhrist to sin. Two elements entering into the atoning work or Christ, each of which, in its bearings, mn:,'t be distinguished from the other-the Divine, and the human. (1) .A.s to guilt. The guilt of the race an accomplished fact; the stain ineffaceable ; the white purity of the infinite Law blotted. What are the bearings of Christ's atonement, divinely and humanly, on this guilt of the past? (a) Divinely: condemnation for ever; (b) huma.nly: expiation for ever. (2) As to sin. An existent, a persistent fact; a. possibility always; a strong power of evil. What are the bearings of Christ's atonement on this sin of the present? (a) Divinely: stamp of condemnation; the. thing which has brought guilt that must be expiated by death, is by that very dear.h a branded thing; (b) humanly : renunciation and conflict ; the thing which is branded, in the atonement, on the part of God, is forsworn on the part of man. 2. -&n,anta to obey. A slight but suggestive difference between the question of ver. 15 and that with which the chapter opens. "Shall we continue in i;in," the apostle had asked, "that grace may abound?" And he had flung a.way =h a thought by the presentation of the believer's new life as a life pledged to God through Christ. In vers. 12-14 a.lao he had insisted on the consistent fulfilment of the pledge. But now he supposes another and more subtle question-Shall we, not "continue" in sin. but sin, once and again, as we may please, presuming on the easily procured pardon of a gracious God? Alas I how this question insinuates itself into the Christian conscio11BDess ! how readily we condone our carelessness by thoughts of the rest.oring mercy of God I But we are grievoU!!ly wrong if we think u, ourselves that sin and obedience may be played with. We have the dread power u, choose our master; but he u a master, and onr choice in either case commits us to a course, and to a CODBequence. The train may be tumed on u, this line or that, but the line must be followed, and the destinatio1ll are wide as the poles apart. Let us look at these three thought&-A choice, a course, a consequence. L A OHOIOE. The false doctrine of law in the necesaarian scheme of morale-so many we~t.e upon tl,e scale. But man's will is not a dead scale, determined by weighta; it is a living thing, and unless its peculiar life be taken into account all calculations must be wrong. True, if we know the caures, we can predict the result, OH, vr.1-28.) THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 173

And certain teachers have said-Those are the causes: man's own susceptible nature, and the divers influences which play upon it. Therefore, given the temperament and the influences, we can predict the result. Very plausible. True, if these are the only oe.uses, the result may thus be known. But the cause of causes is the will itself. Thid is the gree.t factor in the problem. And, after all, when the most scientific calculations have been made, this self-determining power in man may defy all your calculations to predict a right result. Let us not attempt to prove this freedom by elaborate arguments; we need but appeal to each one's consciousness. "I know that I am free; I have power of choice; when I have willed, I know that I might have willed otherwise." This must be each one's true confession. Just as surely as we know that we exist, by the same intuition, which is deeper and truer than all reasoning, do we know that we can yield ourselves to any one of all the manifold motives that are playing upon our wi!L Does not the history of the Fall illustrate this freedom? For what is the essential truth of that history, but that man had it in his power, either to obey God or to gratify himself, and that he chose self-gratification rather than obedience? But the results were not by any means so transient as the choice itself might seem to be. In the highest sense, freedom was gone. There still remained freedom of choice among the various objects of self-gratification, but there was no longer the power to serve Goo as before. A great gulf was fixed between man and God. And in this consists what is called the total depravity of man: totally separated from God, and without the power to return. And certain, moreover, to drift from bad to worse. But under the redeeming influences with which God visits the heart of man, and more especially in view of the great redeeming fact with which God has visited the world, this total depravity becomes in some sense neutralized, man's enfeebled will receives new power, and it is once more possible for him to place his choice on God. The freedom of true duty is once more within his reach; from the depths he may yet climb back to God. Bo, then, taking men as they now are, and especially taking them as we find them in contact with the redeeming truths of the gospel of Christ, we see that each has his alternative choice between godliness and ungodliness, truth and falseness, the right and good, and the wrong and bad, or, in the words of St. Pau.l, between obedience and sin. " Ye yield yourselves:" the supreme fact of every one's life is wrapped up in those words. From childhood upwards good and bad influences contend for the mastery. God and sin ask for our service, and we cannot but" yield ourselves" to the one or the other. We make our choice, whether consciously and with full deliberatenes of purpose, or well-nigh unconsciously and with careless neglect. We choose sin, and thereby set; the seal on our own death; or we choose God, and thereby rise to newness of life. But in either case our own choice determines our course, and the cour.;e to which we commit; ourselves works out its inevitable consequence. II. A COURSE, Let us now consider the course to which our choice in either case commits us. 1. In the one case we become servants, or slaves, of sin. Our Lord's words (John viii. 32-36). Man may refuse to bow to sin; but when he does bow, sin holds him fast. Nay, he m11y yet rise from his thraldom and be free; but every yielding is the taking on of a new chain, and every continuance in sin is the rivetting of the chain. The slave of sin? Oh, it is no fiotion I The man who yields to sin is led c11ptive by 8 master stronger than himself. So with the inebriate, the man of passion, the miser. Yes ; dragged in chains. And yet it is a " free" man, forsooth, who has thus sold himself to serve sin I 2. In the other case ~ b«ome serva"", or slaves, of obedience. The same law works, whatever the material of its working. Hence the degrnding slavery of the servant of sin is but the dark side of the result of that same law which, in its brighter results, is the safeguard and glory of our righteousness. But la not the result sl11very still ? Ah I let us ask, what is slavery? Mere servi-1ntent, earnest, unremitting service-is not. Service is slavery when it is forced. Contrast the service of a Crusader, all d that of a captive among the Moors. It is slavery also when, even if not forced, it is degrading and low. Contrast sfave-trader, and pure, virtuous man enthrnllod. So Epiototus. The service of sin, then, is slavery becnuse it le degrading nnd base; whereas, to yield obedience to God, nud thenceforth to serve him with unremitting ardour and with the enthusiasm of lofty joy, that is not slavery, that is freedom of tho hip;host kind (so John viii. 86). Yes; this the secret of lioorty: the" spirit of ll son" (G11l. iv. 61 7). li4 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [on. vx. 1-23,

III. A CONSEQUENCE. But now let us consider the consequence to whioh euoh a ccurre of conduct in either cRSe must lend. 1. "Sin unto death." Yes, towards this ine,i table resul~ t.he service of sin must tend. A fixity of corrupt oharacter. Recovery of freedom possible now; not always. Death-the death of man's best nature,-thi11_ the doom which the senice of sin ensures. The victims of Circe: so the slaves of sin, But no wizardry e&n undo that death! 2. " Obedience unto righteousness." A fixity again. This the process of all true moral life. So was it to have been with the first man; so was it Tith the second (" yet learned he obedience"). So, doubtless, with the ang,,ls. And so with us: we are fighting towards the crown which Paul desired (Phil. iiL 12; 2 Tim. iv. 7, S), the crown of a. consummate righteousness, or, in other words (Re,. ii. 10), "the crown of life." Such the two consequences of the two ooursea, to one or other of which each mnn, by his free choice, commits himself. But. whereas death is the wages of sin, the eternal life is God's free gift. And to all of us, in words of hope, the voice from heaven says, "Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold on eternal life I "-T. F. L.

\'ers. 3, 4.-Tlu significance of baptism. To suppose that the acceptance of the grace of God in Christ readers us careless about the further committal of sin is to mis- apprehend the nature of redemption. We cannot dissociate the external results of Christ's work from a consideration of its inward effects upon the mind and heart of the man who profits by it. For a practical refutation of the supposition, the apostle points io the acknowledged meaning of the ceremony wherein each believer indicates his close relationship to the Saviour. I. BAPTISM THE snmoL OIi' AN ALTERED LIFE. What can more forcibly set forth an abandonment of former feelings and behaviour than being "dead and buried"? The allusion here to immersion is questioned by none, and a water grave speaks elo- que1H.ly of a changed attitude to sin and the world. We are so constituted that this appeal to the senses powerfully impresses both the actual participator in the act a_nd the spectators of the living picture. II. A snmoL OF OOllPLETE FELLOWSHIP WITH CHRIST. The follower of Christ repeats in his inwacd experience the death, the bwial, and the resurrection of Christ.. These were necessitated by the presence and enormity of sin, and to "put on Christ" as our Redeemer is to adopt his crucifi.xion and subsequent triumph as our expressiou of b&tred ag:ailllit all that perverts the moral order of the world. 'fo be immersed into t.b.e de.ath of Christ is to be completely surrendered to tho claims of the Son of God, and to share his hostility to evil, rejoicing in his conque~t over death and the gravo, and the adverB&IY of mankind. By compliance with his commandment does the dis- ciple signify hie entire dedication to his Master's service. IIL CBARACTEBlB'l'lCB OJI' THIB lIEW LIFE. Emerging from the burial, the candidate rises with Christ as his Example and Companion. His is to be an active life, "a walk," not a dreamy repose of self-absorption into the bliss of Nirvana. The contrast to the old career wa.s exemplified in the resurrection gladness and glory of the Lord. No more was sin to exert its baleful influence; the body of the risen Lord no longer could be tortured with hu::iger and thirst and suffering. The Saviour was limited no longer by material barriers; he was endowed with full authority from on high, and cn,wned with ever-increasing splendour. When the Apostle Paul saw his Lord, the brightness excelled the noonday sun. These triumphs are in their degree repeated in the spiritnal life of the baptized believer. He casts off the works of darkness and puts on the armour of light. He keel's his body under, so that the spirit rules. The voice from heaven procla.imB him Gods beloved son. Inst~ of anguish t~ere is P.eace a,!1d joy. He aits in heavenly places, and God calllleth him always to triumph 1n Clmst Jesua. Such is the ideal life of fellowship with Christ in his resurrection, shadowed forth by the ucent from tha baptismal waters.-S. B. A.
