and hns bought us with his precious blood. He ie enthroned ln our henrts; hP, givea laws to our life. 2. J eeus is rich unto all. We are ae81lred of "the unspeakable riches of Christ,n and are counselled to buy of him "gold tried in the fire, that we may be rich." If" all things are oure," it is because we are Christ's, and G'hrist is Go,l's. He who redeems and rules, supplies the wants of his ransomed ones. He is not, like some of the wealthy of this world, rich for himself; he is rich /w w, rlth boundlessly and inexhaustibly, rich benevolently and for ever. If. THE CONDITIONS UPON WHICH THE LoRDBHIP AND THE WEALTH OP' CHRIST HAY BE ENJOYED, These are stated in two modes. 1. BelieiJing on him is essential to participating in the blessings Christ offers to men. The apostle has previously been insistin.,. upon faith as the means of obtaining the true and Divine righteollBiless, as God's way for man to come to himself and to enjoy his favour. They who have faith shall not be put to shame, shall eurely and eternally be saved. 2. Calling upon him would seem to be a natural result of faith. They who believe in the heart will give their faith utterance by the lips. By this Hebrew expression we may understand both open confession and earnest prayer. By calling upon the Lord's Name, no vain and 811perstitious invocations or repetitions are to be understood, but the sincere entreaty of the soul for deliverance, guidancr,, or help. III. FoR WHOSE BENEFIT CHRIST'S LORDSHIP ABD WEALTH ARE DESimnrn. 1. The limitations of nationality are abolished. The religions of heathenism are local; the deities of heathenism are national and tutelary. Under the older dispensation, Jehovah was revealed as the one God, the God of all the earth; yet the Hebrews too oft.en regarded the Lord as their God, and theirs only. The distinction between Jew and Gentile was, to the Hebrew mind, deep and ineffaceable. To St. Panl largely belongs the honour of giving currency to the true doctrine of Christianity, that religion is one and universal ; that God is the Father of mankind; that Christ is Saviour and Lord of all men; that the middle wall of partition is broken down; that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Gentile. 2. The offers of Christianity are made to all, and its terms and conditions are adapted to all. He is "rich unto all," and his riches are for "whomsoever believeth," for "whomsoever calleth upon his Name." What lan,,,<TDage could be used more fitted to encourage every hearer of the gospel to submit to the Lordship and to seek the true riches of Jesus Christ, the Son of God?

entries.title: ROM 10:12
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Spiritual enrichment. The experience of the aposile was sufficienily large to enable him with confidence to make this sweeping assertion. And the experience of the Church of Christ, through the many centuries which ha,c elapsed since St. Panl thus wrote, enables Christians to make the sllDle assertion with undiminished confidence. In fact, the actual proofs at our disposal o.nd command are overwhelming, both in number and in appropriateness; for, whilst the bestowal of Divine and spiritual wealth has been incess11ntly proceeding, the resources o.re unexhausted and inexhaustible. I. THE RICHES OF THE LORD. In Christ is wes.lth adapted to the enrichment of dependent, needy men. He has in himself: 1. Riches of revelation. 2. Riches of redemption. 3. Riches of ,·eplenishment, owing to the nature and perpetuity of the spiritual dispensation of grace. 4. Riches of resurrection, inasmuch as the true riches endure unto life eternal. I(, THE LIDERALITY WITH WHICH THESE SPIBITUAL RICHES ARE DISPE..~ED, 1. It is becnuse Christ is Lord over o.11, that he is rich unto all. 2. The riches of rroeeming lovo are conferred upon men of every nationality. In the apostolic age, the great distinction which Christianity transcended was that between Jew and Gentile; but, in subsequent times, it has been proved by experience that there is no nation, no class, and no condition incnpable of this Divine enrichment. Ill. THE CONDITION UPON WHICH BPIBITUAL RICHES HAVE BEEN, AND STILL IUY BX, APPROPRIATED, As throughout this chapter, tho apostle here insists upon that spiritual condition of receptivity and application by which all that is good may enter the nature of man. C1\lluJg upon him is an not (1) of repout11nce, (2) of faith, (3) of pmyer, and (4) of nsplro.tlon. .As we exorcise this means of communion, &II things are ours. Vora. 14, 15.-Pi·eaching. Paul was himself brought to the Snviour by thrit S:\'l"iour's 1mmerli11.to interposition. Doubtless he had heard much of Jesus; yet he hriJ. ne\'t!r 800 THE EPISTLE OF PA.UL TO THE ROMANS. [olI. x. 1-21,

trnly known him during his career of unbelief and persecution. It was when Jesus met him by the way that his hostility was overcome, thRt his heart wns melted, thnt bis nature was changed. But this was exceptional treatment. The Lord who, by o. supernatural appeara.noe and voice, called Saul to the knowledge of himself, com- missioned him to preach the gospel to his fellow-men, and made him one of the first, and perhaps the most suocessful, of the innumerable band of preaohers of the cross. We have here-- I. A Drvnra PROVISION. All good is from God. No apostle more constantly insists upon this great truth than does Paul ; and in no treatise is it more prominently set before the mind of the reader than in this Epistle to the Romans. 1. We are told what the ultimate blesmng is which Christianity proffers. It is salvation. Righteousness has reference rather to what is positively given; salvation, rather to the state from which men are rescued by the Redeemer. A worthy end I-worthy even of the interposition of Heaven, of the benevolence of God the Father, of the sacrifice of Christ, of the grace of the Spirit. A deliverance of the spiritual nature from condemnation and from all evil, and the pronsion for the saved of new associations, a new lot, a new hope -a sal.-ation which is final and eternal. 2. We have brought before us the extent to which salvation may be enjoyed, the persons for whose benefit it is proposed. All mankind are qualified to be recipients of this boon upon compliance with the terms pre- scribed. There is no difference in the view of God. The comprehensive term "whollOCVer" is conclusive upon this point. Jews are not excluded; Gentiles are welcomed; the pronsion is for humanity. 3. The text sets before us the conditions upon which this blessing may be enjoyed. It is required (1) that men should call upon the Name of the Lord, i.e. Christ Jesus ; and (2) that they should do this in intelligent and cordial faith: for "how shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?" The expression, "call upon the Name of the Lorci," is full of meaning and beauty. It reminds us whence the blessing of salvation proceeds ; and as the voice, the call, the cry, come from a heart conscious of need and longing for deliverance, it speaks of the spiritual state which prepares for receiving salvation. Thus Christians are spoken of as "all who in every place call upon the Lord." They who act thus glorify God and his promises of faith• fulness. Tbey seek what he has promised to bestow, and they seek with earnestness and confidence. "He is near to all that call upon him in truth." In order to intelligent ca.lling upon the Lord, the apostle reasons, there must be faith. "He that cometh unto him must believe that he is, and that he is a Rewarder of them that seek after him." Faith is the first requirement of the gospel; faith in the glad tidings proclaimed; faith in that Divine Saviour to whom those tidings relate, and who, indeed, is himself the GospeL "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved." An arrangement this in harmony with the wisdom of God, and with the moral nature of man. Dead in unbelief and unspiritnality, the sinner rises in faith into newness of llie, for he lays hold of the grace of God revealed in the Saviour Obrist. Consider how unspeakably rich is the provision here made, and how unepeakab!Y: gr~ious the conditions here proposed. Hearers of the gospel, how can you remam without such a blessing as this when it is put within your reach, and when you are invited to take it, and when the te!'lDJ! upon which you may enjoy it are such that you cannot cavil at them? How can you think of such a Saviour and such a gospel, and remain faithless and unmoved? How can you do other than. from your sin and danger and helplessness call upon One who is "mighty to save "-to "save to the uttermost all that come un~ God by him"? This is the day of visitation. "To-day," says Christ, "if ye will hear my voice, harden not your hearts." II. A HUMAN AGENCY. The apostle brings before us two classes of agents-those who, by the publication of the gospel, are the means of lead~n~ their fellow-men to faith• and those who send forth such preachers upon such a m1es1on. 1. God employs preachers in bringing men to salvation. They have glad tidings of peace, of good things, t.o communicate. As the first bands of returning exiles, bringing good news of a larger company following in their train, were welcome to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, wbu bailed their approa.ch by the mol!ntaine of Judroa; so the preachers of Ohrietianity may well have been welcumed by the spiritually captive tribes and nations whom thoy visited on their errands of grace and evangelization. Thie method of promulgating truth, tb,Jugh not peculiar to our religion., ii very dilltinctive of it. Chrillt chose twelve apost!ee; OH, x. 1-21.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 301

he sent out other seventy also. Defore he left the world he directed and sanctioned per- sonal agency in the ministry of the gospel. Paul instructed Timothy to comm.it the things he had received to faithful men, who should be able to teach others also; tbne arranging for a succession, not of a priesthood, but of a teaching ministry. Christ r.alls out, sanctifies, o.nd blesses the ministry of man to man. Would that there were a more genernl disposition to listen to hie voice and to respond to bis summons," Whom shall I send?" in the ancient language, "Here am I; send me." The auccess which attended the ministry of the apostles and first evangelists was such as to confirm faith in the Divine appointment. God was pleased by the foolishness of preaching to eave them that believed, And every succeeding age has witnessed, in greater or Iese measure, to the efficacy of this wise provision. In our own day literature is so vigorous, and educa.- tion so general, that the press has become a mighty auxiliary and ally to the ministry. Every preacher who has confidence in the Divine origin of his message, and in his own sincerity, will welcome the aide to general intelligence which are afforded by the able and varied literature of these enlightened days. Amongst a Christian co=unity, preaching becomes naturally something more than the publication of the great fundamental facts of the gospel But whilst there is abundant room for instruction, by which the Word of God may be expounded, and the application of religion be shown to all spheres and relationships of life, there is still a pressing need for evangelization. The young have to learn afresh "the first principles of the oracles of God;" the inattentive and careless have to be o.roused by the Word which is as" a fire, and as a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces;" the regions around have to be enlightened by the gospel, which is the true light; the world has yet to be gladdened by the good news of salvation and eternal life. 2. God employs his Church to send forth preachers of the gospel All are not called upon to preach, but, in a sense, all are called upon to send. 'l'rue, the one great Sender is the Divine Head of the Church; and they who are not commissioned by him are without authority, whatever human sanction, credentials, and approval they may enjoy. "The Lord gave the Word, and great was the company of those that published it." We have an instructive instance of the way in which the Lord inspires his people to send forth his servants upon a benevolent mission, in the narrative of the proceedings of the Church at Antioch, when that Church became the second great centre of missionary enterprise. " How shall they preach, except they be sent? "-a query little regarded by very many of the congregutions named after Christ. It is thought enough to leave the matter to individual impulse, wise or unwise, or to consider it the vocation of the pastorate to call out living agencies. Yet, look at; the vast demands of our own day. Clergy of all variety of gift; pastors for congre,,crations ; evangelists for our rural districts ; city missionaries for our great towns; popular itinerant preachers ; colonial missionaries; labourers, by voice and pen and press, among the heathen ; defenders and promulgators of Christian truth in all the departments of literature;-we need all these, of the best and most varied quality, and in increased numbers. In order that Christian society may send out into the world those who shall diffuse the faith of Christ, it is first of all necessary that that society should be in such a condition that from among its members such agencies shall naturally emerge. Mechanical means are of little avail in this matter. Where there is little life there will be little movement. If love to Christ be ohilled by worldliness, no place will be found for love of souls. Out of the fulness of the heart the mouth will speak; when the feeling of the Christian community is strong, its voice will not be silent. The use of any and every means will depend for efficacy upon the sound and living condition of the society in which such means may be employed. It should be habitual with Christian congregations to call out and encourage the exercise of gifts divinely imparted. There are many other gifts beside that of religious instruction and persuasion, and gifts equally precious to God and useful to man. But there are reasons why speech/or Christ needs special culture. Nature.I timidity has to be overcome, and formidable difficulties have to be encountered. It is here that wise counsel and affectionate encouragement come in with especial npprop1intenoss. Almost every youthful speaker has been tempted to renounce this meo.ns of usefulness; nnd often it h!\S happened that a word, providen~ tially spoken, has cheered the diflil.leut and discoum~ed. It must not be forgotten that, if there n.re to be lonrners, there must be tonchers. 1f the Christian Church is to send out proaoher11 and instruotors, it must do something more l\lld better ilil\ll fling tham THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO 'l'HE HOMANS. [ou. x. 1-21.

unfumi~hed on the world. Those who arc t.o influence mon must in the first place be !nfiuenl'~d by men. That community is_ rich which .cont.a.ins a lar~e amount of tonchmg, qmckenmg power. One of our chief dangers 1s lest we should uverestimnte the power of money. There is much which C.'\nnot be purohased by materinl wealth. It is in the abundance of the highest type of Christian oharaoter that spiritual wonlth coni:ists. '\\here there are found the lofty, noble-minded, the holy and the learned, the spiritual and benevolent, nmong the leading spirits of a Church, there the young and ardent and devoted will gather by a subtle magnet.ism, and thence they will derive in tum, by God's ~race, the power of Divine attraction. Hence the importance of seeking a high standar<1 of biblical knowledge and Christian intelligence among all classes in our congregations. And hence, too, the importance of seeking out, and wisely employing, all the ability and culture which a.re devoted to Christ and 118Ilctified to his glory. Can they be said to be truly sent who are thrust forth and then forgotten? Or, rather, does not that Church truly send which follows its agents, whether near or far, with kindly interest, with watchful sympathy, with fervent prayer? Sympathy is invaluable to those who labour, as all Christian servants must do, amid many difficnlties and much opposition. Prayer of intercession is due from every member of the universal Church, and is especially required on behalf of Christian labourers. "Brethren, pray for us, that the Word of God may have free course, and be glorified." In order that the Churches may more adequately fulfil their office as illuminators of a dark world, it ie necessary that there should be a sincerer pity for the multitudes who are in darkness, and a firmer faith in the light which is from heaven. A Church which hesitates as to whether or not it possesses the truth, and has a gospel for mankind; a Church which can look with unconcern upon the prevalence of sin and misery in the world, is not likely to send forth heralds of Christ and tidings of salvation, Faith in the Redeemer, pity for those whom he died to redeem, forgetfulness and denial of self,-these are the conditions of true e,angeliza.tion. It is for us, then., to look up for a renewed baptism of the Holy Spirit, ae a Spirit of life and of power. How otherwise can we rise to fulfil responsibilities so sacred, to discharge duties so momentous ? Hearera of the gospel, seek the Spirit of faith and prayer, that you may be not hearers of the Word only, but doers also! Preachers of the gospel, seek the Spirit of wisdom and fervour, that your words may be with demonstration of the Spirit and of power I Churches of Christ, seek the Spirit of your Master, that you may, feeling your own debt to the Divine, immortal. Saviour, act in the spirit of hie lesson., "Freely ye have received, freely give" I V ers. 16-2L-Israel', tV11,btl,i,ef. The more highly the apostle prized the gqspel, the more sincerely and compassionately did he lament the folly and the guilt of those who deliberately or carelessly rejected it. Especially was his heart stirred to sorrow, when he observed bow generally the glad tidings of life in Christ were rejected by his "kinsmen according to the fiesh." Both upon the peraonal ground of relationship and association., and upon the general ground that Israel's greater privileges involved greater re2p0nsibilities, Paul grieved over the want of faith iL Christ mauifested by eo many of his countrymen. L THE FACT OF lsBAEL's UN13ELIEF. 1. It had been predicted. In that remarkable anticipation of the sufferings and the glory of the Messiah which has won for L;aiah the designation " the evangelical prophet," there occurs an intimation that the Messiah should himself be despised and rejected of men, and that the news of hie salvation should be disregarded by many for whose benefit it was intended. 2. Fact agreed with prophecy. Many sons of Abraham manifested Abraham's faith. Of the early professors and preachers of Christianity, a large proportion were Hebrews. Yet, although individuals welcomed the gospel, the nation as a whole, who by their leaders and repre• 11entative11 had crucified and slain the Lord Jesus, certainly turned away from the message of salvation! which, after his ascension, his apostles. urgently and faithfully proclaimtod. They did not all hearken to the report and obey its summons. II. THE JliEIOUBADLE GUlLT OF lsBAEL'I! TJNDELIEF. This is made apparent by several oowiideratioWI. It appears: 1. From the term, of salvation. "Belief cometh of heariD.g, and hearing by the word of Chrlllt.n No terms could be more righteous, more rtaliOoable, more w accordance with the character of God or the neceHsitics of on. x. 1-21.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 303

men: Compliance with the';D Involves no mental or 80cial eminence, and is equally possible to those of all nations among men. 2. From, the g,m,,;ral dijfuBion of the tidings, Like the very light of the sun, like the voiceleBS witnesa of the heavens the good nowe of salvation soon penetrated into the remotest and darkest places. Eve~ the distant "sons of the dispersion" could not complain that they had been neglected. For the disciples of Christ, so far from keeping the good news to themselves made it a point of conscience and religion to communicate to their neighbours the tidin"s of the advent and the mediation of the Son of God; whilst many, devoting themselv~ to the work of evangelization, deemed no journey too long to undertake and no perils too formidable to endure in the fulfilment of this sacred commission. 3. Even/rc,m. the/ad that many of the less-favowred Gentiles came to beluve. It had been foretold by :lfoses and by the prophet Isaiah that the privileges which the Jews would despise and refuse should be offered to and accepted by the Gentiles. This came to paBS. And it cut the apostle to the heart to remark that his kinsmen were rejecting blessings which the heathen to whom he preached were eagerly welcoming and receiving. 4. From thefvrbearance and gracious invitations of a heavenly Father. Again the apostle has recourse to the language of prophecy. How affecting is the representation here given of the patience, long-suffering, and kindness of God I He " willeth not that any should perish." .Although the people oppose themselves, he does not soon weary of his invitations. He spreads forth his arms, as willing to welcome those who will return from their wanderings and be reconciled to him. So he stands, as it were, all the day long. Still, though he has long proffered grace in vain, the hands which might have been raised to smite &Ye extended to rescue and to bless.

entries.title: ROM 10:1–4
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Israel's strength and weakness. The apostle returns a,,"ain t.o the tender solicitude for the spiritual welfare of Israel which he had already expressed in the beginning of the ninth chapter. He was no blind biiot. He could recognize the good qualities even of those from whom he differed. He knew how far Israel had departed from the truth of God, and yet he is quick to perceive that, even amid their errors and sine, there is- much that is commendable in their character. What an e=ple for every Christian, and especially in these days, when ecclesiastical. divisions are so numerous and so sharply defined, to recognize what is good even in those from whom we differ most widely I I. ZEAL WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE. 1. Israe"es zeal wa., an elemmt of strength. "I bear them record that they have a zeal of God" (ver. 2). The apostle does them the justice of recognizing their zeal for God. Here he could speak with sympathy, the sympathy of persona.I experience. He knew how, before bis conversion to Christianity, he himself he.d been influenced by the same sincere, though mistaken, desire for God's glory. "I am verily a man which a.m a Jew, bom in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia., yet brought up in this oity at the feet of Gamaliel, a..'ld taught according to the perfect manner of the Law of the fathers, e.nd we.s zealous t->ward God, as ye 1111 are this day " (Acts i:xii. 3). Here is the same sympathetic recognition of Jewish zeal This que.lity, when rightly applied, was their strength. It well fitted them to be the bearers of God's message, and the ohannel of his blessings, to the world. A people without zee.l will never accomplish anything permanent or great. 2. Zeal withoot knowledge was their weakness. They had a zeal of God, "but not according to knowledge." Zeal is not necessarily e.n unmixed blessing. Yet there are me.ny who commend earnestness, utterly irrespeotive of the motives from which it proceeds, the methods it adopts, or the ends it hos in view. On this principle the doctrines held or the character exhibited are of small importance, provided only there is earnestness e.nd zeal. Moham- medanism and the Inquisition would therefore bo both laudable, because they exhibited zeal. Zeal without knowledge may become the opened floodgate for a torrent of evil. Zeal in religion may lead to any excesses if it is not restrained e.nd tempered by the wisdom whioh God's Word imparts. II. WonKB WITHOUT l'AITB. "For they being ignorant of God's righteowmess, nnti goi.Di a.bout to lllltQblliih their own rightooUSlless, havci not submitted thelllSelvea uutc 3M THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [ou. x.1-21,

the rightoourness of God" (ver. 3). Thus it is plain t.hat sincerity &nd morality will not sa'l'"e the human soul or procure aooept.auce with God. The essential condition of i:..1lrnti,,n is faith. Faith will lead us to accept God's plan of salvation, and to be guided by his Word in our efforts to obtain it. St. Paul's description of the J ewe hero might be appropriately applied to our Roman Catholic and ritualistic brethren, They too ha'l'"e a zeal for God. Their zeal and earnestness cannot be questioned. But their zeal is often not according to knowledge. They too are " going about to establish their o_wn right.eousness." They substitute works for faith, and by legal observances, by rites and ceremonies, by fastings and penances, they seek to work out a righteousness for themselves. Christ and his Word are too much set aside, and Church and priest and the commandments of men are set up in their place. Let us admit their strength, let us imitate their zeal, while affectionately "speaking the truth in love" we point out and avoid their weakness.-0. H. I.

entries.title: ROM 10:5–13
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The simplicity qf the gospel,. The apostle here contrasts the simplicity of God's plan of sall'&tion with the,e.fforts which men have made to work out a righteousness for themselves. Salvation is gained- !. NoT BY OUR OWN GOOD WORKS. "Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the Law, That the man who doeth those things shall live by them" (ver, 5). If this were the condition of salvation, how hopeless would our condition be I None of us could say that we had made ourselves free from sin, or that our works were perfect and faultless, or that we had fully and faithfully kept all the commandments of God, "Not what these hands have done Could save this guilty soul; . Not what this toiling 11.esh hath bome C.Onld make my spirit whole." Il. NOR BT HIB.A.CULous INTERVENTION. " Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down from above:) or, Who shall descend into the deep?" (vers. 6, 7). The desire which is' here expressed still survives. •Not content with the Word of God and the invisible, but real, spiritual presence of Jesus with his Church, and the power of the Holy Spirit, many zealous Christians think it is necessary to have a more visible manifestation of the supernatural. Hence we have the doctrine of the real presence; alleged appe.a.rances of the blessed Virgin at Lourdes and at Knock; and, on the other hand, an undue stress laid upon the second coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. Vars. 14, 15.-Four questions for every <Jhrisw.,,n. When the great heart of the Apostle Paul burned within:him as he wrote hie Epistles to the Churches, he threw aside ae it were, the calm and stately prose of the quiet thinker and careful writer. He becam; an orator. He saw before him--even in his prison cell-immortal souls, whom he wanted to awaken and arouse. He asked questions, as if he expected an answer to them all. Such questions e.re frequent in this Epistle to the Romans, and on looking carefully over them we see the.t they are not only full of eager earnestness, but also of profitable instruction. In the four questions before us the apostle eeeks to press home upon Christians the absolute necessity of mission work. In the previous chapter he is sorrowing for the unbelief of the Jews, and he begins this chapter by saying that his heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they might be saved. Then, as he goes on, he is led to think of the salvation, not only of the Jews, but also of the whole world. He says, "There is no difference between the Jew and the Gentile: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him. For whosoever shall call upon the Name of the Lord shall be saved." And then, as he thinks of the heathen world lying in darkness, he asks these four questions. I. " How SHALL THEY OALL ON HUtl IN WHOM THEY HA VE NOT BELIEVED ? " In the ordinary dealings of daily life a certain amount of faith in another person is necessary before we can make any request of him. Unless we believe that he hears us, unless we believe that he is both able and willing to give us what we want, we are not likely to ask anything of him. So in spiritual matters, faith in God-the belief that he is, that he hee.rs us, and that he is able and willing to help us-is necessary to snccessful prayer. It is necessary to salvation. But the heathen cannot call upon this gracious God of ours. As a matter of fact, they do not. No doubt, even amid heathen darkness, there are some earnest seekers after God. Certainly, if they call upon him, they shall be saved. But the vast majority of the heathen are without the knowledge of the true God. They are bowing down to pieces of silver and gold, of wood and stone, which cannot hear, or help, or save. 'l'heir very worship is a degradation in it.<!elf. Their religious rites are for the most part horrid cruelties, or foul and nnspeakable lusts. And as for Buddhism, to quote only one authority, Sir Richard Temple, lately,Governor of Bombay, tells us that however excellent and attractive the poetic accounts of it may be, as in the well-known poem, 'The Light of Asia,' the actual Buddhism of India is as degrading as can well be imagined. What they need to know is that there is a God who will hear them when they call upon him. They need to know the.t God is of purer eyes than to behold evil, that the abominations of their la.ad may be put a.way. They need to know of the Lamb of God who beareth a.way the sin of the world, that they may turn from their useless ceremonies and cruel penances. They need to know of a Saviour who gives to all who ce.ll on him salvation, holiness, everlasting life. But "how shall they call on Mm in whom they have not believed," II. "How SHALL THEY BELIEVE IN HIM OF WHOM THEY 11AVE NOT HE.I.RD?. Even Christians need to he.ve the importance of hearing about God more impressed upon them. Some professing Christinns seem to ima,,<Yine that the heart instinctively turns to God, and that in some mysterious way the heathen who have never heard of Gad will come to him. This mistake is fallen into because in Christian lands we have been so accustomed to henr about God from our childhood that we cau hardly imagine it possible not to know nbout him. But the simple refutation of this idea is the actual state of heathen nations. St. Pe.ul, in this very Epistle (eh. i. 21, 25, 28), assures us that though tho heathen had Bt one time a knowledge of God from his works of nature, yet they glorified him not as God, but changed the truth of God into a lie, e.nd there- fore lost the knowledge of God. This is confirmed by the testin1ony of travellers in heathen lands. Missionnrios often. find it very difficult to convey to heathen min,is an idee. of what God is, eo dogrnded lrnve been their notions. It is a long time before UOAiANS, ~ 306 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [ell. x. 1-:u~

a heathen e11n grasp the ide11s of God's holiness and truth and purity, eo 11coustomod la he t-0 think of gods whose qualities are the very opposite of these, Even in our Christia:n land, unhappily, there are places i!1 our large cities eo ne~leoted and degraded that children ha'l"e grown up without bearing about God. And m such oases it baa been found ,ery difficult to con,ey at first an idea of God's being-his greatness, hie holiness, his mercy, and his love. " How shall they believe in l1im of whom. they liaw ,10t J,eard '" Hence, when the heat.hen learn of the love of God and the salvation which is in Christ Jesus, they often ask the question, "Why did you not send and tell us sooner?" No wonder that with sorrow fol hearts they ask the question, as they think of loved ones who have passed away without hearing the glad tidings. How sad. is the e-0ndition of millions of the heathen without the knowledge of the oruoified Saviour! m ... How SBAtL THEY BEAR WITHOUT A PREACHER?" yes, the preaching of the goopel is still the a,,crency that is t-0 regenerate the world. It was the preaching of the gospel that was the means of converting thousands upon the Day of Pentecost. It was the preaching of the gospel which overthrew the idols of ancient Rome. It was the preaching of the gospeliwhich brought about the Protestant Reformation. "The Word," said :Martin Luther over and over a,,a-ain, "it was the Word that did it all." It was the preaching of the gospel that overthrew the idols of Madagascar, and that has already brought civilization and peace and contentment into many of the islands of the sea. It is good t.o circnlat.e the Word of God in every language. But it is necessary also to have the living preachers. " Go ye therefore into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." It needs the living preacher to be a living witness to the trutb and power of the gospel-the full heart overflowing with love to Christ and love to souls; the ripe el:p&ience; the fnlness of the Spirit. The Ethiopian treasurer had the Word of God in his hand as he returned in his chariot from Jerusalem. But he was not savingly converted until Philip began at the Scriptures which he was reading, and " preached unto him Jesus" (Acts viii 36). But the number of missionaries is still very small in comparison with the millions of heathen who have not yet heard the gospel message. "How shall they hear without a preacher?" IV. "How l!lllLL THEY PREACH, EXCEPT THEY BE SENT'/" This is the intensely practical question. If we realize the darkness and misery of heathen lands, if we are really thankful for the unspeakable blessings which the gospel has brought to us, wl:;.at are we doing to send the message of salvation to those who sit in darkness? 1. We oan help ro send out mwionaries lJy our prayers. " The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few ; pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers int.o his harvest." 2. We can help U> send out missionaries by our gifts. We need to understand, not merely the duty of giving, but the privilege of giving. Surely it is a glorious privilege to be a labourer together with God. Upon the Christian Church is laid the responsibility of preaching the gospel to all nations. .And there is this blessed encouragement: 3. If the last of these parts of mission work, of which the apostle speaks, itJ fulfilled, the rest are all sure to follow. If missionaries are sent, then there will be the preaching, the hearing, and, in God's own good time, the believing and the salvation of sonls. His Word shall not return unto him void. Thus by our sending we may be the means of saving.-C. H. L

The gospel does not permit us to regard man as one of the beasts that perish, as he is under so many of the heathen religions. Some of these have no idea of the existence of a soul at all; but in the best of them the soul is either annihilated at death, or transferred to some other creature, or absorbed into the universal being as a drop into the ocean. The gospel, on the other band, teaches that man was made in the image of God; that he has an immortal destiny ; and that, when he had destroyed his own present happiness and future prospects by his own sin, so great value did God place upon him, so great love did his heavenly Father cherish for him, that he sent his own beloved Son to live and die for man's salvation. entries.content: -The freenea, of Balvation. The apostle's heart yeal'Il8 for hie people. For he recognizes their sincerity in much of their grievous mistakin.,.0 of the ways of God. They had zeal for God, though the zeal w11.11 unreasonable and irreli<:rioll8. Unreasonable; for how can man make himself jll8t before God, guilty and sinfnt°aa he is? and why should the Jew think that, if this were poBBible, only one small portion of the race should be suffered to work out its righteousness? Irreligious• for instead oft.he humility as regards one's self, ans the charity aa regards others, which are two essentials of the life in God, there was a proud self-aBBertiveness, and a narrow bigotry. They must learn that God's favour is by grace (vers. 5-11), and for all (vera. 12-21). We have here-the freeness of salvation. I. THE ERROR OF THE JEws. 1. Ignoramoo. "Of God's righteousness." That is, of the fact that the justification of a sinner can only come of God's free grace. Surely their Law might have taught them this: negatively, for it should have made them realize their own utter imperfectness and impotence; positively, for had they not read (Gen. xv. 6) that Abraham was counted righteous through faith in God? and (Hab. ii. 4) that all just ones shall live by faith? 2. Self-sufficiency. "Seeking to establish their own." That is (see GJdet), as a monument, raised, not to God's glory, but to show forth their own achievements. Here was the pride of man, which must be brought down before any way can be made towards God (Matt. v. 3). 3. Disobedi.ena. " Did not subject themselves." For the very faith whereby we receive God's free forgiveness is an act of submission, an abnegating of our false pride, a yielding to a way which is higher and better than our own (see eh, i. 5 ; vi. 17). 4. Fro.stration of the very purport of their own Law. "For Christ is the End of the Law." All was designed to lead to him ; the holy commands were to make them know their guilt and weakness, and crave for pardon and grace ; the sacrifices and ceremonies were at once to stamp the fact of sin more deeply into their consciousness, and to give them a glimmering hope of propitiation and purifying. To Christ all these things directly and indirectly tended ; but the veil was on their eyes, that they "should not look steadfastly on the end of that which was passing away" (2 Cor. iii. 13). II. THE TR)JTII OF Goo. 1. " The righteousness which is of the Law" was, that it ehould be done by man's efforts, conjoined with the grace of God. For, according to God's intent, grace was with the giving of the Law: pardon, for realized imperfection; help, for realized frailty; the coming of Christ, as the end of all its precepts and ceremonial. But if man would ignore this element of grace, there was nothing for him but a penect fulfilling of an impossible righteousness I Doing it, he should live by it. They tried; the world bas tried: the end thereof is death I 2. "The righteousness which is of faith" bath taught us better things. (1) Not the severe effort of the soul, by ecstatic oontemplation, to attain to communion with Heaven : the Buddhist, the Christian mystic. For Heaven has come down to earth; we have but to confess the Sonship of Jesus, au.d live a life in him who has hallowed all life. (Consider the lnc~rnation, and the gift of the Spirit, as illustrating" the Word is nigh thee.") So," the trivial round," etc. (2) Not the painful anguish of the soul, as by a crucifixion, to make atonement for its guilt : the devotee, the ascetic. For the atoaement is made, and, to testify its completeness, he has risen from the dead. We have but to believe this in our heart, and then, "there is now no condemnation." Yes, the faith which works by love: accepting with all our heart the free forgiveness which is through Christ's death, and acknowledging him with our whole life as our true Lord and King. So no shame, but perfect liberty and perfect love.-T. F. L.

l. Tm: U~-n-ERSALITY OF TITE GOSPF.L IS F:VIDENT FROM rrB VERY 1"Rl!:1!:NEBB, If the La~ h&d been able of itself to justify, it might hitve seemed as though the Gentiles were without hope. But when it is perceived thl\t the Law only lMds to Ohriet, and that in Christ a free forgivene..~ is granted to sinful man, at once the conolueion is forced upon us-then t.o every sinful man. And the conclusion is just; even ae Joel h&d foresoon, "Whosoever shall call upon the Name of the Lord shitll be saved." There needs but that faith which is involved in true repentance, a ,villinaness to be eaved by grace alone, and the salvation is ours. Let, then, the true cry for help go up from any human heart, 11.nd it is answered. But it follows that if, according to God's grace, Mlvetion is such that it is, in itself, possible to every man, he must design that it shall be brought within the reach of every man. Hence the succession of questions which Paul asks, arguing that God's design to s&ve sinful man, when calling upon him in truth, implies a design that it should be possible for man to believe in him as God IJJe Saviour, which again implies the he&ring him proclaimed, which again implies a preacher of the glad tidings, which a.,,Cl'll.in implies the sending of the preachers. Yes, if such is the salvation for sinful man, God must have instituted a universal apostolate for the nations. This indeed was so (Matt. xxviil. 19; Acts i. 8). But Paul argues it, that he may justify his own mission, partly; and partly also, we may suppose, to remind them that they, the Jews, should have been the nation of apostles, that this was indeed the very intent of their election, h&d they not made the counsel of God of none effect. 0 glorious calling! 0 grievous forfeiture of high blessing I II. Tms '01,"IVEBSALITY OF THE GOSPEL WAS ANTICIPATED BY THE LAW. What had Moses sa.id to them? "I will provoke you to jealousy," etc. They had provoked God by following aft.er other gods ; God would provoke his people by seeking other peoples (se.e Deut. :o.:xil. 21). lsa.ia.h stated boldly what in the earlier words was more obscurely hinted at," I was fonnd of them," etc. (see Isa.. lxvi.). These, however, are but samples; there wa.s enough in their Law, had not the veil been on their eyes, to show that they were bnt trustees for the world, and that one of their peculiar glories was that the Gentiles should come in the fulness of time t.e do homage to their God (see Isa. lx.). Israel "did know," or at least might have known. \ III. Tms UJ;IVEBSALITY OF THE GOSPEL WAS NOT DICONSIBTENT WITH THE EXOLU• SIDli ol' lsB.A.EL PBOX rre BLESSEDNESS. The terms were, for them as for all, " Whosoever shall call," etc. And, it being impossible to c:a.11 on One whom they had not heard. the hearing was certainly not withheld from them. It wa.s true even of gospel peaching, as of the voices of the heavens (Pa. xix.), that the sound had gone into all the earth. For everywhere the gospel had been preached "to the Jew first." Yes, God had not cut them off from the blessing, but they ha.d cut themselves off. It was trne, u Isaiah had ea.id, "All the day long," etc. So the pa.rabies of Jesus (Matt. xxi., xxii.). They might have been the chosen people for the glorious work of the world's salvation; but the election was broken by their unbelief. So, then, though GoJ might surely choose or lay a.side instruments as he would, in the carrying on of his work, he did not act without reason. It was because the Jews, bei.Dg exalted to heaven, cast themselves down to hell, that they might not be the heralds of his grace. They would not receive it; therefore they could not show it forth.-T. Surely the condition of our" kinsmen according to the flesh" must be uppermost in our tho11ghts, and each man's efforts naturally commence at his own house, his own nei"hbourhood his rmn ~ation. Then, tfae'!/ we:e the descendants of men signally ~Ned in the pt:i-". Their lineage was so d1stmgu1shed, that Paul could not calmly witness the exclusion from the kingdom of God of these sons of patriarchs and prophets. They were in a Bl)",cial sense the "brethren" for whom Christ died. What more affecting to-day than to witness religious apathy in the families of the godly, to see the place of the fathers unoccupied by the children in the house of faith? And the apostle had '!Ii.awns of the splendid results that would ensue if the veil were removed from their hearts, and they should recognize in the Nazarene their wished-for Messiah. What should the receivin.,. of them into the Church be but "life from the dead"? The same reason impels u~ to seek the conversion of many around, whose talents and earnestness might be of such signal service in our ranks. As Saul the perdecutor became Paul the missionary, so we may look upon a bigoted opponent as a potential future enthusia.st in the canse c,f Christ. II. How DID THE APOSTLE'S CONCERN EXPRESS ITSELF? We answer-In hi.s preaching. He ever visited first the Jews and the synagogue in bis tonrs. It was God's design that the gospel should be first preached to his ancient people, that by rejecting or receiving the message they might either fill up the measure of their iniquity and crucify the Saviour afresh, or free themselves from the guilt of their nation and welcome the breaking down of the partition wall between Jew and Gentile. And the writings of the apostle evince his unabated regard and anxiety for the Jews. He declared that he could wish himself "anathema" from Christ, if that self-sacrifice could procure their redemption. We are reminded of the supreme act of self-abnegation by Moses on the mount, when rejecting Jehovah's offer to create from him a new people in the stead of that corrupt and obstinate generation. The apostle's Llngnage breathes the spirit of the croBB of Christ-it is an emanation to the disciple from the Master's self-immolation for the good of men. The prayers of the apostle showed the genuineness of his affectionate solicitude. Prayer is a. thermometer that gauges the warmth of our' desire to save men from misery and ruin. Does not the teacher bring the members of the class before God. in earnest petitions, and the pa.rent his children? We care little for those who a.re never mentioned in our supplications. Let us rememb£>r them where it most avails. ' IIL WHAT CONTBmUTED TO MAKE Tms DEEP CONCERN so NOTEWOBTtIT? It was prayer for men who hated and maltreated him. With rancorous unceasing enmity did the Jews pursue the apostle. They were the chief cause of his imprisonments and tortures, they did their utmost to mar his success and embitter his labours, and at last secured his death. Thinking of their attempts to overthrow the faith of Christian converts, the apostle could use strong language for their discomfiture ; but on his knees, in the solemn presence of the God and Father of all, larger and more generous thoughts possessed his soul, and he forgot all bis personal annoyances in the o'ermastering impulse to seek their salvation. If wronged by any, take the matter to the throne of grace, and you shall begin to pity and then pray for him that did the wrong. It was prayer for those who had proved obstinate, and whose ,aluation Sttmed little likely. No acquaintance with the decrees of God, nor the fact of God's forethought and foreordination, could binder the apostle's entreaties. What a lesson for us not to despair, not to faint I Our mistrust too often paralyzes our intercessions, our human reasonings "limit the Holy One of Israel." -The end of tlie I.aw, 'l'he desire for righteousness has embodied itself in diverse and some of them grotesque forms. Gather together the Pharisee with his phylacteries and ablutions ; the Chin1m1nn burning his bits of paper for ancestral worship; the Hindoo bathing in the sacrod river, or prostrating himself under the idolco.r; the Roman Catholic telling his bearls and porfonuing bis penance; and the moml youth who never omits bis daily portiou of Scripture, or bis morning and evenin~ prayo:S, and would ecllrn to toll an untruth. and one would scarce im:,~ine th:\t the S12 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO Tml BOIIA.NS. Yet the'.I"" all bear witness to man's anxioty to b righte,..,u~ in the sight of the Supreme Deing, and those l\re l\bnormally constituted who IU'e never conscious of this yMrning. It Wll8 not this strong desire for righteousness which the apostle tried to alter in the Jews, but the antiquated imperfect method to which t-hey still clung aft.er the one sure way of justification through faith in Ohrist blld been proclaimed. I. CHRIST THE TERKINATION OF THE LEGAL ECONOMY, The rending of the veil at the Crucifix.ion indi0&ted the passing away of the old dispensation, with all its gorgeous rites and e:i.:terna.l splendour. There arose another order of priesthood, from which the exclusiveness of the former caste was absent. Jesus the High Priest came not of the tribe of Le,·i. It is no longer necessary to become a Jew in order to reap the privileges of access to God. Christ has released. men from the yoke of the Law, with its fasts and fea.st.s, its observance of days and seasons. He has changed our state from pupilage to manhood; from slavery to a " reasonable service." Wherever a Christian is found, there is a spiritual priest and a living temple; wherever Christians meet, there is a holy convocation. The tabernacle disappeared when the temple was erected, and the earthly temple is no longer needed when the glorious building rises, reared without ha.nds. The Jews who would not receive this teaching had to be convinced, by the capture of Jerusalem and the burning of their "beautiful house," that "the old order changed, giving place t.o new." The forerunner of Christ was the last of the Old Testament prophets. IL CHRIST THE DESIGN AND SCOPE OF THE LEVITIOAL DISPENSATION. We cannot understand the Law unless we rega.rd it a.s pointing unmistakably to the coming Messiah, preparing bis way; a preliminary education of man.kind and of one nation in particular; like a st.ock on which a new rose is to be grafted. The sacrifices, the moral and ceremonial precepts, were predictive, were prophecy acted in symbol and type. The chrysalis displays tokens of the winged perfect insect. "The Law hath been our tntor to bring us unto Christ." So that when men inquire, "To what purpose was all this cost of legislation and ritual?" the reply is that it paved the way for something better; it was the "shlldow of good things to come." m CHRIST THE REALIZATION OF THE Moure mEAL, The holiness which the Law ever kept in view, endeavouring to raise men to its standard of righteousness, has been exemplified in Jesus Christ. Wherein the Law was weak, Christ was strong. His condemnation of sin was thorough and effective, and the perfection of his sacrifice renders any subsequent atonement need.less. To enter into the spirit of his offering is to "purge the conscience from dead works" and to give rest and peace to the troubled -the region in which the Law was inoperative. The message of Divine love sounding from the cross has a constraining influence over the affections and life of the Christian, which the Law aimed at and failed to achieve. New Testament saints have frequently attained to an enlightenment of mind and conformity to the Divine will which was sighed &ft.er in vain by patriarch, psalmist, and prophet. Christ brings bis followers into communion with God, and by faith in him a.re they sanctified. Love is proved a stronger principle than terror, knowledge than ignorance, example than precept. In abro!!Bting, Christ fulfils the Law. eo°!iCLUBIO!i. See, then. wha.t faith does. It loolcs at Christ instead of a Law oJ ardina;nces. It iB no longer tied by enactments and fearful of non-compliance, for it beholds the face of Jesus, "the Lamb 8.11 it had been slain." We may trust Christ as our Red<::emer and Guide, without understanding or acknowledging all these points of superiority over the former covenant ; as a w?ma_n kno_ws she will be benefited by a. certain medicine, though she could not name its rngredients, nor state the method of its working; or as a man may jo~rney on the railw~y w_ho comprehends li~tle of th,e application of steam to locomotives, etc. And faith is content to submit to Gods righteuusness, instead of seeking to establish its own. It relies not upon personal desert but upon the provisions of mercy furnished in Christ. It is humble, and triefi not to' patch together a. human garment to hide deformities and deficiencies, Accepting the gracioue offer of God, faith discovers new elements of strength and joy in the very '1Dsition a.l!IIUIIled.-S. In order to obviate the pretence of the gospel being a system complicated to ex~m11;1e and conform to, the ~po_stle ~uotes from_ J?euteronomy (using the passage in ll JUst16able, though Bltered s1gn16ca.t10n) to exh1b1t the simplicity a.nd brevity of the gospel requirements. Nothing impracticable is demanded of would-be converts. 'l'he "word of foith" is close at hand and intelligible, ready to be nttered and trusted. l. THE TWO ESSENTIALS TO ENJOYMENT OF THE BENEFITS OF THE GOSPEL, Belief and confession, 1. BeUef natwrally precedes confesswn, if the latter is not hypocrisy. Speech on religious questions that is not the utterance of a deep-seated conviction is like Ahimaaz running without tidings to deliver. An untimely avowal should be deprecated; the confession should stream forth from the fountain of belief; otherwise the want of correspondence between the outward declaration a.nd the inward a.ssura.nce will work deadly mischief. Let not the child's Catechism be heavily laden. To sensitive minds the ga.p will seem to widen with growing intelligence, and they will deem the alienation from the early standard greater than it is, leading perhar,s to a position of ultimate antagonism. 2. The essentials are few ,n number. Unlike the minute details of the Mosaic ritual, the law of Christ is short and easily comprehended. This apostolic declaration judges our own preaching a.nd creed, showing that we are in danger of making the gate narrower and the road longer to the kingdom than Christ ordained them. The tendency of hoary Christianity is to multiply the requisite articles of doctrine and observance, making the initiation burdensome, the novitiate cumbrous. 3. On the other hand, less than the apostle insisu on cannot prove a bond of Christian fellowship. Occasional commnnion there may be between those who differ respecting the fact of Christ's resurrection, each recognizing the other's sincerity and desire to press forward to the light; but experience attests the impossibility of -enduring religious co-operation on a slighter basis than that laid down in the text. Fundamental divergence of opinion curbs free utterance, checks the fervour of prayer, makes all parties uncomfortable in their association. II. THE PRODUCT OF F AITII. "Righteousness." Distinguish between the assent of the understanding and the trust of the heart. "Believing with" or "in the heart n not only accepts the resurrection of Christ 118 an historical fact, but sees in this a. spiritual truth, that Christ is the Media.tor, the Redeemer, able and willing to work an ethical resurrection in all who commit themselves to his care and tuition. Such a faith rejoices in the great verity; the will gladly submits to Jesus Christ as God's approved Agent of reconciliation. And thus faith imparts righteousness, co=ecting the sinner with the Saviour, the weak with the Strong One, the ignorant with the All-wise. III. THE RESULT OF CONFESSION. "Salvation." As human nature is constituted, the expression of a sentiment in word or deed lends it distinctness and potency. What the orator does for the multitude, when he translates into glowing language their vagne aspirations and inarticulate feelings, clothing, fixing, clarifying, and intensifying them, is what nn open avowal of his religious f&th often effects for the individual. It dis- closes what was wrapped up in the inner being, and the embodiment gives place and form to the idea. Sentiment unexpressed is liable to fade away like vapour uncon- densed. Confession is a real act; it makes the man commit himself definitely to a certain course of behaviour, and assists him to realize his ideal. Most are deficient in moral courage, and all that strengthens determination makes for salvation. It is easier for an avowed than for a secret disciple of Christ to refuse to yield to the solicitations of the worldly, to join them in unprofitable nmusements and practices. Then, too, confession redounds to the glory of God, who honours them that honour him. In heaven it will be no signal tribute to own him, for all there sing his praise. On earth is a sphere of distinction possible by standing up for the true, the right, the good. And so Christ promises to confess those who have confessed him. A m,utly decbrntion may confirm the faith of wavering brethren, and thus saYe ourselves and L,thers. Timidity which sea:d tho lips is n sower retaining tho seed in his bag, and allowing the w11iting soil to go unblessed with golden orops.-S. R. A.

-The nature and beneficence of God, Many surface-distinctions between the Jew and Greek may be drawn by men, but none are recognized by God in such wise III to ino11paoitate some members of the raoe for seeking salvation at his hands. THE EPISTt'E OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [en. x. 1-21,

The text fnrnisbes the basis for auoh a statC1ment of univ-ers&l salvability, In its clel\r enuncinti,)n of the nature of God. By imflication it negatives many theorlea when It RS!;erts that" the same Lord is Lord of all,' and the following olause oontaine mensuro- less rornfort for e'l'ery anxious pmying heart. He ls" rioh unto all that call upon him," I. So1ni: ERRORS OORRBOTED. 1. Polytheism. We might infer the truth of monotheism from the unity of structure visible in the world-Its inhabitants, animals, and plents; from the analogy oh.servable in different kiugdoms of nature; and from the existence of the same laws operating to the remotest star, And the Mosaio Law distinctly enforood the truth, "The Lord our God is one Lord." Nor is the doctrine of the Trinity in unity contradictory. There is the historical faot that wherever Chri!>tianity has prevailed, idolatry has been doomed. The preaching of the fishermen effected what the most potent arguments of Greek philosophy end the keentlllt shafts of ridicule failed to acromplish. 2. Atheism. This is the other extreme; instead of many gods, no God. To attribute to blind force and fortuitous collocation of atoms the order and beauty of design evident in nature and history, is to posit an ineffioient canse for the effects noted. So clearly is this seen, that the favourite attitude of many is to avoid definite assertions, and content themselves with saying, "We cannot be sure; we cannot attain to sufficient knowledge of the Unknowable to prompt our worship.• This is practical atheism, imitated by multitudes who do not deny the authority of the Scriptures, or reject religion on speculative gronnds, yet Jive "without God in the world." Remember that the non-recognition of the Deity does not absolve from religious responsibility. If there be a "Lord of all," he has claims upon your serrice which will not va.nish because of your pleasant dreams and guilty unconcern. 3. Pantheism. He is Lord "of," i.e. "over" all-a Jiving, personal God, above as well as in natnre. He is not to be identified with the universe, nor with his operations. He is different from his acts, as we are not our limbs, our deeds, but are conscious of a li'l'ing will behind these manifestations. The instinct of prayer would be checked at once by the thonght of "calling upon" an abstraction of humanity or unintelligent matter. 4. &cinianism, or the denial of the Deity of Christ. Few stronger passages could be adduced than those in the context to assure us of the apostle's conviction of the di,,anity of the Savionr. In the ninth verse we are taught to "confess Jesus as Lord," and following the emphatic language of the text comes the thirteenth verse, where the prophecy of Joel and the title Jehovah are applied to Christ, the express subject of this chapt.er. All doubt as to the reference is removed by the question, "How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?" since the object or our faith is ever represented as Christ, the manifested God. The only refuge is to deny the competency and inspiration of the apostle, and then we do not get rid of the other Scripture texts which speak of him as the Creator "by whom all things were made," and the Judge "to whom all authority is committed." No declaration of the relationship of the Son to the Father, more available for explanation of the mystery, can we have than "he is the Image of the invisible God." 6. Sectarianism, or Judaism u a system of rites, the embodiment of the narrow bigoted spirit which will admit ooly certain claSl!eB within its pale. Most scornful epithets did the Jews employ with respect to the unprivileged state of the rest o~ mankind; they were "the _drops of the bucket the offscouring of all things." But if the whole world may claim the same Lord, ~ne family dares not arrogat.e to itself all the Divine love and blessing. What is the miserable mperiority of the giant to the dwarf in the view of him who gazes from the mountain-top? The regard of God is to quality, not quantity; he wants the pure gold of repentance and obedience, no matter with what ingredients or amid what l!DJTOundings it may be found. Jesus Christ taught us to abolish caste by the petition, "Oar Fa.ther." In the present conditjon of religions knowledge and feeling, sects may be convenient, almoet iwce1111&ry, but we need not unchristianize those without our borders nor confine our view of aalvation to those who utter the same party shibboleth. IL A'!'BUTH oF OOllFOBTABLE IKPOBT--THE BENEFICENCE OF Gon. 1. His wealth r,errr.ite Mm to do good t<, all. The slowly passing centuries have not enable.i men to fo:.ci out the extent of the Divine riches. The catalogue is cxhaustleee that is being cw:,piloo of the ada.pta.tions, combinations, resources, with which the Creator has furni!!Lt:d ni.an'• home. Then, whi!Bt the mlcroscq>e reveall Innumerable lntlniteslrnnl wowicni, the telescope dileuver• OOUDtlese worlds. And the apoatle delighted In the

use of the word II riches" to describe the mercies of God In redemption. He felt he he.d to publish a purpose of God rich !n _wi~on:i, love, and power, dwarfing all b•irmm 11ystems of reform. The Lord of Cbrist1amty 111 IIO supremely glorioU11 that it wae a. relief to tum away from human poverty in thought ancl means, to contemplate "the treasures of wisdom o.nd knowledge bidden in Christ." 2. B6 is rich, m oil that hi~ creatwes need. Circumlocution offices abound on earth. The kin"' cannot heal the leper, nor the doctor give legal information to the suitor, nor the la;,yer be expected to hee.d the subscription list. But none can seek Christ in vain for spiritual wants. He i11 rich in mercy to the penitent sinner, and to the believer forgetful of bis early vows he is rich in the assurance of forgiveness and succour. The di3appr,inted may find him an unfailing Hope, the bereaved a "God of all consolation;" to the tempted he is the" Way of escape," and to the heated with the straggle of life," the Shadow of a great rock." 3. A benevolent Lord. "Rich unto all." Many a wealthy man is not "rich unto" anybody else-not even unto himself', poor niggardly soul. God sits not as a miser gloating over his goods, or as a king ensconced in the palace, where no cry of the poor or of the anguished can reach him. He delights to give; the glory of God is revealed in blessing his creatures. Love created, BU11tains, enriches, the unive1'3e. We need not fear coming too often or asking too largely. We shall not weary his generosity, or appeal too late to hi.~ exchequer because a more fortunate applicant anticipated our request. Invited tu his banquet, he will not thank you for partaking scantily of the rich fare, lest you should trespass on his bounty. 4. The one restric- ion. Only one condition is to l,e fulfilled-that we " call upon him." This is but reasonable. We receive daily benefits unasked, bat in the concerns of the soul we are treated as intelligent beings, as children whose voice the Father loves to hear. The prayer of mingled contrition and trust purifies and exalts the suppliants, honours and gratifies the Donor or good. The character of the petition manifests the spiritual state or the petitioner. Set the desires not so much upon the promi~es of physical relief as of spiritual blessing, not so much the removal of the trial as strength to bear it, not so much the extraction of the thorn as grace to submit patiently and to see wise purposes subserved by the infliction. What simpler counsel could be given to the heavy-laden sinner than this, "call upon him"? Like Peter amid the waves, cry out, "Lord, save me!" and Divine help shall respond, and you" shall be saved." And when the hour of death draws_ nigh, though we mo.y not be surrounded by taunting foes, and no cruel blows may hasten our departure, yet, like the dying martyr, we may pa.."11 "calling upon the Lord, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."-S. In the previous chapter we saw a Christian patriot lamenting that so many of his fellow~ountrymen, through rejecting God's mercy manifested in Christ Jesus, were becoming mere vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. At the same time, he sees in Divine sovereignty, its incidence and its justice, the real clue to the philosophy of history and the progress of the world. In the present chapter he discusses the rejection of Israel and its reasons, and the nature of that acceptance and salvation which the Gentiles received after the Jews had despised them. In the verses now claiming attention we have the apostle leading his readers up to faith in and confession of a risen Saviour. J. THE MISDIREOTED ZEAL OF THE .APOSTLE'S COUNTRYl!E~. (Vers. 1---3.) The apostle's desire and " supplication " (so Revised Version) for the Jews was that they might be saved. But, alas I their misdirected zeal was preventing their salvation. For instead of submitting to the righteousness which is of God, instee.d of making their way to Cllrist, who is the End to whom the Law when properly understood leads, they were going about with the one object of astablishing their own righteousness. This zoal P11ul knew himself experimentally. For years he also had aimed at Law-keeping, and in his self-ignorance he thought tllat "touching the righteousness which is in the Lo.w" he wns "blameless" (Phil. iii. 6). But the Law-keeping may be in the letter and not in the spirit. The spirit of the Law is love; yet Paul and tho Pharisees tithed mint and anise and cummin, whilo they lived lives of hate, and hesit~lted not to porsocuto Christ-like people even to the death. To keep self-righteousness before the soul ns the end of lifu is simply misdirected zeal. It keeps us nw:\y from Christ and all tho bliss whloh his followship ituplios. his roundabout way, going a.bout to establish his own righteousness, wl\s I\ delusion, a sna.re, a loss, and not a. gain, for it kept him long years from Christ. Let us be clonr that we a.re not under a. simila.r delusion. Let us give up self-righteousneea and ta.ke God's better wav. II. A RISEN SAVIOUll IB THE END OF THE LAW AND OnJECT OF' FAITH, (Ver. 4.) Now, the moment we a.re led t.o take a spiritual view of God's Law, to see that it demands perfect mot'ive as well as decent outward morality, we see that we cannot keep it in its length and breadth; and therefore, instead of living by Law-keeping, we a.re condemned by the Law as its transgressors. Self-righteousness is seen to be selfdeoeption. Condemnation is seen to be our natural state. Then is it that Christ and his perfect righteousness dawn upon our condemned and polluted souls. We see that he has done for us what we cannot do for ourselves, and so the Law serves its purpose when it lays us down at the feet of Christ, to be justified by faith. Instead of trusting our own righteousness, we see in our risen Saviour the true Object of faith and Source of righteousness. We pass out of shame into confidence in his finished work.1 III. Tms 11.ISEN SHIOUR IS EASILY FOU1''D. (Vers. 6-9.) The idea of the human heart is that by some prodigious effort salvation must be secured. Abana and Pharpar are further off, as well as likelier rivers, than this brawling Jordan hard by, and so Naaman cries out, " May I not wash in them, and be clean?" Only ask us to do some great thing in order to salvation, and our self-righteousness will be secured, and we shall be satisfied (cf. 2 Kings v. 12, 13). A far-off salvation suits man's taste the best. Set it in heaven, and he will reek his brains for some ingenious device by which he will fly away and be at rest. Set it beyond the sea, and boats will be built and the voyage nndertaken with alacrity (cf. Dent. xxx. 11-13). Make salvation to consist in a bringing of Christ down from above, and men like Titans will try to scale Olympus. Make salvation to consist in a descent to the lower world to bring Christ up from the dead, and many will try a journey like Orpheus after the lost Eurydice, to bring the Saviour from the shadows. But we have got to see that the risen Saviour is not so far away or so hard to find as thls. As Charles Kingsley once wrote to a la.dy, " My object has been and is, and I trust in God ever will be, to make people see that they need not, u St. Paul says, go up into heaven, or go down to the deep, to find Christ; because he, the Word whom we preach, is very near them, in their hearts and on their lips, if they would but believe it; and ready, not to set them a.float on new and untried oceans of schemes and projects, but ready to inspire them to do their duty humbly and simply where he has put them-and, believe me, the only way to ?'e!!enerate the world is to do the duty which lies nearest us, and not to hunt after ~ far-fet.<:hed ones for onrselves." 1 In the Word of the gospel the risen Saviour comes near to every one of us. We do not require any prodigious effort to reach him, We have simply to opei. the eye of faith, and there he is. IV. THE Jll8E!i S.AVIOUB MUBT BE CONFESSED WREN FOUND. (Vera. 10, 11.) Faith in a risen Saviour wbo is waiting to be found of us must prove its genuineness by the confession of hie Name. It is when we take the Lord's side deliberately that we have tested the reality of our faith. There is a cowardly tendency to helieve, but not confess• to get the benefits of salvation without running a single risk for our Saviour. But' such a selfish, easy-going faith is mere delusion. Whoever really believes in Jesus will not be ashamed to confess him. And conaequently we are encouraged first to believe that God raised Jesus from the dead, and then to confess him as our risen Saviour before men. There is undoubtedly a disposition to separate salvation from confession of G'hrist. It is thought to be wise and prndent to accept of the benefits Christ can offer anti at the same time to be silent about them. "Secret disci pies hip" is thought to be- a maBterpi~ of wJsdom. Every~hing. is thus gained, aud nothing risked or lost. But is everythmg gamed? Is nothrng risked or lost? Is the secret disciple ever likely to become a man of nobility and courage? Does he secure even self-respect? Must he not feel very much as a debtor who is ~]ways trying to shirk his obJigatic,ne and ignr,re the debt? (!r take the ma~tcr .rn. the ~oncrcte. entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The natwral history of faith. From an acconnt of the plan of salvation as faith in and confession of a risen Saviour, the apostle, in the verses now before us, proceeds to consider the natural history of the faith which Jew and Gentile are led to place in the one Lord. For it is most important to know bow faith is induced. And here we notice- I. THE RISEN LORD IS WITHIN EVERY ONE'S CALL. (Vers. 12, 13.) There is no difference in his accessibility to both Jew and Gentile. "He is rich unto all that call upon him." With the sovereigns of this world court-favourites are the rule, and I suppose there is no exception. Only certain individuals get near the king, and are favoured with an audience. But this risen Lord over a.II can be rich unto every one that cares to call upon him. Let Jew or Greek only cry to him, and the needful help will come. This suggests the following comforting thoughts. 1. The throne on which, owr Lord now sits is a throne of grace. He is to sit, indeed, one day on a throne of judgment; meanwhile let us rejoice that he sits on a "throne of grace." It is to help the needy and the lost that he now sits enthroned. We are now under a "reign of grace." We hear a good deal in the present day of a" reign of law:" what consolation it is to think that, so far as Christ is concerned, we are all under a "reign of grace"! 2. He can hear directly every one that calls upon him. Of course, such a fact implies that our risen Saviour is indeed Divine. By virtue of his Divinity, he can hear everybody, whether Jew or Gentile, who cares to call upon him, and can deal directly with them. 'l'he many-voiced cry of lost and tempted souls reaches hia ear e.nd is all interpreted. It is easy to state the case of Christ hearing prayer, but it is overwhelming to imagine what such an arrangement demands from the blessed Being upon the throne. Yet it is sober fact-the whole cry of the race, the bitter cry of lost and tried souls, enters the sympathizing mind of our Divine Saviour and King. 3. He is rich to all the petitioners. Just as when on earth he allowed no one to go empty away, so from his throne of grace on high there is no real petitioner dismissed without relief. He encourages Jew and Gentile alike to call upon him, and then treats us in a way that becomes a King. He does far more "exceeding abundantly for us above all that we ask or think, e.ccording to the power that worketh in us." If we ask him to eave us, he does so with an everlasting salvation. If we ask him to pardon ns, he does so with overflowing love. If we e.sk him to sanctify us, he enables us to die daily unto sin and to live unto righteousness. If we ask him to make us useful, he opens doors of usefulness for us of the most surprising character. In short, " Eye bath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God he.th prepared for them that love him. But he bath revealed them unto us by hie Spirit" (1 Cor. ii. 9, 10). II. BuT AN OMNIPRESENT SA VIOUB NEEDS THE BEAUTIFUL FEET OF ms HERALDS TO DE UPON ALL THE MOUNT.Arns IF lllEN ARE TO KNOW RIS NKARNESS. (Vars. H, 15.) We have seen thl\t the risen Saviour is within every one's call. But he is not palpablt1 to sense. He is unseen. His presence is spiritual. Only by heralds going forth to proclaim the glad tidings of his presence are men led to call upon him. And the heralds address the el\rB of men. By this pa.rtioular a.venue of hearing does tht1 message oome. If men never hear of Jesus, they cannot be ti:tpected to realize his presence or to trust him. And so n propaganda is necessary, and the rui~iouary enterprise is just such a propaganda to brino- before Jew and Gt,ntile the splendid fact thnt a risen Saviour is within each man's ~11. dist.ing11igJuid from any natural reflective enlightenment; while thi\t • heariu"' cometh by the \Vord of God,' ariseth out of a.n express revela.tion uttered from heaven~ in oon4 tnu:t t-0 every system, devioe, or imagination of unassisted human reason," 1 This being ~o, we can underatand how the apostle quotes the rapturous words of the prophet about the beautiful feet of the heralds of glad tidings. The institution of the preaching of the gospel is the most beaut.iful now existing among men. III. THE GLAD TIDINGS HAVE NOT HAD A UNIVERSAL IIEOEPTION. (Vers. 16-18.) In !'Ome oases the heralds have had small success. As Esaias cries, "Lord, who hath believ8'1 our report?" so ha.s many a minister lamented his scant success. For, amid the multitude of compet.ing things and persons palpable to sense, an unseen Saviour gets ignored by many. The problem was not, in the missionary a~e of Paul, as to many not hearing of a Saviour at all-rather was it that so many hearo. of him, yet gave no heed. For the apostle in this passage quotes what in the nineteenth psalm is applied t-0 nature, as if the gospel message, at least in his day, had been as widely proclaimed as the limits of the world allowed. And when we consider the population of the world in Paul's timP, and how it wa.s practically within the grasp of the Roman empire, and t.hat informa.t.ion filteroo down t-0 the distant colonies more surely perhaps than, though not so speedily as, news does nowadays; and when we add to this the magnificent missionary spirit which animated Paul and his associat.es, he had reason to take up the universal. terms and apply them t.o the propa.,aation of the gospel. So that the gospel was more widely proclaimed in the first century in proportion to the population of the globe than it is as yet in the nineteenth. The contrast which now obtains between the revelation of God in nature and the revelation of God_ in the gospel in their respective relations t.o mankind-the one being universal, the other partial in its application-has been largely, if not entirely, due t.o the lack of enterprise and mis- sionary spirit on the part of the Church. .And yet t.oo much may be made of this coutrast, and men may fail to see that the proclamation of a revealed religion is the one way in which God is likely t.o receive attention from his creatures. The followiog quotation from .Archer Butler upon the point will be welcome. "If God were t.o int.erfere at all, they [the deists] maintain, it would be by some universal agency, simple, gene.ml, and obvious, as the laws of his visible creation. '.!'hey smile at the notion of God's greatest exhibition of his will t.o man being acted upon the reduced theatre of a petty province, and made dependent on the chances of human testimony, • In the moral as in the physical world,' exclaims the leader of the sentimental school of deism, • it is ever on a great see.le, and by simple means, that Deity operates.' But what if we ret.ort that it is those very laws of nature 'on a great scale '-those very • lllimple means '-that have cansed God to be forgotten? Not justly, we admit; for they ougl.t eminently to have convinced men of his presence and power: but what of that? We are not now speaking of argumentative propriety, but of actual fact; not of man as he ought to be, but of man as he is. And it is an undeniable fact that it is the permanence and uniformity of the natural laws of the creation tho.t have beguiled men into specnlative, and, still more, int.o practical atheism; that it is the very perfection of the laws which has hidden the Legislator. The band that God bas constructed so wondrously can write, • There is no God ; ' let it be smit with sudden paralysis, and the notion of a.n intervening Avenger will arise; nay, let us at any tim~ behold some strange unique in any of the departments of ~xperience, and it s~rtles our habitual slumber. That is to Bay, as long aa the work lB perfect, we recognize no worker; but the moment it becomes deficient (the very thing which ought logically to produce the doubt) we begin t.o conceive and admit his reality, The more apparently capricious the w~ks of nature, the more they resemble man's; and the more they remind us of direct agency a.nalO!!oWI to the human.
