entries.content:
-The lit1ing sacryio& In the oldest reoords that can be found of the various nations of the e.'U'th, sacrifice is always fonnd to have formed part of their religious sernces. Thus we find an idea universally existing that something was needed to obtain pardon for guilt, and to express gratitnde to the supreme being or beings whom they regarded as the givers and benefactors of their life. But it is only when we come to the religion of Israel that we find the idea of sa.crifice having any influence upon the life. The other na.tions offered sacrifices, but there was no turning away from evil. Kay, in the case of ma.ny heathen countries, their acts of religious worship beoame, and have become, associated with immoral and degrading practices. The religion of Israel, however, tanght the necessity of personal holiness. True, their religion wa.s largely composed of rites and ceremonies, but it was a. religion of pra.ctical mora.lity aL"O. Very plainly the Jewish psalmist recognizes that it is the sacrifice of a broken and contrite heart that is most acceptable to God, a.nd that without this it is vain to offer the blood of bulls and goats. But the high precepts of their religion were sadly neglected by the Jews in later years. In the time of Jesus Christ on earth, the religion of most of them was a religion of ritual and routine. He told the Pharisees that though they outwardly appeared righteous unto men, within they were full of hypocrisy and iniquity. But Jesus came to teach men true religion. The worship that he demands is a worship in ipirit and in truth. The sacrifice tha.t he requires is a sacrifice of our life. He wants the activities and energies of body, soul, and spirit to be consecrated to his service. This is what the apostle means when he speaks of presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice. I. IT IS TO BE A SACRIFICE OF OUR FEELINGS. The whole heart must be given up to God, so that whatever is right may be strengthened, and that whatever is wrong may be taken away. Many Christians render to Christ an imperfect sacrifice in this respect. They keep back part of their life from him. They allow themselves to be dominated by feelings which are inconsistent with his spirit and precepts. They will excw;e them.selves for some besetting sin by saying, "That is my nature; I can't help it." The evil nature is still with ns, it is true; but it is our duty to strive against it, to overcome it. :Moses appears to have been at first a man of hasty and violent temper. Yet the Divine discipline, and no doubt also his own obedience to the Divine will, produced such a change in his character that it is afterwards recorded of him, .. Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men who were' upon the face of the earth." It is a natural thing to be angry when things are said or done to provoke us; but is it Christian? So with the other feelings of envy, of pride, of revenge, of hatred-instead of yielding to them or excnsing them, the true Christian will be ashamed of them and sorry for them, and will do his beet to overcome their influence in his heart. II. IT IS TO BE A SACRIFICE OF OUR AFFECTIONS. The love of God should ever be the chief affection of our heart. Not that we are to love our friends less, but we are to love God more. Hence, when our natural affections become hindrances in the Christian life, they must be restrained and subdued. The strongest temptations to t1e Cbri5tian are not always those that come from the baser part of his nature, but 60 metimes those that come from the purer and better emotions of the soul. The love of a friend-it might seem strange that there should be anything wrong in that. Yet even this affection, right and natural in itself, becomes wrong when it interferes with love to God. The love of home-how can there be anything wrong in that? Yet there is wror:,g in it when it interferes with the call of duty. "He that loveth father or mother more than me," says Christ, "is not worthy of me; and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me." When the din of war begins to resound throughout a land, the man who has dedicated himself to the military 11ervioe of his country does not hesitate to obey the trumpet-call. His farm or his business may require his presence, ar:d °;lay ~uffer ~eriou~ly by his abse~ce.. It is a sore trial v, war himself away from bis Wlfo, from his family, and from lu11 friends, whose fa.cos ht may IJever 11W again in this world. But lwwevcr proesing the claims of his daily work may be, however lltrong his domestic ties, all these CQUJjiderations mus~ now give mr, m.1-21.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 369

wo.y to tho demo.nd of p11tric,tism and of duty. And shall not the Christian soldier encrifico o.11 oarthly affections rather than be unfaithful to Ghrist? Shall he rnt hear the voice of Jesus o.bove all e11rthly voices? Of such complete self-denial Christ himeolf has gi~en ~ls ~he best em~ple. "~~ pie~ not himself." Not merely in his death, but ID his hfo, he gave himself a hvrng sacnfice. When we thiuk of hr,w much we owe to Christ, any sacrifice that we can make will seem but a poor and feeble effort to show our gratitude and our love. Yet we are encouraged to present even our poor so.orifice by the assurance that it will be " acceptable unto God." -C. H. I.

entries.title: ROM 12:2
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-The two likenesses. The exhortation contained in this verse re7ards the human mind as impressiouable, pliable, sU8Ceptible. It is especially add-;.essed to Christians. There are two forms which seek to impress themselves upon the Christian and the image of which every Christian bears in greater or less degree. The one i~ likeness to the world ; the other is likeness to God. I. LIKENESS TO THE WORLD. Against this the apostle warns the Christian: "Be not conformed to this world." 1. The exhortation is mwh needed. The ambition of many Christians is to be as like the world as possible. They talk of the extreme of Puritanism, and speak of being too strict. The danger now is from the extremof worldliness. If I nm to choose, let me have the extreme of being too scrupdom rather than too careless, ultra-conscientious rather than having a conscience that sees no harm in anything. Let me be like Abraham, who would not take from a thread even to a shoe-latchet from the King of Sodom, rather than like worldly minded Lot, who pitched bis tent toward Sodom, and by-and-by came and dwelt in Sodom, though he vexed his righteous soul from day to day with the filthy conversation and unlawful deeds of the people among whom be bad chosen to d we!L Let me be like Elisha rather than Gehazi, like Daniel rather than Belshazzar. 2. OonfOTmity to the world is injurious to the Church. When the Jewish people came in contact with the heathen nations, they began to imitate them, to conform to their customs. The result was disastrous to the spiritual life, aud ultimately to the temporal prosperity of Israel. So it was with the Churches of Asia. Their worldliness proved their ruin. Sardis had a name to live, but it was dead. Laodicea was lukewarm, and neither cold nor bot. We may try as Christians to please the world by conforming to it, but in proportion as we do so we are unfaithful to our Master, and we are displeasing him. "The friendship of this world is enmity against God." 3. The conformity of Christians to the world is in}urious to the world. Some Christians imagine that they will have more influence on the world by becoming more like it. It is a great mistake. If we want to teach children to write, we don't set them imperfect copies. The world was never made better by low ideals. The deities of pa..,cra.n.ism did not elevate humanity. It is not the half-and-half Christian, the worldly minded Christian, whose influence will tell for good upon those around him. If we are to make the world better, it can only be by keeping before us as Christians a high idea.I of what the Christian life ought to be, and by striviug faithfully, and with the help of Divine grace, to live np to it. Christians are living epistles, known and read of all men. What kind of copy are we setting to the world? 4. We are not to imitate the wOTld in its estimate of religion. 'l'be world's idea. of religion is that it is a thing of gloom, an irksome restraint, a we:ll'y bondage, something that it would be desirable to have wheu death is sppl'L'..'\Ching, but which it would be well to live without as long as possible. Too often Uhristi:ms gi,tl encourngement to this idea. Their religion has too little relation to their daily lifo, or a relation of routine form rather than of living and pleasaut association. 5. We a,,, not to imitate the world in its estimate of tlie soul. In the popular estirustion, and in everyday life, the soul is thrust into the background. The chief couceru is how to provide comfort and luxury for thti body. No expense is grudged for these ol~~>cts. Uodily health is scrupulously guMded, nnd rightly so. Educatiou is carefully stteuded to. How anxious parents aro, and rightly so, to secure a i:oo<l educatiou for their children I But how little trouble is taken to instruct them or have them instructed in etornril things I How little care, cronerally, is dovoted to the concerus of the immort:u eo. ul I In this rospoot professing 6hristians aro too linble to be conformed to the world. ']'hoy become too muoh absorbed in the world's busiuess to thiuk ,\$ mu.:h ns they 11ugl1t of thoir own spiritu1111. lifo n11l\ Q' t4o svujs of vthtJrs. Christinu p:\M1ts :\re often U0¥ANB, 2Q 370 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [oR, xn.1-21,

,ery c\ueless in regnrd to the spiritual instruction of their children. Let us not boar the world's likC'ness. "Come ye out from among them, and be yo separate;" "Bo not conformed t-o this world." II. LIKE:S-El'S TO Goo. "But be yo t.rangformed by the renewing of your mind." 1. Th,~. ,s the way to drive out W·eness f.o the tl'orld. Likeness to God will exclude likeness to the world. The more desire we have for God, tho loss wo shall have for the world; the more we think of the soul, the less we shall be anxious about tho body; the more we think of eternity, the less we shall think of this present world; the m0re we think of the judgmcnt of God, the less we shall think of the judgment of men. :!. The first step is the renewing of your mind. An external influence is here implied. We cannot renew our own minds. " Except a man be born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God." This is rightly called the saving change. 'l'o experience this change is the starting-point of the Christian life. It is to pass from death to life. Old things pass away; all things become new. There is a new way of looking at things. Things which we once took pleasure in have no attraction for us now; duties which we once thought irksome now become our delight. This is the result of the Holy Spirit working in us, producing in us likeness to God, transforming us into his image, bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Jesus Christ. 3. Thi.s transformation will soon affect your whole life. (1) It will affect your business. You will no longer regard your business dealings from the merely worldly, but from the Christian standpoint. Your question will not be merely-Will it pay? but-Is it right? (2) lt will affect your companionsliips. The question will be, not-Are they pleasant? but-Are they pleasing to God? are they helpful to my spiritual li:"e? (3) le will affect your amusements. The question will be, not -May I? but-Ought I? Not-Is there any harm in this? but-ls there any good in it? Is it the way in which I would enjoy myself if I knew that I was to die tomorrow? When Achilles Daunt, late Dean of Cork, was a student at Trinity College, Dnblin, be was passionately fond of the drama, and used to go often to the theatre. One e,ening, after coming home and taking up his Bible for his usual evening reading -feeling that the scenes he had just witnessed made it a little irksome to do so-his eye lit on our Lord's words, " He that is not with me is against me.'' 'l'he passage seemed to seize him with an iron grip. He then and there battled out the matter with his own he.art, and did not rise from his knees till he had.resolved to dedicate himself to the Lord. to take his stand boldly as his servant, and never again to enter a theatre. 4. Thu transformation is to be d,eveloped by living near to God. Prayer, and the study of God's Word, are the means of obtaining this likeness to God. It is noteworthy that the same Greek word which is here translated "transformed" is the word which is mied to describe the transfiguration of Christ: " And he was transfigured before them." And when did Christ's transfiguration come to him? When he was on the mountain-top in prayer. "And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glistering" (Luke ix. 29). Prayer is the nue transformation, the true transfiguration, of the soul. Thus here on earth we shall reflect in some measure the image of God until we reach tha.t land where " we shall ba like him, for we shall see him as he is."-C. H. I.

entries.title: ROM 12:3–8
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Divenity and T/111,ity in the <Jhurch of Ohriat. The subject of union among the various branches of the Church of Christ is one to which much attention has of late years been turned. The efforts of the Evangelical Alliance bave been largely directed to secure a more brotherly relationship and more hearty co-operation between the different denominations of Christiane. Some Christians desire an organic union of all sections of the Church, but the passage before us indicates that there may be outward diversity alon" with inward and real unity. L D1VEBBI;Y AND UNITY Il!I' THE BODY. "We have many members in one body, aod all members have not the same office'' (ver. 4). There we have diveraity. What diversity there is between the organs of hearing and seeing, tasting and touching, speaking aod smelling I What a _complex organism is that of he~rt and, brai~, and veins and arteries, and nerves and s10ews I Yet ,here too we have wnity. 'Ihere 1s one body. One life throbs in all the part8. Il. D1VElibITY AND UNITY DT THE Cuoncr.c. "So wo, being many, aro one bodf

in Obrist, and every one members one of another" (ver. 6). There we l,ave diversity. 'l'b~re is. room for di_versHy in Jhe Church of Christ-for valied forms of wor~hip, for varied views of doctrme, for varied methods of Church government. A dull unifr,rmity is undesirable. "Acts of Uniformity" only made more diversity, and produced disrhrd instead of unity. When the Church of England had no room for John Wesley, gh,:i only prepared the way for a larger secession from the ranks of her membership. &>, too, in individual coogregations, there is room for varied gifts and activities. TM-re, also, we have unity. "One body, and every one members one of another." There is the unity of the Spirit, the unity that arises from the common bond of faith in Christ and love to him, of obedience to the same Divine law, and of the inspiring hope of the same heaven. III. Two PRACTICAL LESSONS. 1. A lesson of humi1ity. "For I say, tbrou"'h the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly" (ver. 3). The recognition of the fact that there are varied gifts in the Church of Christ will prevent any one from being unduly proud of any gifts he may possess, or any work he may have done. All the members of the body have need of one another. There is a place for the humble and unlearned workers in the Church of Christ,just as much as for the wealthy and the cultured and the learned. 2. A lesson of C-0'11,C81/,tratwn. Division of labour and concentration of individuals upon particular branches is one of the great principles of modem manufacturing and commerce. St. Paul applies the same principle to Christian work. "Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let'us prophesy according to the proportion of faith; or ministry, let ns wait on our ministering; or he that teacheth, on teaching; or he that exhorteth, on exhortation; he that giveth, let him do it with liberality; he that rnleth, with diligence; he that showeth mercy, with cheerfulness." There are three special spheres of Christian work. (1) Teaching. Under this heo.d may be comprised what the apostle speaks of as "prophecy," "teaching," "exhortation." This is the work of ministers of the gospel, of professors in colleges, of teachers in daily schools and in Sunday schools. There could be no more important work than that of instructing others, moulding immortal souls, inspking old and young with the power of great principles. Wbeu Socrates was asked why he did not commit to writing his philosophic opinions and teachings, hli! answer was, "I write upon human souls. That writing will last eternally." How important that a.11 who engage in any department of teaching shoul,l realize the abiding consequences of their work, and should devote their best energies to it I (2) Ruling. There must of necessity be authority and discipline in the Christian Church. Impenitent offenders against Christian morality need to be excluded. Differences of opinion or quarrels between brethren need to be wisely considered, and breaches bee.led. How necessary that those who nre placed in positions of authority should rule "with diligence," realizing their high responsibility to preserve ihe peace and.maintain the purity of the Church of Christ! (3) Giving. Under this head may be included not only what is here called " giving," but also those branches spoken of e.s "ministering" and " showing mercy." Christians who are not teachers or rulers ought at least to be givers. If they have money to give for Christ's cause, let them give it, and give it, too, with liberality, in no selfish and in no niggard spirit. Every Christian can give something for the building up of the Church of Christ. We can give our time. We can give our attention to the poor, to the sick, to the stranger. Let Christians remember that in the n~tuml body there are no useless or idle members. Each member has its own distinct function, So is it in the Christian Church. There is some special work for every one to do.-C. H. L Vere. 9--21 (omitting vers.11 and 12, for which see below).-Tlw Chnstian'• duty to hisfeZlow-men. In these closing verses of this chapter the apostle sets before us the duty of a Christion man. It is a picture of what the Christian ought to be. What n world it would be if these precepts were carried out, if even every Christian wt1:1 careful to observe them I Six features the apostle mentions which should oho.rsctcriz<l our dealings with others. I. SINCERITY. "Let love be without dh1simulation" (ver. 9). Unreality, falsehood. insinoority, Ulltruthfulness,-these are prevalent ovils in our day. They weaken all 372 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. [m. xn.1-!1.

confident'E' bc-tween mAn and mAn. They destroy don1csUo pence, eoolnl interoourse, and commercial morality. Truthfulness And sincerity Are muoh needed. II. DJFCBTMINATION. "Abhor t.hat which is evil; cleave to that which ia good" (ver. ~). The spirit of indifference is another prevalent evil·of our time. "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil." Dr. Arnold at Rugby, trying to elevate the i:tandard. of ch&l'I\Cter there, found this difficulty-indifference about evil. He said, "What I mmt to see in the school, and what I cannot find, is an abhorrence of evil ; I always think of the psalm,• Neither doth he abhor; that which is evil.'" We want more discrimin&tion. The young espxially need to discriminate in their friendships, and to choose the society of gooJ men and good women. m G~"'EROSITY. "Distributing to the necessity of saints" (ver. 13). In exercising generosity, God's people, our brethren in Christ, should have the first claim upon us. But we are not to limit our attentions to them. "Given to hospitality," we shall show kindness to strangers, just because they are strangers and are away from home and friends. How truly the Christian religion teaches men consideration for others! IV. SYMPATHY. "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (ver. 15). Sympathy is a Christ-like quality. Sympathy for the perishing brought Jesus Christ t.o earth. Sympathy sent Henry Martyn to Persia, Adoniram Judson to Burmab., David Brainerd to the Red Indians, David Livingstone and Bi11hop Han.nington to Africa. Sympathy led Mr. E. J. Mather to brave the dangers of the deep in order to do something for the temporal and spiritual welfare of the deep-sea :fishermen of the North Se&. We want more sympathy for those near us-for the poor, the sick, the suffering, the careless, at our own doors. We need to learn also how to sympathize with innocent enjoyment. The mission of the Christian Church is not a mission of amusement, bnt it can show that it does not frown upon, and can thoroughly enter into, the innocent pleasures and recreations of life. We are not only to "weep with them that weep," but also "rejoice with them that do rejoice." V. HUKILITY. "Mind not high things, but condescend to man of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits." There is too much pride even in the Church of Christ-pride of rank, pride of wealth, pride of learning. The condition of things so severely satirized and rebuked in the second chapter of James is still too common in the Christian Church. The Church of Christ needs to condescend a little more than it does "t.o men of low est.ate." Christian ministers need to think more of the humbler members of their congregations, while they do not neglect the spiritual welfare of the rich. A little more of the humility of Christ would make the Church of Christ and the ministers of religion more respected among the working classes and the poor. VI. PEACEFULNESS. " If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (ver. 18). This peaceful relation may be secured: 1. By not cherishing a vindict-if1t! spirit. "Recompense to no man evil for evil" (ver. 17). "Dearly beloved, avenge not yoarselves" (ver. 19). Offenders against peace would do little harm if they did not find others only too ready t.o take offence. What an example is that of Cranmer!- " To do him any wroDg was to beget A kindneB& from him; for his heart was rioh, Of S11cb fine mould, that if you sowed therein The Beed of bate, it bloBBOmed charity." 2. By meeting enmity with ki'IUVMIB. "BleSB them which persecute you: bless, and curse not" (ver. 14). "Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him d.rin.k: : for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Your kindness will be li.k..e coals of fire to melt h.i.B hardened heart, just as Jaoob's prudent act of kind- IJt,&, following on his prayer, turned away the anger of h.i.B injured brother Esau. Bo we may destroy our enemies, as the Chinese emperor is eaid to have done, by making t,b.tm our friends. ThWI we shall "overcome tvil with good."-C. H. L

entries.content:
-77ie Ohrl,Ua,1,'s dutg to himself. Whlle we are to think of others, we are to think of our11el'f'ea also. Herbert Spencer has contrasted the "religion of enmity,". or the religion of heatheni1m, with what he ea.lie the " religion of amiti," or thB religiun of Ghrii,tiattity. :Uut he epee.kl .. if_ the Chrilltian precept was, "Thou shoJt mt. xn. 1-21.] THE EPIBTtE Ot PAt/L TO TBE ROMANS. 373

love thy neighbour better than thyself." It is not so. The comm.and is "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." ' "To thine own self be trne, And It must follow, as the night the nay, Thou canst not then be false to BDy i.aan." The apostle enumerates some duties which the Christian owes to hilllBelr. I. DILIGFJNOE IN BUSmEsS. Each man should have some definite work or bnsiness in life. Especially should the Christian be free from the sin of idleness. Whatever our work is, let us be diligent in the performance of it. "The hand of the diliuent maketh rich." "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he ·shall stand Wore kings; he shall not stand before mean men." II. EARNESTNESS 011' sPmIT. "Fervent in spirit." It is a strong phrase. Fervent means "burning," "on fire." Yes, we need more Christians who are on fire. It is the enthusiasts who have done the best and most lasting work in the world. They are usually called fanatics at first, but the day comes when their memory is blessed. St. Paul was a fanatic to Festus. Festus could not understand the fire that burned in Paul's heart and in his words. " Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learnin" doth make thee mad." William Wilberforce, the emancipator of the slaves; John H;ward, the prisoner's friend; Samuel Plimsoll, the sailor's friend; Lord Shaftesbury, the friend of the overworked artisan ;-all these men at first were sneered at and ridiculed by the multitude of indifferent and interested men. Earnestness and enthnsia.sm may be incomprehensible to the world, but they are indispensable to the trae Christian. III. A RELIGIOUS sPmIT. "Serving the Lord." That spirit consecrates life, sweetens life, saves life. Prophecy: the spiritual insigl, t the.t apprehends with increasing clearness God's purposes of Baving grace. }[inistry : the official attention to fiae.ncial and business matters of the Church, in which th~ "deacon" wins his good degree. Exhorting: the eam~st pleading with men, that their hearts may be won, or more fully won, to that which jg Divine and good. Such the more official duties. 2. The more private and spontaneous duties are to be similarly performed. Giving: for some who a.re so favoured have it as their special work to hold in trust for others, and to bestow as they have opportunity, the good things of this world. Let this be with all liberality of heart. Ruling: there will be committees for such philanthropic work, and men of enterprise will have it as their special business to lead the way. -0hristian love. Now we come to the great central principle of the Christian life in its social relations among men-true love. And, as the apostle addresses Church-members, he paints this love, by a few vivid strokes, as they owe it to their fellow-members, and also to those that are without. I. First, as members of Christ, they are to love one another. 1. The ethical cliarader o/ this love. It is holy. Not a mere sentimental tenderness, but a love that abhors the evil, in whomsoever found, and cleaves only to the good (comp. Jas. iii. 17, "first pure," etc.). _2. The manifestations of the love. Tender affection, as of the members of one loving family ; self-sacrificing respect, so contrary to the spirit which asks, " Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? The exultant joy of Christian hope, in view of that appearing of our Lord; the patient endurance of trial and pain, by the power of that hope ; the abiding fellowship with God, which ever rekindles the hope and makes it holy. 4. The practical working of this love in the matters of the life that now is. Relief of needy ones, as being the needy ones of God's household ; hospitality to all who for the Lord's sake hnve left their home and rest. 6. The forbearance of this love. When, unhappily, even Christian brethren misunderstand and strive and persecute, they are still to be loved an<l. blessed ; not for auy provocation is cursing to be rendered back. 6. entries.title: ROM 12:1
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-" .A living sac,;fioe." The text suggests to us the spiritul\l teacher's plBtform. He does not so much command or threaten I\S "beseech his brethren." Various terms are, indeed, used in the Authorized Version to translate the word traptUta>..lo,, But the feature of the word is speaking to some one for a pa.rticula.r purpose, to get him to do or refrain from something, to help him in difficulty or console him under trouble. The Saviour is spoken of in John's Epistle as our" Advocate," our Paraclete, according to our Lord's own description of himself when he promised," I will send you another Comrorter." And who has so gre&t a right to speak faithfully as a brother? The very nearness of kin implies affectionate solicitude, precludes evil suspicions. As brethren should the members of Churches stimulate each other with kindly jealousy for each other's welfare. I. THE DEDICATION DESCBIJIED. "Present your bodies a living sacrifice." The law of offerings is not abrogated, is spiritually fulfilled. The daily Ohristian sacrifice is not propitiatory like the Saviour's, but consequent upon that one efficacious atonement, and int.ended in like manner to glorify the righteousness and goodness of God, and to redeem man from evil Sin bas corrupted the entire organism, and the 'sacrifice is to consist of the whole being. The body is expressly named as the part which visibly was immersed in sin, and bowed under idolatry. But as the organ and symbol of the life, and the vehicle of information and action, bringing the powers of the soul into exercise, the surrender of the body to Christian principle means that the entire self is yielded to God. If sacrifice signifies self-denial, there is yet a joy that swallows up the pain of privation in the thought of the honour conferred on the garlanded victim acceptsi by the Most High as an act of worship and praise. Note some of t/i,e qualities of tAu sacri~ It is" living," as contrasted with the dead sacrifices of Jewish rites. True ~on iJ; not a galvanized life, but an inward principle that vivifies the entire frame. The mere saying of prayers, attendance at God's house, the avoidance of ill places and company, is a dead and worthless sacrifice if unaccompanied by love and devotion. The lo't'e of Christ flaming within the body makes it no longer a dull lump of clay, but an illumined spiritual temple. It is a "holy" sacrifice ; the sacredness of consecration to a holy Being rests upon it, and there is real and actual holiness of heart and life. It is "'acceptabl.e," well-pleasing to him who despises not the weak, but rejoices in humble, devout sincerity, where the leaven is cast out in order to a true celebration of the feast. We need not fear the rejection of our offering, since to us has been revealed the proper mode of approach ; nor will the shortcomings and sinful accompaniments that in spite of our best attempts mingle with our words and deeds cause them to be abhorred of him who perceives therein the sweet savour of Christ and incense of the Spirit. The "calves of our lips" will not pollute his courts, nor our "doing good and communicating" pollute his holy altar. We have also a general el,aracterizatwn of the 6(1,(':Tiftce. It is a "reasonabl.e service." It is engaged in and ratified by the highest powers,. the enlighten,ed, in~llect a!ld the quick~ned spirit. Unlike an unmeaning ritual, the SeI'Vlce of the Chnstian 18 to him emblematic of deepest truths. He sees himself not an isolated unit which bas itself merely to please and cherish, but a child of God, a constituent of society, with the obligation and dignity of obedience and self~bnega.tion for the service of God and man. And there is great meaning in the word employed to denote our" service." It compares our lives to the ministrations of tbe priesu! in the temple. Wllen we raise our voices in supplication to the throne, when we seek to lead others to the Saviour of our choice, when we strive to discharge the dntie& of our calling as unto the Lord, when we relieve the distreseed or comfort the afflicted we are 1111 much employed in temple-worship as if, like Aaron, we wore the high priellt's robel!, or, like Zacharias, offered incense before the veil. What a 110blc idea of the vocation of the people of God thia metaphor conveys I Jhpeot not. a on, xn.1-21.J THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 379

path of flowery ease-that the mountains should be levelled and the valleys raised to fo.cilitate your progress I At the aHar say, "I feel the cord that binds me; the knife is keen that severs the tender flesh; the flames are hard tQ bear; but withal I can rejoice tho.t I am exalted to the honour of a holocaust accepted of God, and not consumed but purified by the so.crifice." II. THE WEIGHTY ARGUMENT TO URGE THE DEDICATION, There is a" therefore" in the text; the exhortation is grounded on previous reasoning and previously stated facts. Herein lies the strength of the religious teacher. He may have no excommnnication with bell, book, and candle to pronounce, no fire and sword with which to wrin"' reluctant assent; but he has decisions of a recognized court to allege, and motives J unequalled potency to appeal to, Every one who has to do with machinery knows the importance of motive-power. And Christianity is strong where philosophical systems of ethics are weak. "You admit," the apostle seems to say, "these premisses; now supply the practical conclusion." He has been rehearsing the " mercies of God " to J ewa and Gentiles. Gratitude for the Divine goodness impels to his service, and the hope of future benefits is a lawful constraining force. Surely the grace that has granted pardon, peace, eternal life, is a voice to demand, a magnet to attract to, such a sacrifice as that entreated. Providential mercies cry aloud, "Yield yourselves nnto God." Where shall we begin, how end their recital? There are seasons, such as the beginning of a new year, or the anniversary of a birthday, when the remembrance of the Divine forethought and loving-kindness overwhelms the soul with thankfulness and praise. The darkest night has had its star; in the coldest day some gleam of sunshine bas cheered our landscape. Family and household mercies, blessings bestowed on Church and town and country, fresh discoveries in nature or art, "sweet voices from the distant hills,"- all these renewed compa.ssions of a benevolent God evoke the old inquiry, "What shall I render to the Lord for all his benefits toward me?" The text furnishes the answer, the full New Testament programme, outlined in the psalmist's "cup of salvation" and "thanksgiving," and "payment of vows" and" prayer."-S. R. A.

entries.title: ROM 12:2
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-CJhristian character a metamorphosis. Advice as to conduct, in order to be complete, should be both negative and positive in exhortation; it should say what ought to be done as well as what ought to be avoided. Christianity repels from evil and attracts to goodness. He runs best who not only flees from peril, but knows the refuge for whlch to shape his course. I. NoT THE FABfilON OF THE AGE, BUT THE WILL OF GoD, IS THE TRUE ST.!.~llARD OF DUTY. The Scriptures contrast this world with the kingdom of God. The one is fleeting, the other eternal. The one is carnal, the other spiritual; the one appea· s to the bodily senses, the other is a vision of faith. The kingdom which Christ has established realizes the desire and purpose of God's heart. 'l'hose who enter it are not thereby removed from the sphere of worldly need and influence and activity, but there is a difference in the spirit with which these temporal objects are pursued. A touchstone of value is introduced, and occupations and possessions are appraised :i.ccording to its d.-icisions. The will of God is the Ariadne clew which guides the traveller safely through the maze of shifting opinions and bewildering dictates. The disciple of Christ asks not-What will my com11anions say? what is the prevailing etiquette? what is the code of honour prescribed by the circle to which I belong? or what is the amount of kindness, purity, and justice which will save me from public censure? but-What would God have me do? what will be approve? what is his Divine intent in my upbringing and redemption? From how many petty anxieties is such a man freed, and what noble cares supplant his former subservience to custom! Commerce, politics, the Church, every arena needs suoh men. The face of God is not reflected in his serrnnts like coins stamped with the sovereign's identical image, but varies like the refiectiou of the sky, according to the lo.ke, river, or sea that mirrors its glory. II. A RENEWED MIND IB THE OHANNEL OF TRANSFORMATION, God has created m:ui intelligent, and men act generally according to their perception of the fitness of things. Alter their views, modify their tastes, direct their inclinations, and their ct\l"eer is chan"ed, If they do the same things, they do them with reference to a higher Bein<> and ~ wider lo.ndsoo.pe. Some things loved before appear loathsome now; the eyes ar~ oponod, and tbo old order is desortcd for tho beauties l\lld satisfactions of the new state. THE EPIB1't'E OF' PAUL TO TllE RO:M.iltS. Cott. x.tt. 1-21.

The will of God may be traoed in his works and ways, in oreatton and providenoe ; but Jesus Christ. in the Scriptl11'88 is to us the fullest revelation grantod of the mind of fu-.d, a.nd by etudying hin:i ie the conscionoo quickened, the reason enlightenod, the !Ufection l!l\nctified. Christianity thus works from within out\Vl\rd, It does not try to transfigure appearances by gilding the apples of the tree, or appending fruit to its boughs, bu_t it transforms the sap, and lets the new life produce its appropriate harvest. The renewing of the judgment implies a restoration of man to a primitive condition from which he has fallen. The lineaments of God iu huma.n nature whioh had grown dull, almost obliterat.ed by the wear and tear of a godless existence, are made vivid again. Like the whit.ewash removed from the walls of an ancient edifico, and no longer allowed to conceal the glorious frescoes or carving beneath, so the chamber of the heart is renorated by the reception of the Spirit of Christ, and the defilements nnd deceptions give place to the pristine conception of man in the likeness of God, retouched, remodelled by him who maketh all things new. The blood-stained cross is the measure of devotion to the will of God and of self-sacrifice for the common good. The risen Christ is the ide.al of the future to which Christian hopes turn and to which conformity is lonngly sought. III. TsE COMl'LETER THE TRANSFORMATION, THE MORE SURELY 18 THE WILL OF Goo DISCEID,""ED, Al<"'D THE MORE INTENSELY IS IT PRIZED, It is the universal law condensed into a proverb that "experience teaches." Not all at once can the ear distinguish sounds, or the eye form a.nd colours. Not immediately does the reason discriminate between logical and illogical arguments and procedures, nor the taste discover and apply its canons of judgment. Practice and discipline are required. And it were absurd t,o expect that in the regenerated man the old habits of liking and behaviour conld be thrown off by one effort like a worn-out garment. The man rescued from drowning slowly comes to himself, a.nd gradually does the eye of the saved believer learn to recognize in every place the presence of his Lord, and his ear to at all times catch the faintest whisper of his voice. The early converts made sad blunders in their celebration of Christian ordinances, in their governance of the gifts with which they were endowed, and in their application of Divine morality to the questions of the day. But they were in the school of Christ, and made steady progress, And every advance in k:aowledge and life has confirmed our appreciation of the will of God as being good, and worthy of the utmost maturity of ethical manhood. The Saviour's prayer is the verdict of the saintliest lives, the last word of Christian judgment: "Thy will, not mine, be done." AB an encouragement it may be noted that our standard of duty ever rise!! as we understand better the mind of God and approximate to its requirements. And we must not be disappointed if to ourselves we seem as far off e.s ever from the ideal development. This is only as, in climbing to some mountain summit, the top appears more distant because progress reveals more accurately the total height.-S. R. A.

entries.title: ROM 12:3
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-~ proper estimate of sdf. The fount of knowledge and utterance is the .. grace" of God. The apostle claims to be heard as one who; has received a message, not excocitated a thought, which it is his business to deliver and enforce. This is ever the prophet's function. to announce the mind of God, and he needs continual "grace" to be faithful to the truth, not to hide nor to alter nor to add. L IT :IS NOT SELF-DEPRECIATION wmcH IS HERE COMMANDED. Aristotle's dictum of right action is that virtuous behaviour lies in a mean between two extremes. And whi.lst not a sufficient account, this often serves as a ready criterion. Proper humility is not to be confounded with mock modesty and diffidence on the one hand, nor on the other hand with arrogance and pride. He acts injuriously to himself who, comparing himself with others, despisee what he is and can do, because higher and larger gifts have been bestowed on bis fellows. Such self-despising is ingratitude to God, and casts a slur on the Divine equity. We dare not make light of any post he enables us to fill or of the simplest service he permits UB to render. He who has dignified huma~ity, first by creating it" in his own i~age after his likene~s," and then by the incarnation of his beloved Soo, may expect ID every man a certam reasonable degree of ijelf-respect. And the apostle im~lies t~~t there is ~.'!ay in which each" ought to trunk" of himself, ought to honour his pos1t10n and ab1ht1eH. Shall the lark refus? to trill forth melody in hiB upward flight because he cannot pour forth the lu~c1ou1 on, Xll, 1-21.] THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 381

ohllngeful notes of the nightingale? or the robin refuse to chirp merrily in the winter because ho cannot undertake the long flight of the swallow? Shall the violet withhold its delicious fragrance because the sunflower is so conspicuously gorgeous? or the lofty elm not clap its hands in praise of God because of ita nearness to the wideeprending beech? 'l'hat is not true humility, but scornful indolence, which buries its to.lent in the earth. Of a lowly beast of burden it was said, "The Lord bath neerl of him." II. IT re UNDUE BEL'[l'-EBTEEM WJIICH IB REPROVED. .An immoderate estimate of onr personal worth is unmindful of obvious facts. It forget_s that God regards quality rather than quantity, and that all we possess we have received, even the ability to use our gifts, and by use to augment and perfect our capacity. We gain a humble estimate of our powers by coming into the society of truly great men. AB we measure little hills by, the sky-piercing mountains, so we may profitably turn our thoughts to the almighty and all-wise, the ever-living and holy God. .And, to assist us in our judgments, his grace has sent a pattern of merit in the character and life of his Son, attempering the glory of the Most_ High to our weak vision, and allowing us to see Divine greatness humbling itself to the form of a servant and the death of a criminal. We have to own our imperfect rectitude when we place it side by side with the obedience and righteousness of Christ. As with a douche of cold water, is the most intoxicated with his own grandeur sobered into due modesty. Through pride the angels "kept not their first estate," and it is a favourite device of the tempter to allure men into a sense of self-sufficiency and importance. "Look unto the rock whence ye were hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye were digged." Wounded vanity prevents many II member of the Church from seeking to glorify a lowly position; the foot wants to be where the eye is, and the hand objects to serve the head. The elder brother loses the joy of the prodigal's return. Remember that in the Saviour's reckoning the widow's offering far outweighed the costly contributions of the wealthy. III. THE BULE IB TO BE UNIVEBSALLY APPLIED. "I say to every man that is among you." Every man needs this regulation. The precepts and promises of Scripture addressed to all are only effective as each severally appropriates them. We are individ"ualized in God's sight, not lumped together in the mass. The danger lies at the door of each, and each must calculate his proper worth and position. We cannot do this for 0!le another; to his own Master does each stand or fall. Every Christian has obtained some amount of faith. There are gradations in spiritual as in temporal life, and the rank of honour is according to the service rendered to the body to which we belong. But none is entirely destitute; let none, therefore, be despised or downhearted. All Christians are landed proprietors; an estate large or small is allotted to them to occupy and cultivate. The Spirit distributeth as he will. Our business is not to quarrel with the distribution, but to be diligent stewards of the deposit entrusted to our care. He that is faithful in little or in much shall be rewarded. Such a consideration abates envy and discontent, abolishes boasting and self-complacency.-S. B.~

entries.title: ROM 12:15
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Sympatliy. The two clauses of this verse remind us of the two main emotions of the human breast, of their diverse nature, and their common association. Sorrow ever treads at the heels of joy. The sigh and the laugh may be heard at once. Scarce has prosperity brightened one threshold than adversity overshadows another. As in the plagues, there is light in Goshen and darkness in Egypt. If every house were painted to reveal the condition of the inmates, what startling contrasts would be seen side by side I It is of little use to try and measure the sum of happiness and of misery, to calculate which preponderates in life; better is it to adapt ourselves to these two prevailing states, and by appropril\te words and deeds to evince our sympathy both with those who mourn and those who exult, not shrinking from distress nor envying the fortunate. Many reasons concur in recommending the apostle's injunction. I. GoD BAB MADE MAN A SOCIAL nEING. He is the "God of the families of Israel., The Law commanded convocations, sooial observances; the people encamped not as individuals, but as households and tribes. Besides the appetites and affections that concern ourselves personally, there are others which respect our fellows and cannot be gmtified without their presence. Love, gratitude, pity, all suppose their existen\ ol>jects, so tht1t the mQral coustitut.ion of m&D exhibits the social capacities with which THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS [on. XII. 1-21,

he hRS 't>een endowed. There is a basis for sympathy in our physical nature. Tho appearance of one man acts and reacts on his companions. The mirthful induces merriment in the company, and the entrance of a gloomy countenance damps the spirit~ of e. whole party. Infants are quickly affected by the attitude of those nen.r them; and the lower animals are prone to frisk and leap when their masters are glad, and to be depressed by their melancholy. To shut one's self up in solitude, to take no notice of the circumstances of others, is therefore to sin against the laws of our being. IL JESUS CHRIST BAS PROVIDED FOR TBESlll SOCIAL INSTINCTS IN THE ESTABLISH• KID-"T OF ms CHURCH. He has instituted a community of believers, united for mutual connsel and support. One by one we resort to the Saviour for individual teaching and healing, but "those that are being saved" are" added to the Church," and the visibility of the fact assists in that redemption from selfishness which is the essence of sin. "Bea.r ye one another's burdens" is the recognition of our unity. The limb which shares not in the thrill of pain or plea.sure is on the way to a.trophy, disunion, death. Love and service t.o the Head of the body bind the members together o.s an organism, and love ministers to trouble and enhances joy. Such sympathy cannot, however, be restrict.eel t.o the members of the Church. Family ties lead to efforts for the salvo.iion of outsiders, and a desire for the glory of the Lord and the enlarging usefulness of his kingdom prompts to imitation of his beneficence who co.me to lighten our woes and to augment our gladness. ill. 0UB DEVELOPKJD."T ID,"TQ PERFECl'ION DEllllANDS THE OULTIVATION OF SYMPATHY. It was not "good" for Ad.am to be alone. A high pitch of civilization cannot be reached or maintained in isolation. Left to ourselves, we grow careless of refinement or progress. To shut ourselves up like flowers thai close their petals at the rude blast, t.o crawl inside our shell, and, closing the aperture, to dwell simply on our own satisfactions a.nd uneasinesses, is the pleading of mistaken self-love that overreaches itself and m.isse.s the pure happiness of sharing others' delights and of doing good. Spiritual growth is not attainable any more than physical strength by a life within-doors. Avoid the heat and the icy wind, and health suffers by too-great confinement. What lessoD..& may be learnt from the successes and misfortunes of our neighbours I Their loi may be Oll?II eoon; it were well to be wise betimes. To look on others is to gaze ai a minor that reflects our own image. IV. THE F1JLFILllEliT OF THIS PRECEPT WOULD llllATEBIALLY LIGHTEN THE WBETCHl!lD- BBSS OF ~ WORLD, The savageness of unrestricted competition vanishes where a dne regard is paid io t.he happiness or suffering of our companions. Nothing like a visit from the employer to the homes of his servants, or a sight by the speculator of the misery his UI1just gains have entailed, to abate the fierceness of greed and to remedy grievaru:es and wrongs. The world sorely needs brotherly kindness. Then would men and nations realize that what elevates one raises all, what depresses one truly enriches none. We may note that obedience to the latter clause of the text is perhaps more needful than compliance with the former. The distressed require help, the prosperous can do without it. But any separation of the two duties weakens both. It is not always easy to congratulate a fortunate compeer, any more than to assist the unlucky. No doubt we like t.o buk in the sunshine, and to withdraw from gloom. But the "elder brother" refused to join in the household felicitations, and the .Levite and the Pharisee "'paased by" the wounded traveller. Guard against the mere indulgence of passive sympathy. The rejoicing and mourning of the text imply an active sympathy, and action forms habits of good will and benevolence as Butler has described.. Copy the Redeemer. No ascetic or misanthrope was he, who multiplied the innocent 1?aiety of the marriage feast, and mingled hie tears with those of the weeping Bister1 of La.zaruL Even a hearty grasp of the band adds to joy, and & moistened eye comforts tboae that mourn. The poorest in point of worldly goods may be rich in God-like sympathy. Many a man has been saved from utter despair by the knowledge that another was interested in his welfare.-S. R. A..

A man bas ooen wron"ed 0 by hie neighbour. The feeling of injury begets a desire for retaliation. The rese ntrnent is just, ie a testimony to the sense of righteousnese imbedded in the conscienc'3, But the feeling te!lde to go to~ far, and to become a lo~ging for_ revenge in any shape that may present itself. Here 1s the subtlety of temptation, makmg evil appear as good. Undisguised vice is easy to repel, but a righteous indignation may open the "ate through which unrighteous passion enters like a flood. Thie is one form of the nniv;rsal battle against sin, which ie ever ready to take advantage of lawful natural impulses end to push them to excess. The warning of the text applies, therefore, to the whole sphere of life. All good conduct implies the possibility of the reverse. Solicitation11 to evil are everywhere about us. Physical evil, such as a. painful disease, may become moral evil when it produces murmuring, peevishness, utter idleness, and blasphemy. The struggle is fierce and prolonged, for "we wrestle against powers, against spiritual wickedness in high places." Ae the gifts of God in the material universe are secured at the expense of painful thought and toil, so the blessings of the spiritual life are not to be had at our ease, but only by strenuous wrestling. II. THE METHOD OF WARFARE. "Overcome evil with good." To resist the evil inclination is the first part of the duty, but it is not alone a sufficient maxim. We have a. weapon to wield; we must occupy ourselves in the practice of what is good. Not only arrest the hand that is a.bout to strike an angry blow, but find some service for the hand to render to our opponent. They sin least, are least subject to t.emptation, who a.re engrossed like the Saviour in "doing good." He could move uncontaminated in the presence of "publicans a.nd sinners." The outrush of active benevolence barred the influx of evil. 'l'he moment we try to see if we cannot benefit a would-be foe, we are conscious of a changed sentiment within; we pity instead of hating and condemning; we lose our worse to find our better self. This is a law to1be remembered in all attempts to combat the forces of evil. " Resist the devil; draw nigh to God.." The drunkard ma.y sign the pledge of abstinence, but he needs meetings, society, efforts for others, to occupy his leisure moments. Do not gaze at the Sirens, but make for the home whose pure pleasures will profitably engage your energies. Let the young man have hie stu4y, and his proper recreation, and thus by the pursuit of what is elevating rise above petty meannesses and degrading amusements. III. THE INSPmmo P ATTEBN. Christ is our Exemplar, "who, when he was reviled, reviled not again." He " committed his cause to him that judgeth righteously," and instead of heaping reproaches on his persecutors, prayed for their forgiveness, died for their salvation. The spurious Gospels, with their narrative of the Saviour's boyhood as a scene of vengeance wreaked on his youthful companions for their opposition and insult, condemn themselve11 as contradictory to the after-life of the" meek and lowly" One. He never exerted his power to harm his foes. His only miracles of judgment were on the swine and the barren fig tree. In Gethsemane the band of traitors were awed to the ground, but not injured. He knew that "to whomsoever much is forgiven, the same loveth much." Afterwards " a great company of priests became obedient to the faith." Saul the persecutor was changed by appealing love into Paul the missionary. The Lamb" led to the slaughter" unresistingly has proved himself in victorious submission the "Lion of the tribe of Judah.0 ".Arm yourselves likewise with the same mind." IV. 'l'HE SUCCESS OF TIDS METHOD. Good is stronger than evil because it is on the side of God and the angels; it is backed by eternal laws. Like produces like. Strife leads to more strife; war sows a crop of dragons' teeth that yield a harvest of future enmities and battles. Germany, exaoting a heavy indemnity from France and seizing two foir provinces, has lnid herself under crushing armaments and ceaseless fears of coming roprisnle. The pence principles of Christ, wherever faithfully adhered to, prove their soundness and fruitfulness. 'l'he man who resists not tames the spirit of his opponent. Obstinacy that defies the chilling blllst is forced to relax when the warmth of Christian kindness shines on its oute1· crust. The coals of such a fire do not tlemily bum, but they melt the unjust into contrition and confession. The disuse of duelling has contributed to courtesy nmouget men. We are not lit to take the law into our S8i THE EPISTLE OF rAUL TO THE ROMANS. [oB. XII, 1-11,

own bands and mete out justice, but we C.'lnnot do wrong in cultivating mercy nnd gener,.~ity. He acoordingly proceeds to base his exhorta- tion upon the "mercies of God," and the first matter he urges is becoming individuality, These brethren at Rome ought, t-0 dedicate themselves as living sacrifices unto God, realizing how reasonable such a service is, and exhibiting due unworldliness of character in all things. Let us, then, with Paul as guide, consider the elements of Christian individualism as here set before us. L OUR BODIES A.BX TO BE LAID AS LIVING SACRIFICES ON GoD'S ALTAR. (Ver. 1.) If we ha,e been called with a holy calling, if the risen Saviour has given us the needed helping hand. then we are bound oo realize our obligation to him in dedicating our bodies as" linng sacrifices" unto him. The reason why we can dedicate them as litling sacrifices u: that he has offered the atoning sacrifice our pardon and acceptance require, and we can consequently dedicate ourselves living to his glory. Now, when we look ic.to the order of the Jewish sacrifices, we find that the sin offering ea.me first, then the burnt offering, and then the pea.co offering. The leading idea. in each was at-0nement, consecration, and fellowship. The sin offering emphasized atonement, the burnt offering or holocaust emphasized consecration, and the peace offering emphasized fellowship. Now, the self-dedication to which the apostle here calls us corresponds in the ritual to the burnt offering; and just as in this particular sacrifice the entire ca:::case was consumed in the sacred :fire, so the idea is that our whole personality, body, soul, and spirit, is to be consecrated by the fire of the Holy Spirit to the service of our Lord and Master. The idea, in short, is that our bodies should be organs of the Holy Ghost.. What a holy and blessed thought is thus associated with the body of the believer I It dare not be dedicated to any profane use. It is a holy thing, and is to be I.aid on God's altar and thus dedicated in its entirety to him. Miss Havergal's "Hymn of Consecration" will occur to every one, with the dedication of" hands," and "feet," and "voice," and O lips," and, in a word," all" we a.re, to the glory of our Lord. Dean Goulbnrn, in his suggestive work on the 'Study of the Holy Scriptures,' gives a sk:et.ch upon this passage, from which the following will be found useful : " Consider the members of the body which must thus be yielded: (1) The eyes. The lust of the eye must be monified, and the eye employed in reading God's Word, or surveying his works. (2) '.1.'he ears. We must be' swift to hear' the voice of instruction, and must tnrn away the ear from temptation and from flattery (see Acts :xii 22, 23). (3) The hands. • Let him that i;tol.e steal no more ; but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth ' (Eph. iv. 28). (4) The feet. 'I wu sick, and ye visited me; I was in prison, and ye came unto me' (Matt. :nv. 36). (5) The mouth. 'Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers' (Eph. iv. 29). 'Let your speech be al way with grace, seasoned with salt' (Col iv. 6)." 1 IL WE A.RE TO REALIZE THAT TBIS EJITUIE DEDICATION IS ONLY 0UB REASONABLE SERVICE. (Ver. 1.) It seems at first a large demand. But it becomes reasonable the moment we consider our obligation. If Jesus has dedicated his body in life and in death to our interests and salvation, the dedication of our living bodies in return to him is 6lll'ely a reasonable service. M. de Rougemont has brought out the reasonable character of this self-dedication in his own pointed fashion. The conduct of others is not to be our standard, but the will of God. Worldliness consists essentially in this-making the fashion our standard of life. Now, in this respect we are not to conform to the worldly and pre¥ailing ideas, Saurin has a fine sermon on this verse, in which he exhorts his hearers not to conform to the multitude infaith, or in wfYT'ship, or in morals, or in our exodus at death. 1 And then, if we take the Divine will as our proper standard, we shall :find ourselves "transfigured" (µeTciµ.oprpoiia-6•) by the renewing of our minds, so that . we shall" test" (llorc,µ&(•111)and so come to understand what is that good ar.d acceptable and perfect will of God (cf. Shedd, in loc.). Now, it is in this way, by surrendering ourselves to the Divine idea concerning us, that we shall realize that individuality and influence among men which is so desirable. In fact, we become most original, in the best sense of that term, when we do not try to be original, but simply to be and do what is God's will concerning us. It was the same with our blessed Master. He professed to do nothing of himself, but simply to mediate to men what the Father gave him (John v. 19); and yet he has been out of sight the most original personality which has ever appeared in this world. So will it be with us in our little spheres if we will only e.llow God to transfigure us. IV. SuoII ADANDONllfENT TO TIIE DIVINE WILL SE0UBES DUE SOBRIETY IN OUR ESTIMATE OF OURSELVES. (Ver. 3.) The gospel delivers us from egotism; we dare ncit think highly of ourselves; we can only think of how we are realizing God's will concerning us. And so, as merely mediating God's wiser will, we think soberly and humbly of ourselves. The apostle thus commends to the Romans and to ill men what Leighton calls that "gracing grace of humility, the ornament and safety of all other graces, o.nd what is so peculiarly Christian." Our individualism will thus be found delivered from the egotism and self-esteem of worldly men, and projected al0ng the patA of meekness ond lowliness of heart which the Master trod before us. While belierers are members one of another, we a.re not reduced to a dead level of uniformity, Edification is doubtless to be in the body as every joint supplieth it, but the joints are not all alike; if they were, it would be a curious medley-a conglomeration of mere atoms, ""hich we should have in place of a body. In the body there is subordination of member t.o member, and part to part. The foot is not to usurp the place of the head, nor the hand that of the eye, else will the body be turned upside down, and become a monstro- sity instead of a thing and form of beauty. Consequently, we find that in the apostolic Chnrch there were a variety of offices, and the apostle here specifies the spirit in which they should be filled and their duties discharged. Let us briefly notice the offices as here described. 1. Prophecy. The apostle puts this in the very forefront. Parallel passages go t.o prove that it was most highly esteemed in the apostolic Church. Thus it is placed immediately after the working of miracles (1 Cor. xii. 10). In another place it is spoken af as" the gift of prophecy," and is associated with the ''understanding of all mysteries, and of all knowledge" (1 Cor. xiii. 2). It is further represented as the necessary adjunct t.o speaking with tongues (1 Cor. xiv. 6, 22). And it was evidently regarded as the prime requisite in the edification of the public congregation ; for St. Panl dec!a.res, " If all prophesy, a.nd there come in one that believeth not, or one unlearned., he is convinced of all. he is judged of all: and thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth" (1 Cor. xiv. 24, 25). Now, the more this matter is looked into, the more clearly are we landed in the conclusion that we have the prophetical office continued in Christ's Church in the ministry of the Word. Every minister who is called by Christ to the preaching of the gospel, and endowed by him for the work, is a prophet of the Highest jwt as really as Elijah or John the Baptist. If, then. to any of us this grace of prophecy has been committed, we must exercise it " according to the proportion of faith " ( a.,,al<o')llav .,-ijs 1rltr'l'<"'s). From <Jhurchmansh-ip, which was discussed. by the apostle in the preceding verses, we now pass to the Christian in society ; and our endeavour will be to appreciate the Christian socialism which Paul here inculcates. The great error of the Christless socialism which prevails, alas I in many lands, is that it tries to do from without and by mere material manipulation what can only come from within through the Christian spirit. Into the various forms which socialism has assumed it would be improper here to enter ; but any who wish to get some idea of the subject will do well to get the late Dr. Roswell D. Hitchcock's powerful and compendious treatise on 'Socialism,' where, after treating of "Socialism in General." "Cammunistio Socialism," and "Anti-Communistic Socialism," he reaches his climll in expounding the meaning of "Christian Socialism." 1 Our duty just now is to appreciate the spirit of love which Christianity infuses into society, thereby securing all that socialism could possibly reach by its coarse materialistic methods, and infinitely more. I. CONSIDER THE OHARA0TEB OF LOVE. (Vers. 9, 10.) For this is the one thing needful (1 Cor. xiii.). Well, the apostle tells us it is not to be hypocritical (..,,,,..Jrp,-ros); not to be a. profession, but the reality of love. It is from this loving spirit that Christianity proceeds to the regeneration of society. If, then, we start with a genuine spirit of love, we shall not be found rejoicing at evil, but always abhorring it; while to good at all costs we shall ever cleave. Thus " pure Christian love manifests itself in two phases-the ethical recoil from moral evil, and the cleaving to moral good. The former, full as much 11s the latter, evinces the sincerity of the affection. Indifference towards sin, and especie.lly an indulgent temper towards it, proves that there is no real love of holiness. II. LIFE IN EARNEST. (Vers. 11-13.) Now, when a Christian declines honour, and seeks to put the better man thereinto, it is not that he may shirk work. For, oe a matter of fact, hard work and honour are not inse~rably aseooiated in this world. Hence t.be Christian can show his "zeal for the Lord' while setting no store by honour for it. The ne:i.:t element, therefore, in the Christian life and spirit is earnestness. As Luther puts it, "In regard to ze.al, be not lazy." The Christian will show o zealous spirit in all legitimate lines of effort.1 His life will be intense. And to maintain it in intensity, it will require to be " fervent in spirit," and in all "serving the Lord." The serving of the opportunity, as in some ancient manuscripts, is not so likely, nor so emphatic, as "serving the Lord ; " for the Christian ia one who has learned to serve God in everything-to "do everything as unto the Lord, and not unto men, knowing that of the Lord be shall receive the reward of the inheritance as be serves the Lord Christ" (Col iii. 23, 24). Moreover, with this fervent, faithful spirit there will come a buoy- ancy and hopefulness which is most important in all Christian work; a patience too in tribulation ; a prayerfulness at all times; a liberality towards the saints ; a hospitality &owvds all men. The Christian keeps " open house" because he is open-hearted. Noll", if such an earnestness were infused into all Christian living, society would soon be regenerated. Ill. LIFE lliGNANDlous A!."D snt:PATBETIO. (Vers. 14--16.) Jesus set the great e:i.ample of magnanimity. He blessed his persecutors; he prayed for his murderers; he converted some of them at Pentecost. Hence, if we would carry out his spirit, we must bless them that persecute us; we mw;t meet the weak spirit which descends to intolerance and persecution with the one weapon of blessing. The Christian martyrs have crushed the opposition to the gospel by blessing their persecutors. But we must show sympathy as well as magnanimity, prepared to congratulate those in joy, to weep along with those in tears. Sympathy adds largely to the experience and benefit of life.2 And this sympathy is to be genuine all round; we are to be "of the same mind one towards another." We are not to be selecting for our sympathy those in good positions, but we are to "condea;cend to men of low estate." This is, indeed, the luxury of the Christian Bpirit to be able to take men up in a low condition, and treat them as God has treated us. We are also to avoid being " wise in our own conceits." In this way the Christian will exhibit large-heartedness ; there will be nothing emall or petty about his movements ; he 1l"ill be the noble brother-man in his little sphere that Christ has been and is in the wide sphere of the Church. IV. LIFE LOVINGLY AGGBEBSIVE. (Vers. 17-21.) We pass, lastly, to love encountering opposition, yet triumphing over it. And first we are not to take the law into our own hand and recompense evil for evil Now, the world cannot well understand this Christian spirit. It can appreciate better " the blow for blow " which characterized the early ages. "Thomas Paine, in reference to our Lord's injunction to turn the other cheek to the smit.er, charges Christianity with the 'spirit of a spaniel,' asserting that it destroys proper self-respect, and renders man indifferent to insult and affront" (see Shedd, in Zoe.). But when the Christian is charged to" provide things honest in the sight of all men," the meaning being " things honourable " (Revised Version), then it couples with forbearance true Christian dignity.• In strict accordance with this Christian dignity is to be our living peaceably with all men, if possible. It may be necessary by Christian testimony sometimes to provoke and exasperate worldlinge; but, at the same time pugnacity will be seen not to belong to the Christian spirit. And as for vengeance: let us leave all that with ~od. He will do justly at last. Meanw~le it is our prerogative to feed and give drink to an enemy; and by every means m our power to heap coalB of fire on his head. entries.title: ROM 13:1–7
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content: -LogaUy. There was danger, in the first age of Christianity, lest the nature of the kingdom of the Lord Jesus should be misunderstood even by its subjects, ana misrepresent.ed by those without.. A spiritual empire was a new conception, and carnal minds were prone to confound the dominion over souls with civil and political anthority. Hence the importance and appropriateness of the admonitions so emphatically addressed by the apostle to the Christians of Rome. L 'IllE IXBPIBED CONCEPTION OF CIVIL AUTHORITY. By this the apostle understood the actnally constituted power of the state. The Roman emperor was the head and chief of the greater part of the population of the then known world, and Rome was the centre of political rule and authority. The proconsuls and proprmtors represented in the provinces the imperial majesty and sway of senate and of emperor. But it is evident that the view of civil power taken by the apostle was equally applicable to monarchies and to republics. Whatever the form of government, whatever the designation of the ruler, whatever the rank of the administrator of the law, authority was recognized as of Divine origin and right. It has sometimes been deemed a reproach to the apostle that he should have written thus when Nero was on the throne, But this fact rather emphasizes the principle that the authority is Divine, although the person or persons who wield it may be unworthy of the trust. Nero was at this time under the i.nfl.nence of the wise and moderate counsels of Seneca and of !3urrhus, yet this language which Paul employed would probably have been unaltered had the apostle been writing during th.e subsequent and infamous period of the tyrant's sway. h would be straining thiB passage to cfeduce from it "The right Dinn.e of kings to govern wrong," and it would be nnjUBt to argue from it that it is always unlawful to resist and to dethrone a tyrant. But we may leam to regard subordination, rule, subjection, loyalty, u all part of a Divine order imposed upon human society by the Lord of all. IL THE SOOPE OF LOYALTY, 1. Resped and honour are due from the governed to the governor. Even where there is a Jack of those qualities which command personal r88pect, honour may be rendered to the office which is held, and the duties of which are faithfully fulfilled. 2. The payment of taxc8 and tribute8 is required. In this prectpt Piiul. followed the tkaehing of his Master, "lten<ler unto Cresa.r the things t-J:111.t CJII, xm.1-14.J THE EPIS'l'LE or PAUL TO THE ROMANS. 11re Omear's." Subjects are not reeponeibl e for the l1ll8 maile of the moMy which 18 axa.oted from them by just authority. When a king who hae no constitntione.l right to levy te.xes without the consent of a parliament demands money upon bis own anthority, Buch a demand me.y be refused without disobedience to the injunction of the t,ext. 3. Obedience and subjection are enjoined. The extent and range of this injunction are very large. "Every soul "-very intelligent member of society-is under an obliuation to obey ; and resistance to the ruler is resistance to God, and entails jast pnnishment and retribution. 4. Virtue generally is commended as contribntive to the well-bein"' of society, Good works are to evince the sincerity of the Christian's faith. Th~ Roman law was the highest expression the ancient world attained of jmw~ in the relations subsisting between man and ma.n. It has been the foundation of the codes of many civilized Christian nations in modern times. Obedience to the law was the duty of every good nitizen, every well-wisher of society, every true member of the human family. For the law was the sanction of virtue and righteoasness. Doubtless there have been and are unjust laws; yet it is the duty of the citizen to obey them when obedience does not come into conflict with the higher dnty to God. III. THE GROUNDS OF LOYALTY, These, as adduced by St. Paul, are two. 1. Perwnal considerations a.re advanced. The wrath of the magistrate is to be feared; rulers are a terror to the evil; they that resist shall receive retribution; the ruler bears not the sword in vain. Such motives a.re almost the only motives to which the coarse and vicious are accessible. They a.re motives to which none a.re altogether superior. The consequences of injustice have t.o be borne in mind by those who are liable to the passions of cupidity or of revenge. 2. Religious motives are presented. Government is an ordinance of God, and rulers a.re the ministers of God. A bad subject, then, cannot be a good Christian. In our own days, individualism is carried to such an extent that authority is often disdained and defied, even by those who are by no means the dregs of society, who make pretensions to intelligence and virtne. It is well, therefore, that the inspired teaching shonld be pondered which attaches importance so great to order, patriotism, and loyalty.

entries.title: ROM 13:8–10
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content:
-Love and law. To the unthinking, and at first sight, there seems a contradiction between law, which expresses authority, and is sanctioned by force, and love, which is spontaneous, and is of the heart. Christ himself, however, brought the two into harmony when he said, "If ye love me, keep my commandments;,. and the apostle, in this passage, shows that, really and essentially, the two :ire one. I. THE TRUE PRINCIPLE OF SOCIAL LIFE IS LOVE. The new co=andment which Christ gave was, "Love one another; " and "his peculiar canon of conduct was, "Thou she.It love thy neighbour as thyself." Of this principle we may remark that: 1. It is in harmony with our own constitution. Our true nnture is to live in mutual affection and confidence; it is the depraved nature that devt>lops hatred, malice, and uucharitableness. 2. It is imposed and sanctioned by the Divine Head of the new humanity, the Lawgiver of the spiritual kingdom. 3. It provides the radical cure for human ills. 4. It has not only a negative, it has also a positive virtue; it is the proper and natural origin of the several virtues, supplying their motive, prompting to their exercise. II. THE APPLICATION OF TmB PRINCIPLE IN PRACTICE, The apostle, whose mind WlL9 as thoroughly ethical and practical as it was theological and doctrin,11, traced the working of this principle of love, in preserving human nature and protecting human society from the vices, crimes, and sins which have cursed the world. In this passage he teaches us that love must act in keeping Christians from wronging their neighbours. He whose heart is filled with true love will neither covet nor steal his neighbour's goods, nor take his neighbour's life, nor make inroads upon his neighbour's domestic happiness, nor in any we.y inflict injury upon his neighbour's interests, or deprive him of his rights. For to love our fellow-men is to couut their welfare our own, and to do to them as we would they should do to us. III. '!'HE ACQUISITION OF THIS PRINCIPLE, It may be argued that the counsels of tho apostlo are unpmctical; tbl\t whilst lovo is a cure for human ills, it is not shown how love mBy be acquired, any more than it is how sin may be a'l'oided. But the fact ls that revolation links together the love of man and the love of God. and t~a.:11.:is us THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE ROMANS, [on. xm.1-14.

Christians are addressed as those who know the seasons, who discern the signs of the times, who regard the present as a period of probation, of discipline, of education, and whose gaze is ever forwards, whose hope is in their Lord's return to judge and to save. L Tm: RETBOSPECT OF THE PAST. "The night is far spent." 1. The spiritual night of the world is passing away. entries.title: ROM 13:11–14
entries.author: James Barmby
entries.content: -.Awalce and arm/ It le strange that, at the very commencement of o new dispensation, the prospect of its close should be so often presented to the view, No sooner had Christ's first coming ended, than his people were taught to anticipate bis second coming. Thus the thoughts e.nd affections of C,'hristians are clustered around their Lord, e.nd the revelation of the pa.at suggests the approaching epiphany. The contra.ate of this passage are very striking. When carefully e.nalyzed, they appear- I. As applied to CONDITION, 1. The night of danger is nearly over. This applies to the individual, to any community, to the whore Church. 2. The morning of deliverance is dawning. An inspiration and comfort to the pilgrims, the soldiera, who a.re often oppressed by the gloom of the present perils. '.II. As applied to CHARACTER. 1. The works of night a.re to be abandoned. These belong to the era. which now lies in the remote distance, and from which Christ bas emancipated his people. 2. The life of the spiritual day is to be adopted. If the flesh and its lusts are to be crucified, what is to be crowned? The Lord Jes03 is to be " put on," the armour of light is to be taken and worn; and the Christian soldier is to go forth to meet the coming day, with his face towards the rising sun. with his heart bounding with delight at his great Captain's long-expected ap:i:,earance.

The natural man, on the grounds of mere rea.."On, then, should submit to authority, with deed and with heart. But surely the Christian man should submit on some higher ground than this? It is not only re.ai:onable, it is divinely right, that such submission be rendered to the powers, I. It is right that we: (1) Obey law.
